school-c10-english-a.title: Class 10 English (and Hindi Grammar) — Part A (First Flight (prose), First Flight (poems), Footprints without Feet)
school-c10-english-a.description: Chapter-by-chapter Class 10 English – every First Flight and Footprints chapter and poem, grammar and writing skills – plus Class 10 Hindi grammar, with solved answers, quizzes, chapter tests and revision mock papers.

courses.title: First Flight · A Letter to God (G.L. Fuentes)
courses.summary: A farmer's unshakeable faith, a hailstorm, a letter addressed to God and a kind postmaster – a story full of irony about faith, kindness and misunderstanding.
outcomes: Learners can narrate the story in sequence
Learners can analyse Lencho, the postmaster and the irony in the ending
Learners can explain key words and literary devices
Learners can write exam-ready short and long answers
courses.note: chapter numbering may differ by edition

scenes.text: A farmer's family watches the first big rain fall on their ripe corn field and celebrates.
Within minutes, the drops turn into hailstones – and the harvest is gone.

steps.title: Plot summary
steps.body:
- **Setting:** a lone house on the crest of a low hill in a rural area (Mexico). The farmer **Lencho** knows his field intimately; the corn is ripe, with flowers of kidney beans.
- Lencho hopes for rain. It comes – he compares the big drops to **new coins**.
- A strong wind brings **hailstones** for an hour; the field is destroyed. The family will have no corn that year; they are sad and worried about hunger.
- Lencho has one hope – **help from God**, whose eyes, he was taught, see everything.
- He writes a letter to God asking for **100 pesos** to sow his field again and live until the crop comes, and posts it.
- The **postmaster** laughs, then is moved by the man's faith. He decides to answer it: he collects money from his employees and friends and gives part of his own salary, but can raise only **a little more than half** (70 pesos). He signs the letter “God”.
- Lencho is not surprised to get the money but is **angry** on counting it. He writes a second letter asking God for the remaining 30 pesos, adding that he should **not send it by mail** because the post office employees are “a bunch of crooks”.

steps.title: Author and genre
steps.body: Written by **G.L. Fuentes**, a Spanish-language writer; translated into English. Genre: short story. Main themes: **faith in God, irony, human kindness, ingratitude/innocence**.

steps.title: Solved example: Why did Lencho write a letter to God? (30–40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Cause:** The hailstorm destroyed his entire crop and left the family without food for the year.

**Step 2 – Belief:** He had complete faith that God sees everything and would help.

**Step 3 – Answer:** So he wrote to God asking for 100 pesos to sow again and survive.

steps.title: Solved example: How did the postmaster help Lencho? (30–40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Response:** He first laughed but was moved by Lencho's faith.

**Step 2 – Action:** He collected money from employees and friends and gave part of his salary.

**Step 3 – Result:** He sent 70 pesos with a letter signed “God” to keep Lencho's faith alive.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Lencho asked for 70 pesos – he asked for **100**; he received **70**.
- Writing that the postmaster signed his own name – he signed **“God”**.
- Forgetting that Lencho was **not surprised** to receive money – only angry at the amount.

items: Lencho hopes for rain for his ripe corn
Rain turns into a hailstorm and ruins the field
Lencho writes to God for 100 pesos
The postmaster collects money from colleagues
Lencho receives 70 pesos
Lencho writes again, calling post office employees crooks

quiz.q: How much money did Lencho ask God for?
quiz.why: Lencho asked God for 100 pesos, which he thought was enough to sow his field again. 70 is what he actually received.
Lencho compared the large raindrops to new coins, because he hoped the rain would give a good harvest.
The postmaster answered the letter. He was moved by Lencho's faith and wanted to keep it alive.
Lencho received 70 pesos, a little more than half of the 100 he had asked for. The postmaster could collect only that much.

quiz.q: Lencho's second letter asked God not to send money by
quiz.why: In the second letter he asked God not to send the money by post. He believed the post office employees were crooks who had kept the rest.

scenes.text: A neighbour anonymously pays for Ravi's school fees; Ravi thinks the school clerk kept part of the money.
Kindness can be misunderstood – just like in this story.

steps.title: Characters
steps.body:
- **Lencho:** hard-working farmer who knows his land; simple, innocent and **with unshakeable faith in God** (“an ox of a man” – strong, hard-working); but also **ungrateful and suspicious** towards humans – he calls those who helped him crooks.
- **The postmaster:** fat, amiable; first laughs but is touched by Lencho's faith; **generous and kind** – he does not want to shake that faith. He is satisfied with his good deed.

steps.title: Themes and irony
steps.body:
- **Faith:** Lencho's faith is total – he never doubts God will send money.
- **Kindness:** the postmaster and colleagues help a stranger anonymously.
- **Irony:** (1) the rain Lencho welcomed destroys his crop; (2) the people who actually helped him are called **crooks** by him; (3) the man who trusted God completely distrusts the humans who were God's instruments.
- **Contrast:** strong faith in the invisible God vs weak trust in visible humans.

steps.title: Solved example: Bring out the irony in the story (40–50 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Irony 1:** The longed-for rain turns into hail and destroys the crop.

**Step 2 – Irony 2:** The postmaster and colleagues help Lencho, yet he calls them “a bunch of crooks”.

**Step 3 – Effect:** The ending is both humorous and touching – Lencho's faith in God is matched by distrust of the very people who helped.

steps.title: Solved example: Value-based: What does the postmaster teach us? (40–50 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Value:** Empathy and selfless help – he gave from his own salary to a stranger.

**Step 2 – Spirit:** He wanted to preserve another person's faith rather than mock it.

**Step 3 – Lesson:** Kindness need not seek credit; anonymous help is noble.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling Lencho greedy – he wanted money for **survival and sowing**, not luxury.
- Missing the **double** irony (rain and the “crooks”).

quiz.why: Lencho's main trait is his unshakeable faith in God. Even after losing his crop he wrote to God for help.

options: he did not want to shake Lencho's faith
quiz.why: The postmaster helped because he did not want to shake Lencho's faith in God. It was not duty, fame or payment.

quiz.q: The biggest irony is that Lencho
quiz.why: The biggest irony is that Lencho calls the people who helped him crooks, while he thinks God gave the money. He did not thank the postmaster.

quiz.q: “An ox of a man” suggests Lencho was
quiz.why: 'An ox of a man' suggests Lencho was strong and hard-working, like an ox that works the fields. It does not mean stupid or lazy.
The central themes are faith and kindness, shown by Lencho's trust in God and the postmaster's generosity.

scenes.text: Mira's teacher asks why the writer compares hail to "frozen pearls".
Figures of speech make scenes vivid.

steps.title: Key expressions
steps.body:
- **Crest of a low hill:** top of the hill.
- **Downpour:** heavy rain. **Hailstones:** frozen raindrops falling as ice.
- **Like new coins / frozen pearls:** similes/metaphors that show Lencho's hope and the beauty of the hail.
- **Plague of locusts:** comparison – hail did more damage than locusts.
- **A single hope:** help from God.
- **Amiable:** friendly. **Contentment:** satisfaction.
- **Crooks:** dishonest people.

**Literary devices:** simile, metaphor, irony, personification of nature (wind, rain).

steps.title: Solved example: Identify the device: “The drops were like new coins.” (1 mark)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Device:** Simile (comparison using “like”).

**Step 2 – Meaning:** Raindrops seen as money because rain would bring a good harvest.

steps.title: Solved example: Explain: “The hail did more damage than a plague of locusts.” (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Comparison:** Locusts are known to destroy crops completely.

**Step 2 – Meaning:** The hailstorm was even worse – nothing was left in the field.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling every comparison a metaphor – a **simile** uses “like/as”.
- Mixing up “amiable” (friendly) with “amicable” (settled peacefully).

activity.prompt: Match the word to its meaning

quiz.why: 'Frozen pearls' refers to hailstones, which destroyed Lencho's crop. The phrase describes hail as pearls of ice.
'Like new coins' uses 'like', so it is a simile. A metaphor would say raindrops were new coins.

quiz.q: A plague of locusts is a
quiz.why: A plague of locusts is a swarm of insects that destroys crops, so it is a disaster for farmers.
'Amiable' means friendly. It describes someone pleasant and kind.
'Crest' means the top of something, such as the top of a hill. Lencho's house stood on the crest of a low hill.

scenes.text: Arjun has 10 minutes for a 120-word answer on faith.
He plans: introduction → points with examples → conclusion.

steps.title: How to write a 120-word answer
steps.body:
1. **Introduce** the idea in one line (e.g. “Faith can move mountains”).
2. Give **2–3 points** with evidence from the story.
3. Add a **value/lesson**.
4. **Conclude** in one line. Keep to the word limit; use past tense for narration.

steps.title: Solved example: “Faith is a great virtue.” Discuss with reference to Lencho (120 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Introduce:** Lencho's faith in God is the heart of the story.

**Step 2 – Evidence:** After losing his crop, he does not despair; he writes to God with complete confidence and is not surprised when money arrives.

**Step 3 – Effect:** His faith moves the postmaster and colleagues to collect money – faith inspires goodness in others.

**Step 4 – Limitation:** But blind faith also makes him suspicious of the humans who helped.

**Step 5 – Conclude:** Faith gives strength in crisis, but it should go with trust and gratitude towards people.

steps.title: Solved example: Write the postmaster's diary entry after reading Lencho's second letter (100 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Format:** Date, “Dear Diary”, first person, feelings.

**Step 2 – Content:** Surprise and amusement at being called a crook; satisfaction that Lencho's faith is intact.

**Step 3 – Reflection:** Kindness need not be thanked; he will keep the secret.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Retelling the whole story instead of answering the question.
- Exceeding the word limit; no conclusion.

activity.prompt: Have you ever helped someone who did not know it was you? How did it feel?
activity.hint: Connect your experience with the postmaster's choice.

options: a one-line introduction of the idea
quiz.why: A 120-word answer should begin with a one-line introduction of the main idea. A long quote or the conclusion would not give a clear start.

quiz.q: A diary entry is written in
quiz.why: A diary entry is written in the first person, using 'I', because it records one's own thoughts and events.

options: He was not surprised to receive money
quiz.why: Lencho was not surprised to receive the money, which shows his complete confidence in God. Cursing God or selling his house would show doubt.

quiz.q: A value from the story is
quiz.why: A value from the story is anonymous kindness, as the postmaster helped without being known. Greed, laziness and revenge are not shown as values.

quiz.q: A good long answer ends with
quiz.why: A good long answer ends with a conclusion or lesson, which sums up the main point. A new topic or a question leaves it unfinished.

questions.q: Where was Lencho's house?
options: On the crest of a low hill
questions.why: Lencho's house stood on the crest of a low hill, from where he could see the valley and his field.

questions.q: What destroyed Lencho's crop?
questions.why: A hailstorm destroyed Lencho's crop. It came after the rain he had hoped for.

questions.q: Whom did Lencho write to?
questions.why: Lencho wrote his letter to God, because he believed God would help him.

questions.q: How much did Lencho ask for?
questions.why: Lencho asked God for 100 pesos to sow his field again.

questions.q: What did the postmaster do first on reading the letter?
questions.why: On reading the letter the postmaster laughed heartily at first. Then he became serious, moved by Lencho's faith.

questions.q: How did the postmaster raise the money?
options: From employees, friends and his own salary
questions.why: The postmaster raised money from his employees and friends and gave part of his own salary. This was an act of charity.

questions.q: Why did Lencho get angry?
questions.why: Lencho got angry because he received only 70 pesos, 30 less than he had asked for. He believed the post office employees had taken the rest.

questions.q: Assertion: Lencho was not surprised to receive money. Reason: He had complete faith in God.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true: Lencho was not surprised to receive money, because he had complete faith that God would help. So the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Assertion: Lencho thanked the post office staff. Reason: They collected money for him.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: The assertion is false: Lencho did not thank the post office staff; he called them crooks. The reason is true, as they collected the money.

questions.q: The comparison of raindrops to new coins shows Lencho's
questions.why: Comparing raindrops to new coins shows Lencho's hope of a good harvest. Rain meant money from his crop.

questions.q: Which best describes the ending?
questions.why: The ending is ironic and humorous, because Lencho trusts God and blames the people who actually helped him.

questions.q: Why did the postmaster sign the letter “God”?
options: To preserve Lencho's faith in God
questions.why: The postmaster signed the letter 'God' to preserve Lencho's faith in God. He wanted to keep Lencho's belief alive.

questions.q: Which statement about Lencho is most accurate?
options: He trusted God completely but distrusted the humans who helped him
questions.why: Lencho trusted God completely but distrusted the humans who helped him. This contrast creates the story's irony.

questions.q: If the postmaster collected 70 pesos and Lencho needed 100, what fraction did he send?
questions.why: The fraction sent is 70 out of 100, which is 70/100 = 7/10.

questions.q: Which theme pair fits best?
questions.why: The themes that fit best are faith and irony. The story is not about war, science or revenge.

questions.q: “The hail did more damage than a plague of locusts” is a
questions.why: The sentence compares the hail's damage to that of locusts, showing it destroyed everything. It is a comparison, not a prayer or a joke.

courses.title: First Flight · Nelson Mandela: Long Walk to Freedom
courses.summary: An extract from Nelson Mandela's autobiography: the inauguration of South Africa's first democratic, non-racial government in 1994, apartheid, the meaning of courage, twin obligations and the true meaning of freedom.
outcomes: Learners can describe the inauguration and its significance
Learners can explain apartheid and the sacrifices of freedom fighters
Learners can explain Mandela's ideas on courage, obligations and freedom
Learners can write exam-ready answers using key ideas
courses.note: chapter numbering may differ by edition

scenes.text: Heads of state from many countries gather at the Union Buildings in Pretoria.
Jets fly overhead as Nelson Mandela takes the oath as South Africa's first Black President.

steps.title: The ceremony
steps.body:
- On **10 May 1994**, **Nelson Mandela** was sworn in as President of South Africa at the amphitheatre of the **Union Buildings, Pretoria** – the country's **first democratic, non-racial government**.
- Dignitaries and leaders from more than 140 countries attended – the largest gathering of international leaders on South African soil.
- **Two Deputy Presidents** were sworn in: **Mr de Klerk** first (as second Deputy President), then **Thabo Mbeki** (as first Deputy President).
- Mandela pledged to liberate the people from bondage of poverty, deprivation, suffering, gender and other discrimination.
- **Jets, helicopters and troop carriers** of the South African forces flew over the Union Buildings – a display of the military's loyalty to democracy. The generals who would have arrested Mandela a few years earlier now saluted him.
- **Two national anthems** were sung: whites sang “**Nkosi Sikelel' iAfrika**” and Blacks sang “**Die Stem**” – the old anthem of the Republic – symbolising reconciliation.

steps.title: Apartheid
steps.body: **Apartheid** was a political system that separated people according to their race. In South Africa, the white minority ruled; Black people were denied rights. Mandela spent about **three decades in prison**, much of it on Robben Island. In the last decade of the 20th century the apartheid regime was dismantled and replaced by a government in which all races are equal.

steps.title: Solved example: Why was the inauguration a significant event? (40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Change:** It marked the end of apartheid and the birth of a democratic, non-racial government.

**Step 2 – Recognition:** Leaders from over 140 countries attended, showing world support.

**Step 3 – Symbol:** Military salute and two anthems showed reconciliation.

steps.title: Solved example: What did the military display signify? (30 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Display:** Jets, helicopters and troop carriers flew past.

**Step 2 – Meaning:** It showed the military's loyalty to democracy and to a freely elected government – generals now saluted the man they once arrested.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up the anthems – whites sang **Nkosi Sikelel' iAfrika**, Blacks sang **Die Stem** (each the other's anthem) – a sign of unity.
- Saying de Klerk became President – he was sworn in as **second Deputy President** (Thabo Mbeki became first Deputy President).

statements.s: Mandela was sworn in on 10 May 1994.
De Klerk took the oath before Thabo Mbeki.
statements.why: De Klerk was sworn in first, as second Deputy President.

statements.s: Leaders from over 140 countries attended.
Apartheid meant equal rights for all races.

quiz.why: The ceremony was held at the Union Buildings in Pretoria, the seat of government of South Africa.
Apartheid is racial segregation, the system that separated people by race in South Africa.
The two Deputy Presidents were de Klerk and Thabo Mbeki. Tambo and Sisulu were ANC leaders, not these Deputy Presidents.
The military flypast showed the armed forces' loyalty to democracy and to the new government.
Singing the two anthems symbolised reconciliation and unity between the races.

scenes.text: Before her first debate, Asha's hands shake. Her coach says courage is not the absence of fear.
Mandela said the brave person is one who conquers fear.

steps.title: Depths of oppression, heights of character
steps.body:
- Mandela felt that South Africa had paid a terrible price: thousands of people suffered and sacrificed for freedom. He believed the **depths of oppression created heights of character**. He named patriots like **Oliver Tambo, Walter Sisulu, Chief Luthuli, Yusuf Dadoo, Bram Fischer, Robert Sobukwe** – people of extraordinary courage, wisdom and generosity.
- **The country's greatest wealth is its people** – finer and truer than the purest diamonds.
- **Courage:** he learnt that courage was **not the absence of fear but the triumph over it**. The brave man is not he who does not feel afraid, but he who conquers that fear.
- **Goodness:** no one is born hating another because of skin colour, background or religion; people learn to hate, and if they can learn to hate, they can be taught to love – love comes more naturally to the human heart.

steps.title: Twin obligations
steps.body: Every man has **twin obligations**: to his **family** (parents, wife, children) and to his **people, community and country**. In a civil and humane society, each can fulfil both. But in South Africa, a man of colour who tried to live as a human being was **punished and isolated**; he was torn from his family and forced to live a life of secrecy and rebellion. Mandela put his people before his family – not by choice but by necessity.

steps.title: Solved example: What does Mandela mean by “depths of oppression create heights of character”? (40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Meaning:** Extreme injustice produced people of great courage and wisdom.

**Step 2 – Example:** Leaders like Tambo, Sisulu and Luthuli rose to fight apartheid.

**Step 3 – Message:** Suffering can bring out the best in human beings.

steps.title: Solved example: What are the twin obligations and why could Mandela not fulfil both? (50 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Define:** Obligation to family and to people, community and country.

**Step 2 – Problem:** Under apartheid, working for his people meant being punished, imprisoned and separated from family.

**Step 3 – Result:** He chose his people's freedom, not by choice but because the system left no other way.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Mandela was never afraid – he admitted feeling fear; courage was **conquering** it.
- Treating “twin obligations” as two jobs – they are duties to **family** and **society/country**.

activity.prompt: Match the idea to its meaning
pairs: Duty to family and to the nation

quiz.why: According to Mandela, courage is not the absence of fear but the triumph over it. The brave person conquers fear.

quiz.q: Mandela called South Africa's greatest wealth
quiz.why: Mandela said South Africa's greatest wealth was its people, not its gold or diamonds.
His twin obligations were to his family and to his country, as he describes in the extract.

options: hate and can be taught to love
quiz.why: Mandela believed people learn to hate, and can therefore be taught to love, which comes more naturally to the human heart.

quiz.q: Which leader is named by Mandela?
quiz.why: Mandela names Oliver Tambo, along with other leaders like Sisulu and Luthuli. He does not name Gandhi, King or Lincoln in this way.

scenes.text: As a boy, Mandela thought freedom meant running in the fields and staying out at night.
As a young man he wanted to earn and marry – later he saw that his people were not free.

steps.title: How Mandela's idea of freedom changed
steps.body:
1. **As a boy:** freedom meant running in the fields near his mother's hut, swimming in the stream, roasting mealies, riding bulls – freedom to do as he liked.
2. **As a student/young man:** he wanted basic, honourable freedoms – to stay out at night, read what he pleased, go where he chose; then to achieve his potential, earn a living, marry and have a family.
3. **Realisation:** his boyhood freedom was an **illusion**; not only he but his **brothers and sisters were not free**. The hunger for his own freedom became a **hunger for the freedom of his people**.

**Oppressor and oppressed:** the oppressor must be liberated just as surely as the oppressed. A man who takes away another man's freedom is a **prisoner of hatred**, locked behind the bars of prejudice and narrow-mindedness. Both are robbed of their humanity.

steps.title: Solved example: How did Mandela's understanding of freedom change? (60 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Childhood:** Freedom to play and roam.

**Step 2 – Youth:** Personal freedoms – to read, go out, earn, marry.

**Step 3 – Maturity:** Realised his people were not free; his hunger became for his people's freedom – which made him a fighter and turned a frightened young man into a bold one.

steps.title: Solved example: Why does Mandela say the oppressor is not free? (40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Idea:** The oppressor is a prisoner of hatred, prejudice and narrow-mindedness.

**Step 2 – Effect:** He too is robbed of his humanity.

**Step 3 – Conclusion:** True freedom needs liberation of both the oppressed and the oppressor.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing that Mandela wanted only his own freedom – it became a hunger for the **freedom of his people**.
- Missing the point that the **oppressor** too needs liberation.

activity.prompt: Order the stages of Mandela's idea of freedom
items: Freedom to run in the fields as a boy
Freedom to stay out at night and read what he pleased
Freedom to earn, marry and raise a family
Realisation that his people were not free
Hunger for the freedom of all people, oppressed and oppressor

quiz.q: As a boy Mandela thought he was
quiz.why: As a boy, Mandela thought he was born free. This was an illusion, because the apartheid system did not allow it.

options: a hunger for his people's freedom
quiz.why: His hunger for personal freedom became a hunger for the freedom of his people.

quiz.q: The oppressor is a prisoner of
quiz.why: Mandela says the oppressor is a prisoner of hatred, prejudice and narrow-mindedness.

quiz.q: Who must be liberated, per Mandela?
quiz.why: Mandela says both the oppressed and the oppressor must be liberated. The oppressor is also robbed of his humanity.

quiz.q: The change in his idea of freedom made him
quiz.why: His changed idea of freedom made him bold, not frightened. It turned a fearful young man into one who would act.

scenes.text: Kabir must give a speech on "Courage" at assembly.
He borrows the idea "courage is triumph over fear" and adds examples.

steps.title: Key lines (paraphrased) to use in answers
steps.body:
- Courage = triumph over fear.
- People learn to hate; they can be taught to love.
- Depths of oppression create heights of character.
- Twin obligations – family and nation.
- Oppressor and oppressed both need liberation.
- The country's greatest wealth is its people.

steps.title: Solved example: Long answer: “Mandela's life is an example of sacrifice for the nation.” (120 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Introduce:** Mandela put his people's freedom above personal comfort.

**Step 2 – Sacrifice:** He spent about three decades in prison and lived apart from family – unable to fulfil his duty to them.

**Step 3 – Vision:** He fought apartheid and later sought reconciliation, not revenge.

**Step 4 – Result:** He became the first President of a democratic, non-racial South Africa.

**Step 5 – Conclude:** His life shows courage, selflessness and forgiveness.

steps.title: Solved example: Extract-type: What is meant by “an extraordinary human disaster”? (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Meaning:** Apartheid – a long period of racial discrimination.

**Step 2 – Why disaster:** It caused immense suffering and divided society for decades.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Quoting long passages from memory – use **short paraphrased ideas**.
- Forgetting the date (10 May 1994) and place (Pretoria).

activity.prompt: Write three sentences about a time you conquered a fear.
activity.hint: Use Mandela's idea: courage is not the absence of fear but triumph over it.

quiz.why: 'Extraordinary human disaster' refers to apartheid, which caused great suffering. It does not mean an earthquake, flood or war.

quiz.q: Mandela's message after victory was of
quiz.why: Mandela's message after victory was reconciliation, not revenge or war.

quiz.q: A speech on courage can use the idea
quiz.why: A speech on courage can use Mandela's idea that courage is the triumph over fear, not the absence of it.
Mandela's inauguration took place in 1994 on 10 May, after the first democratic elections.
His twin obligations show a dilemma between duty to family and duty to the nation.

questions.q: When was Mandela sworn in?
questions.why: Mandela was sworn in on 10 May 1994 at the Union Buildings.

questions.q: Where?
questions.why: The ceremony took place at the Union Buildings in Pretoria.

questions.q: Apartheid means
questions.why: Apartheid means racial segregation. It is the opposite of democracy, freedom and equality.

questions.q: Who took the oath first among the two Deputy Presidents?
questions.why: De Klerk took the oath first among the two Deputy Presidents; he was sworn in first as the second Deputy President, then Thabo Mbeki.

questions.q: Mandela said the greatest wealth of his country is
questions.why: Mandela said his country's greatest wealth is its people, not its army, minerals or gold.

questions.q: Courage, according to Mandela, is
questions.why: For Mandela, courage is the triumph over fear. A brave man feels fear but conquers it.

questions.q: Assertion: The military flypast was significant. Reason: It showed the forces' loyalty to democracy.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true: the flypast was significant because it showed the forces' loyalty to democracy. So the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Assertion: Mandela fulfilled both his twin obligations fully. Reason: South Africa was a humane society.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are false: Mandela could not fulfil his obligations fully under apartheid, and South Africa was not a humane society then.

questions.q: Why does Mandela say the oppressor must be liberated?
options: He is a prisoner of hatred and prejudice
questions.why: The oppressor must be liberated because he is a prisoner of hatred and prejudice, robbed of his humanity.

questions.q: Which shows reconciliation?
questions.why: Singing of both anthems shows reconciliation and unity. Banning the old anthem or arresting generals would show division.

questions.q: What turned Mandela from a frightened young man into a bold one?
questions.why: His desire for his people's freedom turned Mandela from a frightened young man into a bold one. It was not money, fame or travel.

questions.q: “Depths of oppression create heights of character” means
options: extreme suffering produced people of great character
questions.why: 'Depths of oppression create heights of character' means that extreme suffering produced people of great character. It does not say oppression is good.

questions.q: Case: A student learns to hate a group from others and later becomes friends with them. Which Mandela idea fits?
options: People learn to hate and can be taught to love
questions.why: The student fits Mandela's idea that people learn to hate and can be taught to love. Love comes more naturally to the human heart.

questions.q: Mandela spent about how long in prison?
questions.why: Mandela spent about three decades, 27 years, in prison.

questions.q: Which statement best summarises the extract?
options: A celebration of freedom with reflections on courage, sacrifice and humanity
questions.why: The extract is a celebration of freedom with reflections on courage, sacrifice and humanity. It is not comic, a travelogue or a war diary.

questions.q: Mandela's boyhood idea of freedom was
questions.why: Mandela's boyhood idea of freedom was an illusion. He later realised that he and his people were not free.

courses.title: First Flight · Two Stories about Flying
courses.summary: Two stories about fear and flight: Liam O'Flaherty's young seagull who must overcome fear to fly, and Frederick Forsyth's pilot guided through a storm by a mysterious black aeroplane.
outcomes: Learners can narrate both stories in sequence
Learners can analyse the theme of fear and self-confidence
Learners can discuss the mystery in The Black Aeroplane
Learners can write exam-ready answers
courses.note: chapter numbering may differ by edition

scenes.text: A young seagull sits alone on a ledge. His brothers and sister have flown; he is afraid his wings won't hold him.
His mother holds a piece of fish just out of reach…

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- The young seagull is **alone on his ledge**; his two brothers and sister had flown the day before. He is afraid to fly – the sea below looks vast.
- His parents scold him, threaten to let him starve, and ignore him. He sees his family flying, eating and enjoying.
- He is **hungry** – he has had nothing to eat since the previous night.
- His **mother** flies close with a piece of **fish** in her beak, stopping just out of his reach. Maddened by hunger, he **dives at the fish** with a scream – and falls into space.
- For a moment he is terrified; then his wings spread and he **flies**. His family praise him.
- He lands on the **green sea**, his legs sink, he panics, then floats. He is no longer afraid.

steps.title: Author and theme
steps.body: Author **Liam O'Flaherty** (Irish). Themes: **fear of the unknown**, **self-confidence**, the role of **parents/mentors** in pushing a child to independence; hunger as the motivator.

steps.title: Solved example: Why was the seagull afraid to fly? (30 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Fear:** He thought his wings would not support him over the vast sea.

**Step 2 – Lack of confidence:** Though his siblings had flown, he lacked faith in himself.

steps.title: Solved example: How did the mother make him fly? (40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Trick:** She flew towards him with fish in her beak and stopped just out of reach.

**Step 2 – Hunger:** Maddened by hunger, he dived at the fish.

**Step 3 – Result:** He fell, then his wings opened and he flew.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the father gave the fish – it was the **mother**.
- Missing that **hunger** finally overcame fear.

items: The seagull is alone on the ledge, afraid to fly
His family ignores him and he grows hungry
His mother brings fish close but out of reach
He dives at the fish and falls
His wings spread and he flies
He lands on the sea and floats

quiz.q: How many siblings had flown before him?
quiz.why: Two brothers and a sister had already flown before the young seagull, but he was still afraid.

options: Hunger at the sight of fish
quiz.why: Hunger at the sight of fish made him finally dive. His mother held a piece of fish out of his reach to tempt him.
The mother held the fish, tempting the hungry seagull to fly.
He landed on the green sea, not on a rock or ledge. He floated, which gave him confidence.
The story mainly shows overcoming fear, as the seagull learns to fly.

scenes.text: A pilot flies an old Dakota from Paris to England at night, dreaming of breakfast at home.
Ahead, huge black storm clouds – and not enough fuel to go around them.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- The narrator, a pilot, is flying an old **Dakota** aeroplane from **Paris to London** (England) for an English breakfast with his family.
- He sees huge **black storm clouds**. He has too little fuel to fly around them, so he **takes the risk** and flies into the storm.
- Inside the clouds, his **instruments fail** – the compass spins, radio is dead. He is lost.
- A **black aeroplane** without lights appears; its pilot waves to follow. The narrator follows, and is guided out of the clouds to a runway.
- He lands safely, but the black plane has disappeared.
- In the control room, the woman says **no other aeroplane was flying** that night – only his was on the radar. The mystery remains: who was the pilot?

steps.title: Author and theme
steps.body: Author **Frederick Forsyth**. Themes: **mystery**, **risk-taking**, **divine help** or unknown help in crisis; narrated in the **first person**, which makes it suspenseful.

steps.title: Solved example: Why did the pilot fly into the storm? (30 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Problem:** He did not have enough fuel to fly around the clouds.

**Step 2 – Choice:** He wanted to get home for breakfast, so he “took the risk”.

steps.title: Solved example: What makes the ending mysterious? (40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Event:** After landing, the black aeroplane vanished.

**Step 2 – Fact:** The control tower said no other plane was flying; radar showed only his.

**Step 3 – Mystery:** So who guided him? Possibly divine help or his imagination.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying he flew from London to Paris – it was **Paris to England (London)**.
- Claiming the black plane landed with him – it **disappeared**.

statements.s: The pilot flew an old Dakota.
He had plenty of fuel to fly around the clouds.
The black aeroplane had lights on.
The control room confirmed a second plane.
statements.why: No other plane was on radar.

quiz.why: The pilot was flying to England, from where he had started his journey back.

quiz.q: Why did his instruments stop working?
quiz.why: His instruments stopped working inside the storm clouds, so he had to fly blind.
A mysterious black aeroplane guided him out of the storm and to a safe landing.

quiz.q: The woman in the control room said
quiz.why: The woman in the control room said that no other plane was flying, so the black aeroplane could not have been there.
The story is narrated in the first person, by the pilot, which makes it feel immediate.

scenes.text: One hero is pushed by a mother's trick; the other is guided by an unknown pilot.
Both face fear in the air.

steps.title: Common threads and differences
steps.body:
- **Common:** both are about **flying** and **facing fear**; both heroes receive help at a crucial moment.
- **Seagull:** fear of the **unknown**, overcome by **hunger and the mother's encouragement** – a story of growing up.
- **Pilot:** a **risky decision**, then a crisis, rescued by **mysterious help** – a story of suspense.
- **Lesson:** fear can be overcome; help sometimes comes from unexpected places; confidence grows from experience.

steps.title: Solved example: Compare the help each hero received (50 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Seagull:** His mother used fish to lure him – practical, motivating help.

**Step 2 – Pilot:** An unknown black plane guided him – mysterious help.

**Step 3 – Common:** Both were helped at the moment of crisis and survived.

steps.title: Solved example: Was the pilot right to take the risk? (40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Against:** It was careless – he endangered passengers by entering storm clouds.

**Step 2 – For:** He lacked fuel to go around.

**Step 3 – Judgement:** Risks should be calculated; safety first.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Saying both heroes were helped by family – only the seagull was.

items.text: Control room finds no other plane

quiz.why: Both stories are about flying and facing fear: the seagull's first flight and the pilot's storm.

quiz.q: The seagull's fear was overcome by
quiz.why: The seagull's fear was overcome by hunger, which pushed him to dive at the fish.
The pilot's rescue was mysterious, since the black aeroplane that guided him was not known to the control room.

quiz.q: Which hero took a risky decision?
quiz.why: The pilot took the risky decision to fly into the storm clouds. The seagull's act was a leap, not a calculated risk.
Both stories show that fear can be overcome, whether by hunger or by determination in danger.

scenes.text: Zoya is scared of the deep end of the pool, like the young seagull at the ledge.
Her teacher asks her to write about it, linking it to the story.

steps.title: Answer-writing tips
steps.body:
- For character questions, give **trait + evidence**.
- For “what would you do” questions, give a **reasoned opinion**.
- For mystery endings, mention **possible explanations** rather than claiming certainty.

steps.title: Solved example: Long answer: “Fear is overcome by action.” Discuss with reference to the young seagull (120 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Introduce:** The seagull was paralysed by fear of the vast sea.

**Step 2 – Evidence:** Scolding and threats did not help; only when hunger forced him to dive did he discover his wings could hold him.

**Step 3 – Point:** Action replaced imagination; confidence came after the first attempt.

**Step 4 – Link:** Like a child learning to swim or speak on stage.

**Step 5 – Conclude:** Courage grows by doing.

steps.title: Solved example: Diary entry of the pilot after landing (100 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Format:** Date, first person, emotions.

**Step 2 – Content:** Fear in the clouds, relief on seeing the black plane, shock at the control room's reply.

**Step 3 – Reflection:** Gratitude to the unknown pilot; resolve not to take such risks.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Writing “the seagull was lazy” – he was **afraid**, not lazy.

activity.prompt: Describe a time you did something for the first time despite fear.
activity.hint: What pushed you – like hunger pushed the seagull?

quiz.why: A good character answer includes a trait plus evidence from the text. A quote alone or just the title does not explain the character.
The young seagull was afraid to fly, even though his siblings had done it.
The pilot's experience shows mystery and luck, since he was guided by a plane that no one else saw.
A diary entry needs a date and is written in the first person. An address of the receiver, headline or subject line belong to other formats.
'Courage grows by doing' fits the seagull, who learned to fly by actually trying it.

questions.why: 'The Black Aeroplane' was written by Frederick Forsyth.

questions.why: The young seagull was afraid of flying over the sea, not of fish or other birds.

questions.q: Why couldn't the pilot fly around the storm?
questions.why: The pilot could not fly around the storm because he had no fuel to spare. So he took the risk of flying through it.

questions.q: Assertion: The seagull flew when he dived at the fish. Reason: Hunger overcame his fear.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true: the seagull flew when he dived at the fish, because hunger overcame his fear. So the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Assertion: The control tower guided the pilot. Reason: His radio was dead.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: The assertion is false: the control tower did not guide him, the black aeroplane did. The reason is true, since his radio was dead.

questions.q: What does the mother's act show?
questions.why: The mother's act of tempting the seagull with fish shows wise encouragement, tough love to help him fly.

questions.q: Which statement about the black aeroplane is correct?
questions.why: The black aeroplane disappeared after guiding the pilot, and no one else had seen it.

questions.q: The first-person narration in The Black Aeroplane
questions.why: First-person narration in 'The Black Aeroplane' adds suspense and immediacy, because we see events through the pilot's eyes.

questions.q: Case: A student refuses to try public speaking until a teacher gives her a tiny role she cannot refuse. Which story fits?
questions.why: The student who refuses to try public speaking until she is given a role she cannot refuse fits 'His First Flight', where the seagull flies because of need and encouragement.

questions.why: The pilot's risk was flying into storm clouds, since he had no fuel to go around.

questions.q: Which possible explanations fit the ending?
options: Divine help, a ghost pilot or his imagination
questions.why: The ending is open, so possible explanations include divine help, a ghost pilot or the pilot's imagination.

questions.q: Which common message unites both stories?
options: Help arrives in crisis and fear can be conquered
questions.why: The common message is that help arrives in crisis and fear can be conquered, as shown in both stories.

questions.why: The seagull had not eaten since the previous night, so he was very hungry.

courses.title: First Flight · From the Diary of Anne Frank
courses.summary: Extracts from the diary of a Jewish girl who later hid from the Nazis: why she writes, her friend “Kitty”, her family background, and her clever response to a strict maths teacher who kept punishing her for talking.
outcomes: Learners can explain why Anne kept a diary and called it Kitty
Learners can describe Anne's family background and school life
Learners can narrate the Mr Keesing episode
Learners can write exam-ready answers on Anne's character
courses.note: chapter numbering may differ by edition

scenes.text: On her 13th birthday, Anne receives a diary.
She has family and many friends, yet she feels she has no one to confide in.

steps.title: Key ideas
steps.body:
- **Anne Frank** was a Jewish girl in Amsterdam (Netherlands). She received a diary on her **13th birthday**.
- She felt that **paper has more patience than people** – she could write things she couldn't say.
- She had loving parents, a 16-year-old sister, and about thirty people she could call friends, but **no true friend** to share deep thoughts. So she imagined the diary as her friend and named it **Kitty**.
- She believed no one would be interested in the musings of a thirteen-year-old girl – yet her diary became one of the world's most widely read books.
- Her family history: father **Otto Frank** married at 36, mother at 25; sister **Margot** born in Frankfurt in 1926, Anne in 1929. Being Jewish, the family emigrated from Germany to Holland (1933) where her father started a company. Her grandmother died in 1942; Anne still lights a candle for her. Life was full of anxiety because of Hitler's anti-Jewish laws.

steps.title: Solved example: Why did Anne call her diary Kitty? (30 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Need:** She had no true friend to confide in.

**Step 2 – Choice:** She imagined the diary as a friend and named it Kitty to make it feel real.

steps.title: Solved example: “Paper has more patience than people.” Explain (30 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Meaning:** Paper listens without judging or interrupting.

**Step 2 – Context:** Anne could share feelings with her diary that she could not tell people.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Anne had no friends – she had **many**, but no **true** friend.
- Mixing up her age – she got the diary on her **13th** birthday.

statements.s: Anne got her diary on her 13th birthday.
Anne had no friends at all.
statements.why: She had many but no true friend.

statements.s: Kitty was Anne's cat.
Anne's family moved from Germany to Holland.

quiz.why: Anne named her diary Kitty, and wrote her entries as letters to Kitty.

quiz.q: Why did Anne keep a diary?
quiz.why: Anne kept a diary because she had no true friend to share her thoughts with.
Anne's father was Otto Frank, who later published her diary.
Anne wrote that paper has more patience than people, because she could write freely without being judged.
Anne's family was Jewish, which is why they were persecuted by the Nazis.

lessons.title: Mr Keesing and the chatterbox essays

scenes.text: Mr Keesing, an old maths teacher, keeps scolding Anne for talking in class.
He gives her extra homework – an essay on "A Chatterbox".

steps.title: The episode
steps.body:
- Mr Keesing was annoyed with Anne for **talking too much** in class.
- **First punishment:** an essay on **“A Chatterbox”**. Anne argued convincingly that talking is a **student's trait** and that she inherited it from her **mother**, who also talked a lot – one cannot do much to break an inherited trait. Mr Keesing laughed.
- **Second punishment:** an essay on **“An Incorrigible Chatterbox”**. Anne wrote it; Mr Keesing had no complaints for two lessons.
- **Third punishment:** an essay titled **“Quack, Quack, Quack, Said Mistress Chatterback”**. Anne, with help from her friend **Sanne** (good at poetry), wrote a **poem** about a mother duck and a father swan with three baby ducklings who were bitten to death by the father because they quacked too much.
- Mr Keesing **took the joke the right way**; he read the poem aloud in class and to other classes, and from then on he let Anne talk and never assigned extra homework. He even began making jokes himself.

steps.title: Solved example: How did Anne justify talking in her first essay? (40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Argument 1:** Talking is a student's trait.

**Step 2 – Argument 2:** It is inherited from her mother, who is also talkative.

**Step 3 – Conclusion:** One cannot do much to change an inherited trait – so she would try but couldn't promise.

steps.title: Solved example: How did Mr Keesing change? (40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Before:** Strict; punished her with extra essays.

**Step 2 – Turning point:** He enjoyed the witty poem and read it to classes.

**Step 3 – After:** He allowed her to talk and stopped extra homework – showing a sense of humour.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Anne wrote all three essays alone – Sanne helped with the **poem**.
- Calling Mr Keesing cruel throughout – he **changed** and took the joke well.

Essay: Quack, Quack, Quack, Said Mistress Chatterback (a poem)

scenes.text: Anne's family later went into hiding during the Second World War.
Her diary, published after the war, became one of the most read books in the world.

steps.title: Anne's character
steps.body:
- **Witty and intelligent** – turned punishment into a joke.
- **Sensitive and introspective** – felt lonely despite friends.
- **Frank and honest** – wrote her true feelings.
- **Confident** – argued with her teacher logically.

**Historical context:** the Frank family, being Jewish, faced Nazi persecution; they later hid in a secret annexe in Amsterdam. Anne died in a concentration camp in 1945. Her father **Otto Frank** survived and published the diary. (This historical context is beyond the extract but helps understanding; handle the topic with sensitivity.)

steps.title: Solved example: Describe Anne's character with evidence (60 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Witty:** Wrote a funny poem to answer the teacher.

**Step 2 – Sensitive:** Felt she had no true friend; confided in Kitty.

**Step 3 – Logical:** Argued that talking was inherited and a student trait.

steps.title: Solved example: Why is the diary important? (40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Personal:** A teenager's honest thoughts and feelings.

**Step 2 – Historical:** A record of Jewish life under Nazi persecution, read worldwide.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Overstating – the extract itself is mostly about school and feelings; keep facts from the chapter central.
