courses.title: First Flight · Glimpses of India
courses.summary: Three short pieces about India's diversity: the traditional baker (pader) of Goa, the land and people of Coorg, and a journey to the tea gardens of Assam with legends about tea.
outcomes: Learners can describe the Goan baker and his place in village life
Learners can describe Coorg's geography, people and traditions
Learners can retell the legends of tea and facts about Assam tea
Learners can write exam-ready answers
courses.note: chapter numbering may differ by edition

scenes.text: In a Goan village, children wake to the "jingling thud" of the baker's bamboo staff.
He carries a basket of loaves and bangles of bread.

steps.title: Key points
steps.body:
- The writer (**Lucio Rodrigues**) recalls childhood in Goa and the **Portuguese** heritage of bread-making. The Portuguese may have left, but the **bakers (paders)** remain; the furnaces and mixers still exist.
- The baker came **twice a day** – morning selling, and evening returning with an empty basket. His **bamboo staff** made a **jingling thud** to announce his arrival.
- Children ran to him for **bread-bangles**, not to brush teeth – they ate them with tea.
- Bread is essential at **marriages** (sweet bread **bol**), **parties**, **feasts**; **bebinca** cake for **Christmas**; sandwiches for a daughter's **engagement**.
- Bakers wore a single-piece long frock called **kabai** (to the knees); later a shirt and trousers shorter than full-length and longer than half-pants.
- Bakers collected bills **monthly**, recorded on a wall with pencil. Baking was a profitable profession – a baker's **plump body** was a sign of prosperity (people said “look at his plump body” to describe a well-fed person, like a jackfruit).

steps.title: Solved example: Why is the baker important in Goan village life? (40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Daily need:** He supplied bread twice a day.

**Step 2 – Festivals:** Bol for marriages, bebinca for Christmas, sandwiches for engagements.

**Step 3 – Tradition:** He keeps the Portuguese bread-making heritage alive.

steps.title: Solved example: What did the baker wear? (20 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Old:** A single-piece long frock, the kabai, reaching the knees.

**Step 2 – Later:** A shirt and trousers shorter than full length.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling the baker's staff a drum – it is a **bamboo staff** making a jingling thud.
- Confusing bol (marriages) with bebinca (Christmas).

activity.prompt: Match the bread item to the occasion

quiz.q: A baker in Goa is called
quiz.why: A baker in Goa is called a pader. A dhobi is a washerman, a vaid a doctor and a mali a gardener.
The baker announced his arrival with the jingling thud of a bamboo staff, not with a bell or horn.
In the lesson, the baker collected his bills monthly, not daily or weekly. The pader came every day to sell bread but settled accounts once a month.
Bebinca, a Goan layered sweet, is essential for Christmas, as the lesson says. It is not tied to Onam, Eid or Diwali.

quiz.q: A plump body was a sign of
quiz.why: A plump body was a sign of prosperity, so bakers who looked well-fed were seen as doing well. It did not mean illness or poverty.

scenes.text: Rohan's family drives to Coorg (Kodagu) in Karnataka, through coffee estates and misty hills.
They raft on the Kaveri and see monks in red robes at Bylakuppe.

steps.title: Key points
steps.body:
- **Coorg (Kodagu)** is the smallest district of **Karnataka**, between **Mysuru and Mangaluru**; a piece of heaven – evergreen rainforests, spices, **coffee plantations**.
- **Best time to visit:** **September to March**; weather is perfect with some showers.
- **People – Kodavus:** a fiercely independent martial race, possibly of **Greek or Arabic descent**; one story says part of **Alexander's army** settled here; another theory links them to Arabs because they wear a long black coat with an embroidered waist-belt – the **kuppia**, similar to the **kuffia** of Arabs and Kurds.
- Known for **hospitality** and **tales of valour**. The **Coorg Regiment** is one of the most decorated in the Indian Army; **General Cariappa**, the **first Army Chief** of independent India, was a Coorgi. **Kodavus are the only people in India permitted to carry firearms without a licence.**
- **River Kaveri** gets its water from the hills and forests of Coorg; **mahaseer** (a large freshwater fish) abounds. Adventure sports: river rafting, canoeing, rappelling, rock climbing, mountain biking.
- **Brahmagiri hills** – panoramic view; **Nisargadhama** island reached by rope bridge; **Bylakuppe** – India's largest Tibetan settlement, Buddhist monks in red, ochre and yellow robes.

steps.title: Solved example: Why are the Kodavus thought to be of Greek or Arab descent? (40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Greek theory:** A part of Alexander's army is said to have settled in Coorg.

**Step 2 – Arab theory:** Their long black coat (kuppia) resembles the Arab kuffia.

steps.title: Solved example: What makes Coorg special for tourists? (40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Nature:** Rainforests, coffee estates, Kaveri river with mahaseer.

**Step 2 – Adventure:** Rafting, canoeing, rock climbing, trekking.

**Step 3 – Culture:** Hospitable Kodavus; Bylakuppe Tibetan settlement.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Placing Coorg in Kerala – it is in **Karnataka**.
- Saying all Indians can carry guns without licence there – only **Kodavus** are permitted.

statements.s: Coorg is the smallest district of Karnataka.
The best time to visit is April to June.
General Cariappa was a Coorgi.
Bylakuppe has a Tibetan settlement.

quiz.why: Coorg lies between Mysuru and Mangaluru in Karnataka, as the lesson says. The other pairs name different regions.
The kuppia is a long black coat worn by Kodavus, with a red sash. It is not a dance, fish or sword.
Mahaseer is a large freshwater fish found in Coorg's rivers. It is not a hill, coffee type or bird.
Kodavus are the only people in India allowed to carry firearms without a licence, a unique right. They cannot carry elephants and swords alone is not the right.
The river Kaveri flows from Coorg, where it rises. Ganga, Krishna and Narmada rise elsewhere.

scenes.text: Pranjol and his friend Rajvir travel by train to Assam; tea bushes stretch for miles.
Rajvir tells legends about how tea was discovered.

steps.title: Key points
steps.body:
- **Pranjol** (from Assam; his father manages a tea garden) and **Rajvir** (from Delhi) are classmates travelling to Assam during summer vacation. Rajvir has read about tea.
- Over **80 crore cups** of tea are drunk every day throughout the world (as stated in the text).
- **Legends:** (1) **Chinese legend** – Emperor **Shen Nung** noticed a few leaves of a twig falling into his boiling water; the water tasted delicious – tea was discovered. (2) **Indian legend** – **Bodhidharma**, an ancient Buddhist ascetic, **cut off his eyelids** because he felt sleepy during meditation; ten tea plants grew out of the eyelids; the leaves banished sleep when put in hot water.
- Tea was first drunk in **China** as early as **2700 BC**; words like *chai* and *chini* are from Chinese. Tea came to Europe in the **sixteenth century**, first drunk more as medicine than as a beverage.
- **Assam** has the largest concentration of plantations in the world. They visit **Dhekiabari Tea Estate**. Tea-pluckers with bamboo baskets on their backs pluck the newly grown leaves. The **second flush** (sprouting period from **May to July**) yields the best tea.

steps.title: Solved example: Narrate the two legends of tea (60 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Chinese:** Emperor Shen Nung boiled water; a few leaves fell in; it tasted delicious – tea.

**Step 2 – Indian:** Bodhidharma cut his eyelids to stay awake while meditating; ten tea plants grew from them; their leaves banished sleep.

steps.title: Solved example: Why is the “second flush” important? (20 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Fact:** It is the sprouting period from May to July.

**Step 2 – Value:** It yields the best tea.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Bodhidharma was Chinese emperor – he was a **Buddhist ascetic**; Shen Nung was the emperor.
- Writing that tea reached Europe in ancient times – it came in the **16th century**.

pairs: Chinese emperor in the tea legend
Buddhist ascetic who cut his eyelids

quiz.why: Pranjol and Rajvir were travelling to Assam, as the lesson says. Rajvir was surprised by the tea gardens.

quiz.q: The Indian legend of tea involves
quiz.why: The Indian legend of tea involves Bodhidharma, who is said to have cut off his eyelids to stay awake. Shen Nung is the Chinese emperor in the Chinese legend.

quiz.q: Tea came to Europe in the
quiz.why: Tea came to Europe in the 16th century, according to the lesson. It was drunk in China much earlier.

quiz.q: The best tea is from the
quiz.why: The lesson says the best tea is the second flush, picked from May to July. It is not the first flush or winter tea.
Pranjol's father manages a tea garden, which is why the boy knows about tea. He is not a teacher, baker or pilot.

scenes.text: Students design a brochure about three Indian regions.
Food, people and landscape show India's diversity.

steps.title: Linking the three pieces
steps.body:
- **Goa:** food culture and Portuguese heritage; traditional profession.
- **Coorg:** landscape, martial people, adventure tourism, coffee.
- **Assam:** tea plantations, legends and history of tea.
**Common thread:** India's rich **diversity** – each region has its own traditions, foods and stories.

steps.title: Solved example: Long answer: “Glimpses of India shows India's cultural diversity.” (120 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Goa:** Paders keep the Portuguese bread tradition alive; bread marks festivals.

**Step 2 – Coorg:** Kodavus' martial traditions, hospitality, coffee and adventure sports.

**Step 3 – Assam:** Tea gardens, legends of Shen Nung and Bodhidharma.

**Step 4 – Conclude:** Together they show unity in diversity.

steps.title: Solved example: Write a short notice for a school trip to Coorg (50 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Format:** School name, NOTICE, date, heading.

**Step 2 – Content:** Destination, dates (October), cost, items to carry, last date, contact.

**Step 3 – Sign:** Name and designation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Mixing details between the three pieces (e.g. mahaseer in Assam).

quiz.why: The Goa piece mentions Portuguese heritage, since the bakers' bread-making traditions come from the Portuguese. Assam and Coorg are not linked to it.
The Coorg piece features adventure sports, such as rafting, canoeing, rock climbing and trekking.

quiz.q: Which piece is set on a train journey?
quiz.why: 'Tea from Assam' is set on a train journey, with Pranjol and Rajvir travelling. Goa and Coorg are not train-journey pieces.
The common theme of these three pieces is India's diversity, in food, places and culture. They are not about war, sports only or science.
A notice must include a heading and a date, and give the information clearly. A poem, dialogue or story is not a notice format.

questions.q: Author of “A Baker from Goa”
questions.why: 'A Baker from Goa' was written by Lucio Rodrigues. Ruskin Bond, Lokesh Abrol and Arup Kumar Datta wrote the other pieces.

questions.q: Coorg is in
questions.why: Coorg is in Karnataka, between Mysuru and Mangaluru. It is not in Goa, Kerala or Assam.

questions.q: The Chinese emperor in the tea legend
questions.why: The Chinese emperor in the tea legend was Shen Nung. Bodhidharma is in the Indian legend.

questions.q: Bread-bangles were eaten by children with
questions.why: Children ate bread-bangles with tea, as the lesson describes. It is not eaten with milk, curry or jam.

questions.q: The best season to visit Coorg
questions.why: The best season to visit Coorg is September to March, as the text says. It is not only December or April–June.

questions.q: The second flush is from
questions.why: The second flush is the tea picked from May to July, according to the text.

questions.q: Assertion: Kodavus may be of Arab descent. Reason: Their kuppia resembles the Arab kuffia.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true: Kodavus may be of Arab descent, and their kuppia resembles the Arab kuffia, which supports the theory. So the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Assertion: Goan bakers have vanished since the Portuguese left. Reason: Bread is not used at festivals.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are false: Goan bakers have not vanished since the Portuguese left, and bread is essential at festivals like Christmas.

questions.q: Who was the first Army Chief from Coorg?
questions.why: The first Army Chief from Coorg was General Cariappa, as the lesson says. Thimayya, Manekshaw and Rawat are other officers.

questions.q: Which describes the baker's arrival?
questions.why: The baker's arrival is described as the jingling thud of his bamboo staff. It was not a horn, song or bell.

questions.q: Tea was first drunk in China as early as
questions.why: Tea was first drunk in China as early as 2700 BC, according to the text.

questions.q: Which is TRUE of Bylakuppe?
questions.why: Bylakuppe is the largest Tibetan settlement in India, near Coorg. It is not a Goan village, dam or tea estate.

questions.q: Case: A tourist wants rafting, coffee estates and a Tibetan monastery in one trip. Where?
questions.why: Coorg offers rafting, coffee estates and a Tibetan monastery (Bylakuppe) in one trip. Goa, Delhi and Assam do not offer all three.

questions.q: Why was a plump baker a common sight?
options: Baking was profitable and bakers were well-fed
questions.why: A plump baker was a common sight because baking was profitable and bakers were well-fed. They were not ill or athletes.

questions.q: Which pair is correct?
questions.why: 'Bebinca – Christmas' is the correct pair, as bebinca is essential at Christmas. Kuppia belongs to Coorg and mahaseer to Coorg's rivers.

questions.q: Over how many cups of tea are drunk daily worldwide according to the text?
questions.why: The text says over 80 crore cups of tea are drunk daily worldwide.

courses.title: First Flight · Mijbil the Otter (Gavin Maxwell)
courses.summary: The author's funny and touching account of keeping an otter, Mijbil, from Iraq: getting him, his water-play, the chaotic journey to London and people's guesses about what animal he was.
outcomes: Learners can narrate how Maxwell got Mijbil and their bond
Learners can describe Mij's habits and play
Learners can narrate the air journey and the London episodes
Learners can write exam-ready answers
courses.note: chapter numbering may differ by edition

scenes.text: Grieving the death of his dog Jonnie, the author travels to southern Iraq.
Two Arab boys bring him a sack – inside is a baby otter.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Early in 1956 the author, **Gavin Maxwell**, travelled to **southern Iraq**. After his dog **Jonnie** died, he wanted an **otter** as a pet instead of a dog. A friend suggested he get one from the **Tigris marshes**, where otters were common.
- At **Basra**, while waiting for mail, he returned to his room one evening to find two Arabs with a sack containing an otter – sent by his friend.
- He named it **Mijbil** (Mij). It was of a race previously unknown to science and was named **Maxwell's otter** (*Lutrogale perspicillata maxwelli*) by zoologists.
- For the first 24 hours Mij was aloof and indifferent; then he began to accept the author and climbed into his bed to sleep.

steps.title: Mij at play
steps.body:
- Mij loved **water** – he went mad with joy in the bathtub, rolling and splashing; he even learnt to **turn on the tap**.
- He would play for hours with a **rubber ball** and marbles; otters, the author observes, are extremely playful and will play with almost anything.
- He walked on a leash like a dog and pulled towards water pipes and puddles.

steps.title: Solved example: Why did Maxwell want an otter? (30 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Loss:** His dog Jonnie had died; he did not want another dog.

**Step 2 – Idea:** A friend suggested an otter from the Tigris marshes, where they were common.

steps.title: Solved example: How did Mij show his love for water? (40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Bathtub:** He plunged and splashed madly in the bath.

**Step 2 – Taps:** He learnt to turn on the tap himself.

**Step 3 – Walks:** He pulled towards water and played in puddles.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Maxwell bought Mij in London – he got him in **Basra, Iraq**.
- Saying Mij was friendly from the first minute – he was **aloof** for 24 hours.

items: Maxwell's dog Jonnie dies
He travels to southern Iraq
Two Arabs bring an otter in a sack
Mij is aloof for a day
Mij sleeps in Maxwell's bed
Mij learns to turn on the bath tap

quiz.why: Maxwell got Mij in Basra, Iraq, where he went to explore the marshes. London is where he took the otter later.
Maxwell's dog was named Jonnie, who had died.
Mij's species was later named Maxwell's otter after Gavin Maxwell, because it was a new subspecies.

quiz.q: For the first 24 hours Mij was
quiz.why: For the first 24 hours Mij was aloof and indifferent, showing little interest in Maxwell.
Mij loved to play with a rubber ball, along with marbles.

scenes.text: Airlines would not carry animals in the cabin; Mij had to travel in a box.
Mij tore the box lining, bled, and then escaped in the aeroplane.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- The airline (bound for **Paris and then London**) would not allow animals in the cabin; Mij had to go in a box as baggage, at the author's feet.
- An hour before the flight, Maxwell put Mij in the box; Mij tore the lining to shreds and **bloodied** himself trying to escape. With no time to fix it, Maxwell reached the airport with Mij in a damaged box.
- During the flight Mij **escaped** and ran through the aeroplane; passengers panicked (a woman screamed “A rat!”). Maxwell searched, his face covered in curry from a passenger's plate as he dived for Mij.
- A kind **air hostess** offered to let Mij stay on Maxwell's knee – he cuddled in and Maxwell was grateful.
- In **London**, people could not identify Mij; they guessed he was a **baby seal, a squirrel, a walrus, a hippo, a beaver, a bear cub, a leopard** – and a labourer even asked if it was a **“brontosaur”**.

steps.title: Solved example: What happened when Mij was put in the box? (40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Reaction:** He panicked and tore the lining.

**Step 2 – Injury:** He bled from his mouth and paws.

**Step 3 – Effect:** Maxwell had to take him to the airport in a damaged box, leading to the escape on the plane.

steps.title: Solved example: Why were Londoners' guesses funny? (40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Unfamiliar:** Few people had seen an otter.

**Step 2 – Guesses:** Seal, squirrel, walrus, hippo, beaver, bear cub, leopard, brontosaur.

**Step 3 – Humour:** Wild, mismatched guesses show ignorance and create comedy.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Mij flew in the cargo hold – he was in a box **at Maxwell's feet** in the cabin.
- Forgetting the **air hostess's** kindness.

statements.s: Airlines allowed animals in the cabin freely.
statements.why: He had to travel in a box.

statements.s: Mij escaped during the flight.
The air hostess let Mij sit on Maxwell's knee.
Londoners immediately knew Mij was an otter.

quiz.why: Mij travelled in a box at Maxwell's feet on the plane.

quiz.q: What did Mij do to the box?
quiz.why: Mij tore the lining of the box during the flight, trying to escape from fear.
An air hostess helped during the flight, giving Maxwell a towel and a bowl of water.

quiz.q: A passenger screamed that Mij was a
quiz.why: A passenger screamed that Mij was a rat, when he escaped from the box.

quiz.q: Which was NOT a London guess?
quiz.why: Nobody guessed 'otter' in London; people guessed things like a brontosaur, a beaver or a walrus.

lessons.title: Humour, style and the human–animal bond

scenes.text: Your pet has moods, games and tricks – just like Mij.
Maxwell writes about Mij with affection and gentle humour.

steps.title: Style and themes
steps.body:
- **First-person narrative** with **humour**: curry on the author's face, the brontosaur guess, Mij's tantrums.
- **Close observation** of animal behaviour – play, water-love, attachment.
- **Bond and responsibility:** Maxwell cares for Mij's comfort; the story shows love and the challenges of keeping an unusual pet.
- Note: wild animals should not be taken as pets today; laws (e.g. India's Wildlife Protection Act) protect many species.

steps.title: Solved example: Give two humorous incidents (40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Incident 1:** Maxwell's face got covered in curry while chasing Mij in the plane.

**Step 2 – Incident 2:** A London labourer asked if Mij was a brontosaur.

steps.title: Solved example: How do we know Maxwell loved Mij? (40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Care:** He worried about Mij's injuries and comfort in the box.

**Step 2 – Patience:** He searched the plane and was grateful when Mij settled on his knee.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Missing the humour – exam questions often ask for **funny incidents**.

activity.prompt: Match the moment to its feeling

quiz.why: The narrative is in the first person, told by Gavin Maxwell using 'I'.
The curry on Maxwell's face is a humorous incident, from the time the chapter shows him laughing with Mij. Jonnie's death and Mij bleeding are not humorous.

options: a bond between human and animal
quiz.why: The story shows a bond between a human and an animal.
Otters are described as extremely playful creatures.

quiz.q: Today, wild animals as pets are
quiz.why: Today, keeping wild animals as pets is often restricted or protected by law, to protect wildlife. It is not always allowed.

scenes.text: Arjun writes a paragraph about his dog's habits in Maxwell's style.
He adds one funny moment and one caring moment.

steps.title: Tips
steps.body:
- For narrative questions, keep **sequence**: Iraq → Basra → playing → box → flight → London.
- For character questions, use **evidence** (aloof, playful, water-loving, attached).

steps.title: Solved example: Long answer: Describe Mij's journey from Basra to London (120 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Problem:** Airline rules – box at feet.

**Step 2 – Box:** Mij tore the lining, bled.

**Step 3 – Flight:** Escaped; chaos; curry on Maxwell; air hostess let Mij sit on his knee.

**Step 4 – London:** People guessed seal, beaver, brontosaur.

**Step 5 – Conclude:** Humour and care mark the episode.

steps.title: Solved example: Write Mij's diary entry (as Mij) after the flight (80 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Voice:** First person, playful.

**Step 2 – Feelings:** Fear of the box, excitement of running, comfort on the knee.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Saying Mij reached New York – he went to **London** (via Paris).

activity.prompt: If you could keep any animal, what would you need to care for it properly?
activity.hint: Think food, space, water, laws and kindness.

quiz.why: The correct journey order is Iraq to Paris to London, as Maxwell travelled with Mij from Basra.
Mij's key traits are being aloof at first, playful and water-loving. He was not fierce, silent or lazy.

quiz.q: A diary in Mij's voice uses
quiz.why: A diary in Mij's voice would use the first person, 'I'.

quiz.q: Why did Mij tear the box?
quiz.why: Mij tore the box out of fear and a wish to escape, as he was in an unfamiliar place.
Maxwell's gratitude was towards the air hostess, who helped him with Mij during the flight.

questions.q: Mijbil was a
questions.why: Mijbil was an otter, a water-loving animal that Maxwell kept as a pet.

questions.q: Maxwell got Mij in
questions.why: Maxwell got Mij in Basra, in Iraq.

questions.q: Mij loved
questions.why: Mij loved water, as otters do.

questions.q: Maxwell's dog Jonnie had
questions.why: Maxwell's dog Jonnie had died, so he was looking for a new companion.

questions.q: Mij learnt to
questions.why: Mij learnt to turn on the bath tap, which shows his intelligence and playfulness.

questions.q: Who was kind during the flight?
questions.why: An air hostess was kind during the flight, helping Maxwell with Mij.

questions.q: Assertion: Mij bled before the flight. Reason: He tore the box lining trying to escape.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true: Mij bled because he tore the box lining trying to escape. So the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Assertion: Londoners recognised Mij easily. Reason: Otters were common pets in London.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are false: Londoners did not recognise Mij easily, and otters were not common pets in London.

questions.q: The zoological name honours
questions.why: The zoological name honours Maxwell, as Mij's species was named Maxwell's otter.

questions.q: “A brontosaur” guess shows
questions.why: The guess 'a brontosaur' shows public ignorance and adds humour, since nobody guessed it was an otter.

questions.q: Why did the airline refuse animals in the cabin?
questions.why: The airline refused animals in the cabin because of its rules about animals, which is why Mij had to travel in a box.

questions.q: Which statement best sums up the chapter?
options: A humorous account of the bond between a man and an unusual pet
questions.why: The chapter is a humorous account of the bond between a man and an unusual pet. It is not a war story, travel guide or science report.

questions.q: Case: A pet refuses its carrier and hurts itself before a trip. Which episode is similar?
questions.why: A pet that refuses its carrier and hurts itself matches Mij and the box, where he tore the lining and was hurt trying to escape.

questions.q: Mij was of a species previously unknown to
questions.why: Mij belonged to a species previously unknown to science, so it was later named after Maxwell.

questions.q: Which sequence is correct?
options: Jonnie dies → Iraq → Mij arrives → box → flight → London guesses
questions.why: The sequence is: Jonnie dies, Maxwell goes to Iraq, Mij arrives, the box, the flight and the London guesses. Other orders mix the events.

questions.q: Where did Mij sleep after he accepted Maxwell?
questions.why: After accepting Maxwell, Mij slept in Maxwell's bed, showing trust.

courses.title: First Flight · Madam Rides the Bus (Vallikkannan)
courses.summary: Eight-year-old Valli's carefully planned bus ride to town, her independent spirit, the joking conductor, and her first encounter with death when she sees a cow killed on the road.
outcomes: Learners can narrate Valli's planning and journey
Learners can describe Valli's character and her interactions
Learners can explain the turning point and the theme of death
Learners can write exam-ready answers
courses.note: chapter numbering may differ by edition

scenes.text: Valli watches buses pass her house every day. She secretly saves every coin she gets.
She asks quiet questions and learns: town is six miles away; the fare is thirty paise each way.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Valliammai (Valli)**, an **eight-year-old** girl, watched the street from her front doorway; the most fascinating thing was the **bus** that travelled between her village and the nearest town.
- She **secretly gathered information**: the town was **six miles** away, the fare was **thirty paise one way**, and the trip took **forty-five minutes**; the bus left at 1 p.m. and she could be back by 2:45 p.m. – during her mother's afternoon nap.
- She **saved sixty paise** by resisting temptations – peppermints, toys, balloons, merry-go-round rides.

steps.title: Solved example: How did Valli plan her journey? (40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Information:** Listened to conversations and asked questions – distance, fare, time.

**Step 2 – Money:** Saved sixty paise by resisting sweets and rides.

**Step 3 – Timing:** Chose the afternoon when her mother napped.

steps.title: Solved example: What sacrifices did Valli make? (30 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Temptations:** She did not buy peppermints, toys or balloons.

**Step 2 – Rides:** She skipped the merry-go-round – showing determination.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the fare was 60 paise one way – it was **30 paise each way** (60 total).
- Saying her mother knew – she went **secretly**.

activity.text: The town was ___ miles away. The fare was ___ paise one way. The trip took ___ minutes.

quiz.why: Valli was eight years old, a small child who dared to ride the bus alone.
Valli saved 60 paise, enough for the fare to town and back.
The town was six miles away from Valli's village.

quiz.q: When did she plan to go?
quiz.why: Valli planned to go during her mother's afternoon nap, so her mother would not know.
Valli's careful planning shows she was determined and resourceful. She was not fearful, lazy or careless.

scenes.text: The conductor teases: "Hurry up, madam!" Valli replies she can climb on her own.
She refuses to sit with the "elders" and insists on a window seat.

steps.title: On the bus
steps.body:
- The bus was **new**, painted white with green stripes, with cushioned seats. Valli climbed in confidently; the **conductor** jokingly called her **“madam”**.
- She refused help, stood on the seat to look out, and was annoyed when an **elderly woman** asked her about going alone; Valli replied curtly.
- The view: a canal, palm trees, grassland, distant mountains, blue sky; she laughed with glee when a **young cow** ran in front of the bus, tail high, and the driver had to honk.
- In town she stayed in the bus (the conductor offered a drink; she **refused**, saying she had no money and would not accept his treat).
- She took the same bus back, paying another thirty paise.

steps.title: Solved example: How did Valli show independence on the bus? (40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Climbing:** She refused help to get in.

**Step 2 – Seat:** Insisted on a window seat, standing to look out.

**Step 3 – Refusal:** Declined the conductor's free drink – she paid her own way.

steps.title: Solved example: How did Valli treat the elderly woman? (30 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Attitude:** She found her questions intrusive.

**Step 2 – Reply:** She answered sharply that she could look after herself – showing pride.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Valli got off and explored the town – she **stayed in the bus**.
- Calling the conductor rude – he was **friendly and joking**.

statements.s: The conductor called Valli "madam" as a joke.
Valli accepted a free drink.
Valli explored the town market.
A young cow ran in front of the bus on the way.

quiz.why: The conductor called Valli 'madam', which amused her and made her feel important.

options: she did not want a favour she couldn't pay for
quiz.why: Valli refused the drink because she did not want a favour she could not pay for. It was her self-respect.

quiz.q: What made Valli laugh on the way?
options: A young cow running ahead of the bus
quiz.why: A young cow running ahead of the bus made Valli laugh on the way.
Valli preferred the window seat, to watch the scenery.
The bus was new and white with green stripes, as the story describes.

lessons.title: The return and the turning point

scenes.text: On the way back, Valli sees the same young cow lying dead by the roadside.
Her excitement fades; she no longer looks out of the window.

steps.title: Death and growing up
steps.body:
- On the return trip, Valli saw the **young cow** that had run before the bus earlier now **lying dead** by the roadside, hit by a vehicle.
- She was deeply shaken; the beauty outside lost its charm. She **stayed in her seat** and did not look out.
- Back home, her aunt and mother talked about death; Valli understood more than they knew.
- **Theme:** a child's **first encounter with death** – the transience of life; joy and sorrow sit side by side; growing up.

steps.title: Solved example: What was the turning point in Valli's journey? (40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Event:** She saw the dead cow on the return journey.

**Step 2 – Effect:** Her joy turned into sadness; she stopped looking out.

**Step 3 – Meaning:** Her first, sobering realisation of death.

courses.title: First Flight · The Sermon at Benares

outcomes: Learners can narrate how Siddhartha became the Buddha

scenes.text: A young prince, protected from all suffering, rides out and sees a sick man, an old man, a funeral and a monk.
He leaves the palace to seek the truth – and attains enlightenment under a tree.

steps.title: Siddhartha's journey
steps.body:
- **Gautama Buddha** (563 BC – 483 BC, as given in the text) was born a prince, **Siddhartha Gautama**, in northern India. He was shielded from suffering and married a princess; they had a son.
- When he went out hunting/riding, he saw **a sick man, an aged man, a funeral procession and a monk begging for alms**. These sights moved him so much that he went out into the world to seek **enlightenment** about the sorrows he had witnessed.
- He wandered for **seven years**, then sat under a **peepal tree**, vowing to stay until enlightened. After seven days he was enlightened; he renamed the tree the **Bodhi Tree** (Tree of Wisdom) and became the **Buddha** (the Awakened or Enlightened).
- He preached his **first sermon** at **Benares** (Varanasi), most holy of the dipping places on the Ganges.

steps.title: Solved example: What sights changed Siddhartha? (30 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Sights:** A sick man, an old man, a funeral and a monk begging.

**Step 2 – Effect:** He realised suffering is universal and left to seek enlightenment.

steps.body:

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Saying he gave the first sermon at Bodh Gaya – he was **enlightened** at Gaya; the **sermon** was at **Benares**.

lessons.title: Kisa Gotami and the mustard seed

scenes.text: Kisa Gotami's only son dies. In grief she carries the body from house to house asking for medicine.
The Buddha asks her for a handful of mustard seed – from a house where no one has died.

steps.title: The story
steps.body:
- **Kisa Gotami** had an **only son**, who died. In her grief she carried the dead child to all her neighbours, asking for medicine; people thought she was out of her senses.
- A man directed her to the **Buddha**. He asked her to bring a **handful of mustard seed** from a house where **no one had lost a child, husband, parent or friend**.
- She went from house to house. People were willing to give mustard seed, but every house had lost someone: “The living are few, but the dead are many.”
- Weary and hopeless, she sat by the wayside, watching city lights flicker and be extinguished. She realised that **human life is like those lights** – death is common to all; she had been **selfish in her grief**.
- She buried her son and went to the Buddha, who gave her the sermon.

steps.title: Solved example: Why did the Buddha ask for mustard seed? (40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Method:** Not as medicine but as a lesson.

**Step 2 – Discovery:** She would find that every family had faced death.

**Step 3 – Outcome:** She realised death is universal and her grief was selfish.

steps.body:

**Step 2 – Lesson:** Lives too are lit and then go out – death is the fate of all.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the Buddha gave her medicine – he gave her a **task** to teach a lesson.
- Saying she found a house with no death – she found **none**.

lessons.title: The sermon: grief, death and peace

scenes.text: Ripe fruits fall early; clay pots break. So too do mortals.
The Buddha says grief only brings more pain; the wise do not grieve.

steps.title: Message of the sermon
steps.body:
- **Life is brief and combined with pain.** There are no means by which those born can avoid dying.
- **Similes:** as **ripe fruits** are in danger of falling early, mortals are always in danger of death; as **earthen vessels** made by the potter end in being broken, so is the life of mortals.
- Young and old, foolish and wise – all fall into the power of death.
- Neither father can save son nor kinsmen their relations; mortals are carried off one by one like an **ox led to the slaughter**.
- The wise do not grieve, knowing the terms of the world. **Weeping and grieving** do not bring peace of mind; they bring greater pain and make the body suffer. The dead are not saved by lamentation.
- One who has drawn out the arrow of lamentation, complaint and grief will obtain **peace of mind**; he who has overcome sorrow will be free from sorrow and blessed.

steps.title: Solved example: What does the Buddha mean by “the wise do not grieve”? (40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Understanding:** The wise know death is inevitable and universal.

**Step 2 – Effect:** Grief only increases pain and harms the body.

**Step 3 – Path:** Accepting this brings peace of mind.

steps.body:

**Step 2 – Clay pots:** All earthen vessels break – all lives end.

**Step 3 – Ox to slaughter:** Death takes people one by one, helplessly.

courses.title: First Flight · The Proposal (Anton Chekhov)
courses.summary: A one-act farce in which a nervous neighbour comes to propose marriage but ends up quarrelling about land and dogs – a satire on the upper classes and marriage for property.
outcomes: Learners can summarise the play scene by scene
Learners can analyse Lomov, Natalya and Chubukov
Learners can explain farce, satire and humour devices
Learners can write exam-ready answers
courses.note: chapter numbering may differ by edition

scenes.text: Lomov arrives in a tailcoat, very nervous, to ask for Natalya's hand.
Within minutes, they are shouting about who owns the Oxen Meadows.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Setting:** Chubukov's country-house in Russia (19th century). One-act play by **Anton Chekhov**; a **farce**.
- **Ivan Vassilevitch Lomov**, a neighbour (35, healthy but hypochondriac), arrives in evening dress. **Stepan Stepanovitch Chubukov**, a landowner, suspects he has come to borrow money, but Lomov asks for his daughter **Natalya Stepanovna**'s hand. Chubukov is delighted and calls her.
- Before Lomov can propose, he mentions his **Oxen Meadows**; Natalya insists they belong to **her family**. A heated quarrel follows; Chubukov joins, insults fly (Lomov has palpitations, his foot “has gone to sleep”). Lomov leaves.
- When Natalya learns he came to **propose**, she becomes hysterical and demands he be brought back.
- Lomov returns; they soon quarrel again – this time about whose dog is better: Lomov's **Guess** or Natalya's **Squeezer**.
- Lomov collapses; they think he is dead. When he revives, Chubukov forcibly makes them kiss and accept the marriage – and they immediately start quarrelling again, while Chubukov calls for champagne.

steps.title: Solved example: Why did Lomov visit Chubukov? (30 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Purpose:** To propose marriage to Natalya.

**Step 2 – Reasons:** He was 35, wanted a quiet, regular life, and Natalya was a good housekeeper, not bad-looking and educated.

steps.title: Solved example: What were the two quarrels about? (30 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – First:** Ownership of the Oxen Meadows.

**Step 2 – Second:** Whose dog was better – Guess or Squeezer.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the meadows were called “Cow Meadows” – they are the **Oxen Meadows**.
- Mixing the dogs: **Guess** is Lomov's, **Squeezer** is Natalya's.

steps.title: Character sketches
steps.body:
- **Lomov:** 35, wealthy landowner, **nervous, hypochondriac** (palpitations, numb foot, twitching eyebrow), quick-tempered and argumentative; wants marriage for a settled life, not love.
- **Natalya:** 25, **sharp, quarrelsome**, proud of her family property; practical – she wants the marriage too (becomes hysterical when she learns of the proposal).
- **Chubukov:** landowner, **cunning, opportunistic and hot-tempered**; pleased to marry off his daughter to a wealthy neighbour; insults Lomov in quarrels but then forces the engagement.

**Common trait:** all three are materialistic and argumentative – marriage is a matter of **property and convenience**.

steps.title: Solved example: Character sketch of Lomov (60 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Health:** Hypochondriac – palpitations, numbness.

**Step 2 – Temper:** Nervous yet quarrelsome; insists on his rights.

**Step 3 – Motive:** Wants a wife for a quiet, regular life – practical, not romantic.

scenes.text: Two adults scream about who owns a small meadow and whose dog runs faster.
Exaggeration makes the trivial seem huge – that is farce.

steps.title: Devices
steps.body:
- **Farce:** comedy with exaggerated, improbable situations and quick action.
- **Satire:** Chekhov mocks the upper classes' **greed for property** and the idea of **marriage as a business deal**.
- **Irony:** a man who comes to propose ends up insulting the bride; the quarrels continue even after engagement.
- **Humour devices:** physical comedy (Lomov's fits), name-calling, sudden changes of mood (Natalya), absurd arguments over trivial matters.

questions.why: Chekhov satirises upper-class greed and marriage for property. It is not about priests, farmers or children.

questions.q: Chubukov's nature
questions.why: Chubukov is opportunistic and hot-tempered, welcoming the proposal for gain and quickly quarrelling.

questions.q: Which shows irony?
options: A man who comes to propose ends up insulting the bride
questions.why: It is ironic that a man comes to propose and ends up insulting the bride. Dogs barking or a coat are not ironic.

questions.q: Case: Two neighbours argue for an hour about a fence worth almost nothing. Which play does this resemble?
questions.why: Two neighbours arguing for an hour about a trivial thing resemble The Proposal, where land and dogs cause quarrels.

questions.q: Lomov wants to marry because
options: he wants a quiet, regular life at 35
questions.why: Lomov wants to marry because he wants a quiet, regular life at 35. He is not forced and does not need money.

questions.q: Which sequence is correct?
options: Proposal request → Meadows quarrel → recall → dogs quarrel → forced kiss
questions.why: The correct order is: proposal request, Meadows quarrel, Natalya's recall, dogs quarrel, then forced kiss. Other orders mix the events.

questions.q: Why is the ending comic?
options: They are engaged yet keep quarrelling while champagne is called for
questions.why: The ending is comic because they are engaged yet keep quarrelling, while champagne is called for.

questions.q: Natalya's full name
questions.why: Natalya's full name is Natalya Stepanovna, as she is the daughter of Stepan Stepanovitch Chubukov.

courses.title: First Flight · Poems I (Dust of Snow, Fire and Ice, A Tiger in the Zoo, How to Tell Wild Animals, The Ball Poem)
courses.summary: Five poems explained line-by-line in your own words: Robert Frost's two short poems, Leslie Norris on a caged tiger, Carolyn Wells's comic guide to wild animals, and John Berryman on a boy's first lesson in loss.
outcomes: Learners can explain the central idea of each poem
Learners can identify poetic devices (symbol, rhyme scheme, alliteration, contrast, humour)
Learners can answer extract-based and short-answer questions
Learners can compare themes across poems
courses.note: chapter numbering may differ by edition

scenes.text: Meena had a bad morning – nothing went right.
Then a bird shook water drops on her from a tree, she laughed, and the day felt better.

steps.title: What the poem says
steps.body:
- The poet was in a **sad, regretful mood**. A **crow** sitting on a **hemlock tree** shook down the **dust of snow** on him.
- This small, unexpected act of nature **changed his mood**; he felt refreshed, and the part of the day he had **rued** (regretted) was saved.
- **Message:** small moments in nature can heal sadness and change our outlook.

steps.title: Poetic devices and tone
steps.body:
- **Symbols:** the **crow** and **hemlock** (a poisonous tree) are usually symbols of gloom/ill omen; yet they bring joy – a contrast that shows good can come from unexpected sources. **Snow** = freshness, purity, joy.
- **Rhyme scheme:** abab cdcd. Two stanzas, one long sentence.
- **Tone:** reflective, uplifting.

steps.title: Solved example: How did the dust of snow change the poet's mood? (30 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Before:** He was sad and regretful.

**Step 2 – Event:** A crow shook snow on him from a hemlock tree.

**Step 3 – After:** He felt refreshed; the rest of the day was saved from regret.

steps.title: Solved example: Why does Frost choose a crow and hemlock? (30 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Usual meaning:** Both suggest gloom or death.

**Step 2 – Twist:** Here they cause happiness – showing joy can come from unlikely sources.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the poet saved a whole day – he saved **some part** of a day he had rued.
- Calling hemlock a flowering, happy tree – it is **poisonous**.

items.back: Usually ill omen – here brings joy
Poisonous tree – here part of a happy moment

quiz.q: The bird in the poem is a
quiz.why: The bird in 'Dust of Snow' is a crow, which shakes snow dust from a hemlock tree.
The tree is a hemlock, a tree in the poem. It is not a pine, oak or maple.
'Rued' means regretted. The poet had regretted part of his day before the crow changed his mood.
The poem's rhyme scheme is abab, with alternate lines rhyming.
The message is that small moments can change mood. The snow dust lifted the poet's gloom.

scenes.text: Some scientists say the world may end in fire; others say in ice.
Frost links these to human desire and hatred.

steps.title: What the poem says
steps.body:
- Some say the world will end in **fire**, some in **ice**.
- From his experience of **desire**, the poet sides with fire.
- But if the world had to perish twice, he knows enough of **hatred** to say that ice is also **great** and would **suffice**.
- **Fire = desire/greed/passion; Ice = hatred/indifference/coldness**. Both can destroy the world.

steps.title: Poetic devices and tone
steps.body:
- **Symbolism:** fire and ice. **Contrast/antithesis** between two opposite forces.
- **Rhyme scheme:** aba abc bcb. Short, conversational, ironic tone.
- **Theme:** human emotions – unchecked desire and hatred – are destructive.

steps.title: Solved example: What do fire and ice stand for? (30 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Fire:** Desire, greed, lust, passion – they spread rapidly.

**Step 2 – Ice:** Hatred, coldness, indifference – they harden hearts.

**Step 3 – Point:** Both can destroy the world.

steps.title: Solved example: Why does the poet say ice would “suffice”? (30 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Experience:** He has seen enough hatred.

**Step 2 – Meaning:** Hatred is powerful enough to destroy the world too.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking the poem literally only as science – it is about **human emotions**.
- Saying the poet prefers ice first – he first holds with **fire**.

pairs: If the world were destroyed two times

quiz.why: In 'Fire and Ice', fire stands for desire, which can destroy the world with passion.
Ice stands for hatred, which is cold and destructive.
The poet first says he holds with fire, meaning desire, as the world might end that way.
'Suffice' means be enough. Ice would be great and would suffice to destroy the world.
The main device in 'Fire and Ice' is symbolism, with fire and ice standing for desire and hatred.

lessons.title: A Tiger in the Zoo (Leslie Norris)

scenes.text: At the zoo, Aarav watches a tiger walk up and down along the bars.
He imagines the tiger free in a jungle near a water hole.

steps.title: What the poem says
steps.body:
- The tiger **stalks** the few steps of his **cage**, quiet with rage; his stripes are like velvet.
- **What he should be doing:** lurking in the **long grass** near the **water hole**, hunting plump deer; snarling around houses at the jungle's edge, terrifying the village.
- **Reality:** locked in a **concrete cell**, he ignores visitors; at night he hears patrolling cars and stares at the **brilliant stars** with his brilliant eyes.
- **Message:** wild animals belong in their natural habitat; captivity takes away their freedom and dignity.

steps.title: Poetic devices and tone
steps.body:
- **Contrast** between cage and jungle (stanzas alternate).
- **Alliteration:** “quiet rage”… “pads/padding”, “velvet quiet”; **imagery** of claws, fangs, eyes.
- **Personification** of the tiger's feelings (rage, ignoring visitors).
- **Rhyme scheme:** abcb in most stanzas.

steps.title: Solved example: Contrast the tiger in the cage with the tiger in the wild (40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Cage:** Paces a few steps, quiet with rage, ignores visitors, stares at stars.

**Step 2 – Wild:** Lurks in grass near water hole, hunts deer, terrifies villagers.

**Step 3 – Point:** Captivity robs him of freedom and power.

steps.title: Solved example: Why does the tiger ignore the visitors? (30 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Feeling:** He is angry and helpless.

**Step 2 – Meaning:** He feels no connection with those who enjoy his captivity.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the tiger is happy in the zoo – he is **angry and helpless**.
- Missing the **stanza-wise contrast**.

quiz.q: The tiger is “quiet with rage” because
quiz.why: The tiger is 'quiet with rage' because he is caged, imprisoned and angry. He is not ill or sleepy.

quiz.q: In the wild he would hunt
quiz.why: In the wild he would hunt plump deer. In the zoo he is confined.
At night he stares at the brilliant stars, longing for freedom.
The poem contrasts cage and jungle: the tiger's life in the zoo and his life in the wild.
'A Tiger in the Zoo' was written by Leslie Norris. Robert Frost wrote 'Dust of Snow' and 'Fire and Ice'.

lessons.title: How to Tell Wild Animals (Carolyn Wells)

scenes.text: Kabir reads a comic poem that "teaches" how to identify animals – by what they do to you!
If it hugs you hard, it's a bear…

steps.title: What the poem says
steps.body:
- A humorous guide to identifying animals:
- **Asian Lion:** large, tawny, roars at you as you die.
- **Bengal Tiger:** noble wild beast with black stripes on yellow, who greets you.
- **Leopard:** spots; it is useless to roar or cry when it springs on you.
- **Bear:** hugs you very hard.
- **Hyena:** comes laughing/smiling.
- **Crocodile:** weeps while eating its prey.
- **Chameleon:** has no ears or wings, sits on a tree and changes colour – you can hardly see it.
- **Message:** humour about the dangers of wild animals; the joke is that you learn their identity only when it is too late.

steps.title: Poetic devices and tone
steps.body:
- **Humour and irony**; **deliberate misspelling** for rhyme (“lept” for “leapt” to rhyme with “leopard”; “dyin’” to rhyme with “lion”) – **poetic licence**.
- **Alliteration** (“noble wild beast”, “black stripes”).
- **Idiom:** “crocodile tears” = false tears.
- **Rhyme scheme:** varies; playful.

steps.title: Solved example: How can you identify the bear and the hyena? (30 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Bear:** It hugs you very hard.

**Step 2 – Hyena:** It comes smiling/laughing at you.

steps.title: Solved example: What is the humour in the poem? (40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Method:** Identification happens only when the animal attacks.

**Step 2 – Irony:** The reader learns the animal's name at the cost of life.

**Step 3 – Device:** Funny rhymes and poetic licence.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking the poem as a serious science guide.
- Saying the chameleon has big ears – it has **no ears and no wings**.

activity.prompt: Match the animal to how you can tell it
pairs: Roars at you as you die
Black stripes on yellow, greets you
Spots; useless to cry when it springs
No ears or wings; changes colour

quiz.why: The crocodile weeps while eating, which gives the idiom 'crocodile tears' (false tears).
The chameleon is described as having no ears or wings, and it changes colour.
The tone of 'How to Tell Wild Animals' is humorous, not tragic or angry.
Misspelling a word to make a rhyme is poetic licence, a freedom allowed to poets.
'How to Tell Wild Animals' was written by Carolyn Wells.

scenes.text: A boy's ball bounces down the street and into the water.
He stands staring, trembling – it was more than a ball.

steps.title: What the poem says
steps.body:
- A boy loses his **ball**; it bounces down the street and into the **water** (harbour). He stands rigid, trembling, staring at where it went.
- The poet does not intrude; he does **not offer money** for another ball – it would be worthless, because the boy must learn the **epistemology of loss** – the knowledge of how to bear loss.
- Money is external; the boy must learn that **some things, once lost, cannot be bought back**. He is learning the first lesson of growing up: **responsibility** and how to stand up after loss.

steps.title: Poetic devices and tone
steps.body:
- **Symbol:** the **ball** = childhood/possessions/memories; **water** = the world of loss.
- **Free verse**, reflective tone.
- Key phrase: **epistemology of loss** – understanding the nature of loss.

steps.title: Solved example: Why doesn't the poet buy the boy another ball? (30 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Reason:** Another ball cannot replace the memories and attachment.

**Step 2 – Lesson:** The boy must learn to accept loss – the epistemology of loss.

steps.title: Solved example: What is the “epistemology of loss”? (30 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Meaning:** Knowing what it means to lose something and learning to live with it.

**Step 2 – Growth:** It is part of growing up and taking responsibility.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the poem is about a cheap ball – it is about **loss and growing up**.
- Saying the poet consoles the boy with money – he **does not**.

statements.s: The poet offers the boy money for a new ball.
The ball symbolises childhood and memories.
Epistemology of loss means learning to bear loss.
The poem is written in strict rhyme.

quiz.why: In 'The Ball Poem', the boy's ball went into the water (the harbour) and was lost.
The boy learns the 'epistemology of loss', that is, what it means to lose something you love.

options: The loss cannot be replaced by buying
quiz.why: Money is worthless here because the loss cannot be replaced by buying a new ball. The boy must learn to bear it.
The ball symbolises childhood and possessions, and its loss is a lesson in loss and growing up.
'The Ball Poem' was written by John Berryman.

questions.q: Which poem is by Robert Frost?
questions.why: 'Dust of Snow' is by Robert Frost. 'The Ball Poem', 'Amanda!' and 'Fog' are by other poets.

questions.q: In “Fire and Ice”, ice stands for
questions.why: In 'Fire and Ice', ice stands for hatred, and fire stands for desire.

questions.q: Which animal hugs you very hard?
questions.why: The bear hugs you very hard, as 'How to Tell Wild Animals' describes.

questions.q: The tiger in the zoo stares at
questions.why: The caged tiger stares at the brilliant stars at night, thinking of freedom.

questions.q: Hemlock is a
questions.why: Hemlock is a poisonous plant, so the tree adds a sad mood in the poem.

questions.q: “Crocodile tears” means
questions.why: 'Crocodile tears' means false tears, shown for show rather than real grief.

questions.q: Assertion: The poet does not buy the boy a new ball. Reason: He wants the boy to learn to bear loss.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true: the poet does not buy the boy a new ball because he wants him to learn to bear loss. So the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Assertion: The caged tiger is content. Reason: He ignores the visitors.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: The assertion is false: the caged tiger is angry, not content. The reason is true, because he ignores the visitors.

questions.q: The rhyme scheme of “Dust of Snow” is
questions.why: The rhyme scheme of 'Dust of Snow' is abab cdcd, so alternate lines rhyme.

questions.q: Which device is central to “Fire and Ice”?
questions.why: Symbolism is central to 'Fire and Ice', as fire and ice stand for desire and hatred.

questions.q: Extract: “…has saved some part of a day I had rued.” What changed?
questions.why: 'Has saved some part of a day I had rued' shows the poet's mood changed because of the crow and the snow.

questions.q: Which poem uses poetic licence in spelling for rhyme?
questions.why: 'How to Tell Wild Animals' uses poetic licence in spelling for rhyme, such as misspelt words.

questions.q: Which two poems share the theme of loss/negative emotions shaping life?
options: Fire and Ice and The Ball Poem
Dust of Snow and How to Tell Wild Animals
A Tiger in the Zoo and Fire and Ice
questions.why: 'Fire and Ice' and 'The Ball Poem' share the theme of emotions and loss shaping life.

questions.q: In “A Tiger in the Zoo” the stanzas mainly
questions.why: In 'A Tiger in the Zoo', the stanzas alternate between the cage and the wild, to contrast the tiger's present and what he longs for.

questions.q: Which statement best describes “Dust of Snow”?
options: A small natural event lifts a gloomy mood
questions.why: 'Dust of Snow' is about a small natural event lifting a gloomy mood. It is not about a snowstorm or winter sports.

questions.q: How can you tell a chameleon?
options: No ears, no wings, changes colour
questions.why: A chameleon has no ears or wings and changes colour, as the poem says.

courses.title: First Flight · Poems II (Amanda!, The Trees, Fog, The Tale of Custard the Dragon, For Anne Gregory)
courses.summary: Five poems explained in your own words: Robin Klein's nagged child, Adrienne Rich's trees moving out of the house, Carl Sandburg's cat-like fog, Ogden Nash's comic “cowardly” dragon, and W.B. Yeats on outer beauty and true love.
outcomes: Learners can explain the central idea of each poem
Learners can identify metaphor, symbolism, imagery, humour and dialogue form
Learners can answer extract-based and short-answer questions
Learners can compare themes such as freedom, appearance and courage
courses.note: chapter numbering may differ by edition

scenes.text: "Sit straight! Finish your homework! Don't eat chocolates!" – Riya hears this all day.
She imagines being a mermaid, free in the sea.

steps.title: What the poem says
steps.body:
- Amanda is a young girl constantly **nagged** by an adult (probably her mother): don't bite nails, don't hunch shoulders, sit straight, finish homework, tidy your room, clean shoes, don't eat chocolate (acne), don't go out in the sun, stop sulking.
- Amanda escapes into **fantasies**: she imagines being a **mermaid** drifting in a languid emerald sea; an **orphan** roaming the streets, free, making patterns with bare feet in the dust; **Rapunzel** in a tower who would never let down her hair.
- **Message:** excessive nagging hurts a child's freedom; children need space and understanding.

steps.title: Poetic devices and tone
steps.body:
- **Dramatic monologue** with alternating stanzas: instructions vs Amanda's imagination (shown in **brackets/italics**).
- **Imagery:** emerald sea, silence golden, freedom sweet.
- **Allusion:** Rapunzel (fairy tale).
- **Tone:** of the speaker – irritated; of Amanda – dreamy, resentful.

steps.title: Solved example: Why does Amanda want to be an orphan? (30 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Reason:** No one would nag her.

**Step 2 – Image:** She could roam freely and make patterns in the dust.

steps.title: Solved example: What does the poem suggest about parenting? (40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Problem:** Constant correction suffocates the child.

**Step 2 – Reaction:** Amanda withdraws into fantasy and sulks.

**Step 3 – Lesson:** Guidance should be balanced with freedom and kindness.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking Amanda really is a mermaid – these are **imaginary escapes**.
- Missing the alternating structure (instructions vs fantasy).

quiz.why: Amanda imagines being a mermaid, drifting in the sea, to escape the scolding.
Amanda is told not to eat chocolate because it gives acne, in the mother's scolding.
Rapunzel is a fairy-tale character who lived in a tall tower. Amanda alludes to her to imagine freedom.

options: nagging and a child's need for freedom
quiz.why: The poem is about constant nagging and a child's need for freedom.
'Amanda!' was written by Robin Klein.

scenes.text: Potted plants on a balcony lean towards the open sky.
In this poem, trees inside a house move out to the empty forest.

steps.title: What the poem says
steps.body:
- The trees inside the house are **moving out into the forest**, which has been empty all these days – no bird sits there, no insect hides, the sun buries its feet in shadow.
- All night the roots work to disengage from the floor cracks; leaves strain towards the glass; small twigs stiff with exertion; long-cramped boughs shuffle under the roof.
- The poet sits writing long letters, barely mentioning the departure; the moon is broken like a mirror; by morning, the forest is full of trees again.
- **Interpretation:** a literal reading (nature reclaiming space) and a **symbolic** one – **women breaking free** from domestic confinement (Rich was a feminist poet).

steps.title: Poetic devices and tone
steps.body:
- **Personification:** trees move, strain, shuffle.
- **Imagery:** the moon broken like a mirror; sun burying its feet.
- **Symbolism:** trees = suppressed women/nature; house = confinement; forest = freedom.
- **Free verse.**

steps.title: Solved example: Why is the forest empty? (30 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Reason:** All the trees are inside houses.

**Step 2 – Effect:** No bird can sit, no insect hide, no sun can bury its feet in shadow.

steps.title: Solved example: What could the trees symbolise? (30 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Symbol:** Women confined to homes.

**Step 2 – Movement:** Moving out = seeking freedom and identity.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Reading the poem only literally – mention the **symbolic** meaning too.

statements.s: The forest is full at the start.
Trees move out at night.
The moon is described as broken like a mirror.
The poem is in strict rhyme.

quiz.why: In 'The Trees', the trees are moving out into the forest, away from the house.
The poet sits writing letters in the house, while the trees move away.
The house symbolises confinement, while the trees and forest symbolise freedom.
The main device is personification, since the trees are shown as moving like people.
'The Trees' was written by Adrienne Rich.

scenes.text: Early morning, fog creeps over Mumbai harbour silently.
Like a cat, it sits for a while, then moves on.

steps.title: What the poem says
steps.body:
- The **fog comes on little cat feet** – silently.
- It **sits looking** over the harbour and city on **silent haunches**, then **moves on**.
- **Central idea:** the poet compares the fog to a **cat** – silent arrival, watchful sitting, quiet departure.

steps.title: Poetic devices and tone
steps.body:
- **Extended metaphor:** fog = cat (no “like/as”).
- **Free verse**, very short (six lines); vivid **imagery**.
- “Haunches” = hindquarters on which a cat sits.

steps.title: Solved example: How is fog like a cat? (30 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Arrival:** Silent, on little feet.

**Step 2 – Behaviour:** Sits watching on silent haunches.

**Step 3 – Departure:** Moves on quietly.

steps.title: Solved example: Identify the main figure of speech (20 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Device:** Metaphor (extended).

**Step 2 – Why:** Fog is described directly as having cat feet and haunches.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Calling it a simile – there is **no “like/as”**; it is a **metaphor**.

activity.prompt: Match the cat image to the fog

quiz.why: In 'Fog', fog is compared to a cat that comes on little cat feet.
The comparison without 'like' or 'as' is a metaphor: fog comes on little cat feet.
The fog looks over the harbour and city, as a cat looks over its surroundings.

options: hind legs/hips on which an animal sits
quiz.why: Haunches are the hind legs or hips on which an animal sits, as the fog-cat sits.
'Fog' was written by Carl Sandburg.

lessons.title: The Tale of Custard the Dragon (Ogden Nash)

scenes.text: Everyone teases Custard the dragon for being a coward.
When a pirate attacks, only Custard fights.

steps.title: What the poem says
steps.body:
- **Belinda** lived in a little white house with a black kitten **Ink**, a grey mouse **Blink**, a yellow dog **Mustard**, and a little pet dragon **Custard**.
- Custard had big sharp teeth, spikes on top, a mouth like a fireplace, a chimney for a nose, daggers for toes – yet he was a **coward** who cried for a nice safe cage. Others boasted of bravery and teased him.
- A **pirate** with pistols entered. Everyone fled/hid – Belinda cried for help, Ink and Blink ran, Mustard fled. **Custard** jumped, snorted, and **ate the pirate**.
- Afterwards, the others again boasted they would have been braver, and Custard was still called cowardly; he still cried for a nice safe cage.
- **Message:** true courage shows in action, not boasting; appearances deceive.

steps.title: Poetic devices and tone
steps.body:
- **Ballad** form with **rhyming couplets (aabb)**; humour and **irony**.
- **Alliteration:** “little black kitten”, “mouth like a fireplace”.
- **Similes/metaphors:** mouth like a fireplace, chimney for a nose, daggers for toes.
- **Repetition** of the refrain-like line about the realio, trulio little pet dragon.

steps.title: Solved example: What is ironic about Custard? (40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Appearance:** Fearsome – teeth, spikes, fiery mouth.

**Step 2 – Reputation:** Called a coward who wants a safe cage.

**Step 3 – Action:** Only he fights the pirate – the “brave” ones run.

steps.title: Solved example: Describe how each character reacted to the pirate (40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Belinda:** Cried for help.

**Step 2 – Ink, Blink, Mustard:** Ran/hid in fear.

**Step 3 – Custard:** Leapt and gobbled the pirate.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Mixing names: **Ink** = kitten, **Blink** = mouse, **Mustard** = dog, **Custard** = dragon.

quiz.why: Custard, the dragon, ate the pirate. The others ran away.
Custard cried for a nice safe cage, because he was the cowardly dragon.
The rhyme scheme is aabb, in rhyming couplets.
'The Tale of Custard the Dragon' is a ballad, a narrative poem.
The poem was written by Ogden Nash, known for humorous verse.

scenes.text: A young woman wonders if people like her only for her looks.
An old man says only God loves us for ourselves alone.

steps.title: What the poem says
steps.body:
- A **dialogue** between the poet-speaker and **Anne Gregory**, a young woman with beautiful **yellow hair** (“great honey-coloured ramparts at your ear”).
- The speaker says no young man will ever love her for herself alone, only for her **yellow hair**.
- Anne replies that she can **dye her hair** brown, black or carrot – so young men would love her for herself.
- He answers that he heard an **old religious man** say that **only God** could love her for herself alone and not her yellow hair.
- **Theme:** **outer beauty vs inner worth**; human love is often based on appearance; true unconditional love is divine.

steps.title: Poetic devices and tone
steps.body:
- **Dialogue form** in three stanzas; **rhyme scheme** abcbdefe (approximately).
- **Metaphor:** “honey-coloured ramparts” – hair like protective walls; “yellow hair” = outer beauty.
- Tone: gentle, philosophical.

steps.title: Solved example: Why does Anne want to dye her hair? (30 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Wish:** She wants to be loved for her inner self, not looks.

**Step 2 – Plan:** Changing hair colour would test that.

steps.title: Solved example: What does the old man's statement mean? (30 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Statement:** Only God can love a person for herself alone.

**Step 2 – Meaning:** Human love is influenced by appearance; divine love is unconditional.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Saying Anne's hair was black – it was **yellow/honey-coloured**.

statements.s: Anne had yellow hair.
The speaker says young men will love her for herself alone.
Anne plans to dye her hair.
The old man says only God loves us for ourselves.

quiz.q: The poem is in the form of a
quiz.why: 'For Anne Gregory' is in the form of a dialogue, between the speaker and Anne.
'Ramparts' are protective walls, used as a metaphor in the poem.
The theme is outer beauty versus inner worth, since hair colour should not decide love.

quiz.q: Who can love Anne for herself alone?
quiz.why: Only God can love Anne for herself alone, not for her yellow hair.
'For Anne Gregory' was written by W.B. Yeats.

questions.q: Amanda imagines being
questions.why: Amanda imagines being a mermaid, an orphan and Rapunzel, to escape being nagged.

questions.q: “Fog comes on little cat feet” is a
questions.why: 'Fog comes on little cat feet' is a metaphor, since fog is described as a cat without 'like' or 'as'.

questions.q: Custard is a
questions.why: Custard is a dragon, the cowardly dragon of Ogden Nash's poem.

questions.q: Anne Gregory's hair is
questions.why: Anne Gregory's hair is yellow, which the speaker says should not decide her worth.

questions.q: In “The Trees”, the forest is initially
questions.why: In 'The Trees', the forest is initially empty, and the trees return to it.

questions.q: Who fled when the pirate came?

questions.why: Appearances versus reality is common to both: Custard looks cowardly but acts bravely, and Anne is loved for her hair, not herself.

courses.title: Footprints · A Triumph of Surgery (James Herriot)
courses.summary: A vet's humorous account of Tricki, a pampered, overfed Pekinese, and how a little discipline – not surgery – cured him.
outcomes: Learners can narrate Tricki's illness and cure
Learners can analyse Mrs Pumphrey and Herriot
Learners can explain the irony of the title
Learners can write exam answers on pet care and pampering
courses.note: chapter numbering may differ by edition

scenes.text: Tricki, a rich lady's Pekinese, is so fat he waddles and gasps.
The vet decides the "treatment" is a stay at his surgery.

steps.title: Plot summary
steps.body:
- **Mrs Pumphrey**, a rich widow, loves her dog **Tricki** so much that she **overfeeds** him – cream cakes, chocolates, malt, cod-liver oil, Horlicks – and stops his walks. He becomes **grossly fat**, lethargic, refuses food, vomits and pants.
- The narrator, vet **James Herriot**, advises a strict diet and exercise, but Mrs Pumphrey cannot resist Tricki's pleading eyes.
- Herriot takes Tricki to his **surgery for two weeks** to “treat” him. He gives him **no food for two days, only water**; Tricki then joins the other dogs, races and plays, and regains health.
- Mrs Pumphrey sends **fresh eggs, wine and brandy** daily to “build up” Tricki – which Herriot and his colleagues enjoy.
- When Tricki returns healthy and bouncing, Mrs Pumphrey, overjoyed, calls it **“a triumph of surgery”**.

steps.title: Solved example: Why was Tricki taken to the surgery? (40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Condition:** Overfeeding and no exercise made him fat and ill.

**Step 2 – Problem:** Mrs Pumphrey could not follow the diet advice.

**Step 3 – Solution:** Herriot took him away to control his diet and exercise.

steps.title: Solved example: How was Tricki cured? (30 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Diet:** No food for two days, only water, then a controlled diet.

**Step 2 – Exercise:** Playing with other dogs.

**Step 3 – Point:** No medicine or operation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Tricki had an operation – there was **no surgery**; the title is ironic.
- Saying the eggs and wine were for Tricki's diet – Herriot and staff **consumed** them.

items: Mrs Pumphrey overfeeds Tricki
Tricki becomes ill and lethargic
Herriot takes him to the surgery
No food for two days, then play with other dogs
Mrs Pumphrey sends eggs, wine and brandy
Tricki returns healthy – “a triumph of surgery”

quiz.why: Tricki was a Pekinese, a small dog breed belonging to Mrs Pumphrey.
Tricki fell ill because of overfeeding and no exercise, not infection or old age.

quiz.q: How long was Tricki at the surgery?
quiz.why: Tricki stayed at the surgery for two weeks, until he recovered.
Mrs Pumphrey sent eggs, wine and brandy to the surgery for Tricki, which shows her foolish indulgence.
No, there was no operation. Tricki was cured by diet and exercise, so the title is ironic.

scenes.text: A grandmother keeps feeding her grandson sweets because she loves him.
Love without wisdom can harm – like Mrs Pumphrey's.

steps.title: Character sketches
steps.body:
- **Mrs Pumphrey:** wealthy, kind-hearted but **foolishly indulgent**; loves Tricki like a child; cannot say no; easily upset; generous with gifts.
- **Herriot:** **practical, wise and tactful** vet; understands that the dog needs discipline, not medicine; handles the owner gently; slightly guilty about enjoying the gifts.
- **Tricki:** pampered, lazy at first; becomes active and lively when given a normal dog's life.

steps.title: Solved example: Character sketch of Mrs Pumphrey (60 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Loving:** Treats Tricki like a child.

**Step 2 – Indulgent:** Overfeeds and cannot refuse him – causing illness.

**Step 3 – Generous/naive:** Sends lavish gifts and believes surgery cured him.

steps.title: Solved example: How does Herriot show wisdom? (40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Diagnosis:** Recognises overfeeding as the problem.

**Step 2 – Tact:** Takes the dog away instead of arguing.

**Step 3 – Method:** Uses diet and exercise.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Calling Mrs Pumphrey cruel – she is **loving but unwise**.

quiz.q: Mrs Pumphrey is best described as
quiz.why: Mrs Pumphrey is loving but foolishly indulgent, spoiling Tricki with food. She is not strict or cruel.
Herriot is practical and tactful, as he treats Tricki without hurting Mrs Pumphrey's feelings.
Tricki recovered because of discipline and exercise. No medicine or surgery was used.
Herriot felt slightly guilty about the gifts, as Tricki's ill-health was not caused by them but he did not use them.
At the surgery Tricki played with other dogs, which gave him exercise and company.

scenes.text: A school nutrition week talks about junk food and exercise.
Tricki's story is a funny lesson about both.

steps.title: Themes
steps.body:
- **Over-indulgence harms:** love must be balanced with discipline.
- **Health = diet + exercise**, not medicine alone.
- **Irony and humour:** “triumph of surgery” with no surgery.
- **Rich people's excess** contrasted with the sensible vet.

steps.title: Solved example: Why is the title ironic? (30 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Claim:** Mrs Pumphrey calls the cure a triumph of surgery.

**Step 2 – Fact:** Tricki was cured by diet and exercise – no surgery at all.

steps.title: Solved example: What lesson does the story teach parents? (40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Lesson:** Too much pampering spoils children.

**Step 2 – Balance:** Love should include healthy limits on food and screen time, and encourage play.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Missing the **irony** of the title.

statements.s: The title is ironic.
Love always means giving more food.
Exercise helped Tricki recover.
The story is tragic.

quiz.why: The title is ironic, because there was no surgery, yet Mrs Pumphrey thought the 'triumph of surgery' saved Tricki.
The main theme is the dangers of over-indulgence, as Tricki was made ill by too much food and no exercise.
The tone of the story is humorous, with gentle comedy about Mrs Pumphrey and her dog.
Health needs diet and exercise, as the story shows. Medicine alone or sweets would not help.
'A Triumph of Surgery' was written by James Herriot, a vet.

scenes.text: Arjun prepares a speech on "Pamper less, love more".
He uses Tricki as his example.

steps.title: How to score
steps.body:
- Long answers (120 words): introduce → 3 points with evidence → value/lesson → conclusion.
- Use characters' names correctly.
- For creative tasks (diary, letter, speech), keep the format and stay true to the story.

steps.title: Solved example: Long answer: “Pampering can harm.” Discuss with reference to Tricki (120 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Introduce:** Excessive love without discipline can be harmful.

**Step 2 – Evidence:** Mrs Pumphrey's cakes, chocolates and lack of walks made Tricki ill.

**Step 3 – Cure:** Herriot's diet and play restored him.

**Step 4 – Lesson:** Parents and pet owners must balance affection with healthy habits.

**Step 5 – Conclude:** Real care sometimes means saying no.

steps.title: Solved example: Herriot's diary entry on Tricki's return (100 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Format:** Date, first person.

**Step 2 – Content:** Tricki's transformation; Mrs Pumphrey's joy and the “triumph of surgery”.

**Step 3 – Feelings:** Amusement and slight guilt about the gifts.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Retelling the whole plot instead of answering the question.
- Ignoring the word limit.

activity.prompt: Is there a habit of yours that feels loving but is actually unhealthy?
activity.hint: E.g. late-night snacks, too much screen time – what would Herriot advise?

quiz.q: A diary entry by Herriot is in
quiz.why: A diary entry by Herriot is written in the first person, using 'I'.
'Pamper less, love more' fits Mrs Pumphrey's lesson, as she loved Tricki but spoiled him.
The cure took about two weeks, the time Tricki spent at the surgery.
The vet's method was diet and exercise, not surgery, pills or injections.
Mrs Pumphrey was overjoyed to see Tricki healthy again, and she praised Herriot.

questions.q: Tricki's owner
questions.why: Tricki's owner was Mrs Pumphrey, a rich widow who spoiled him.

questions.q: Tricki's problem
questions.why: Tricki's problem was overfeeding, which made him fat and ill.

questions.q: Who is the narrator?
questions.why: The narrator is James Herriot, the vet who treats Tricki.

questions.q: For the first two days Tricki got
questions.why: For the first two days Tricki got only water, to cut his overeating.

questions.q: What did Mrs Pumphrey send daily?
questions.why: Mrs Pumphrey sent eggs, wine and brandy daily, which shows her over-indulgence.

questions.q: Tricki regained health by
questions.why: Tricki regained health by playing with other dogs, which gave him exercise.

questions.q: Assertion: The title is ironic. Reason: Tricki was cured without any surgery.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true: the title is ironic, because Tricki was cured without any surgery. So the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Assertion: Mrs Pumphrey followed the diet advice. Reason: She was strict.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are false: Mrs Pumphrey did not follow the diet advice, and she was not strict but over-indulgent.

questions.why: Herriot's method of diet and exercise shows he was practical, not cruel, lazy or greedy.

questions.q: Mrs Pumphrey's main flaw
questions.why: Mrs Pumphrey's main flaw is over-indulgence, spoiling Tricki with food. She is not mean or cruel.
