questions.why: A child given junk food and no outdoor play who becomes unwell matches 'A Triumph of Surgery', where Tricki is made ill by overfeeding and no exercise.

questions.q: Why did Herriot take Tricki away?
options: Mrs Pumphrey couldn't enforce discipline at home
questions.why: Herriot took Tricki away because Mrs Pumphrey could not enforce discipline at home. He needed to control the dog's diet and exercise.

questions.q: Which best describes the tone?
questions.why: The tone is gentle humour, with comic treatment of Mrs Pumphrey's fussing. It is not a tragedy or suspense story.

questions.q: Which statement is the central irony?
options: A cure by fasting and play is praised as surgery
questions.why: The central irony is that a cure by fasting and play is praised as surgery. No operation was done.

options: Wealth can lead to unwise excess
questions.why: The story suggests wealth can lead to unwise excess, as Mrs Pumphrey's money led her to spoil the dog.

questions.why: Tricki was a Pekinese, a small long-haired breed.

courses.title: Footprints · The Thief's Story (Ruskin Bond)
courses.summary: A young thief befriends a trusting writer, steals his money, and then – changed by trust and the hope of education – returns it.
outcomes: Learners can narrate the theft and the return
Learners can analyse Hari Singh and Anil
Learners can explain the themes of trust and transformation
Learners can write exam answers
courses.note: chapter numbering may differ by edition

scenes.text: A boy runs to the railway station in the rain with stolen money.
The train leaves – but he does not get on.

steps.title: Plot summary
steps.body:
- The narrator, a **15-year-old** thief (calling himself **Hari Singh**), approaches **Anil**, a young writer (about 25), watching a wrestling match, and asks for work.
- Anil cannot pay but agrees to give him food in return for cooking. Hari's cooking is bad, but Anil is kind; he **teaches Hari to write his name** and promises to teach him whole sentences and to add numbers.
- Hari steals small amounts from the daily shopping. One day Anil comes home with money from selling a book to a publisher and tucks the bundle of notes under his mattress.
- At night Hari **steals the money** and runs to the station for the **Lucknow Express**, but he **cannot board** – he realises he would lose the chance to be educated and Anil's trust. He wanders in the rain and returns, **slipping the wet notes back** under the mattress.
- Next morning Anil gives him a **fifty-rupee note** as wages, saying they will start writing sentences. Hari notices the note is **still wet** – Anil knew but forgave silently.

steps.title: Solved example: Why did Hari not board the train? (40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Doubt:** He thought of Anil's trust and kindness.

**Step 2 – Loss:** Leaving meant losing the chance to learn and become a big man.

**Step 3 – Decision:** He returned to put the money back.

steps.title: Solved example: How do we know Anil knew about the theft? (30 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Clue:** The fifty-rupee note he gave Hari was still wet.

**Step 2 – Meaning:** Anil had found the wet notes but chose silent forgiveness.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Anil caught Hari red-handed – he **never accused** him.
- Writing that Hari boarded the train – he **did not**.

items: Hari meets Anil at a wrestling match
Hari cooks for Anil and learns to write his name
Anil brings home money from a publisher
Hari steals it at night
Hari misses the Lucknow Express on purpose
He returns the wet notes; Anil gives him a wet fifty-rupee note

quiz.why: Hari Singh was fifteen years old, a young thief.
Anil was a writer, who took Hari in as a servant.
Hari ran to catch the Lucknow Express, planning to escape with the money.
The money was hidden under the mattress, where Hari stole it from.

quiz.q: Anil showed he knew by giving
quiz.why: Anil showed he knew about the theft by giving Hari a wet note, which had been under the wet mattress.

scenes.text: A shopkeeper forgives a boy who shoplifted and offers him a job.
Trust can change people – that is Anil's way.

steps.title: Character sketches
steps.body:
- **Hari Singh:** clever, experienced thief who studies his “victims”; yet **sensitive**; longs for education; his **conscience** awakens; ends up honest.
- **Anil:** kind, trusting, **easy-going** writer; generous (gives food and lessons); **forgiving** – he knew about the theft yet treated Hari with dignity.

steps.title: Solved example: Character sketch of Anil (60 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Kind:** Gives Hari shelter, food and lessons.

**Step 2 – Trusting:** Leaves money where Hari could find it.

**Step 3 – Forgiving:** Knew of the theft but said nothing; gave wages with the wet note.

steps.title: Solved example: How does Hari change? (40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Before:** A cunning thief who changes names.

**Step 2 – Turning point:** At the station he realises the value of education and trust.

**Step 3 – After:** He returns the money and chooses to learn.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Calling Anil careless – he is **trusting** by nature.

quiz.why: Anil's main trait is trust and kindness; he trusted Hari and forgave him silently.

options: Anil's trust and the hope of learning
quiz.why: Hari's conscience was awakened by Anil's trust and the hope of learning. He was not stopped by police or fear of jail.
Hari was an experienced thief, who studied his victims carefully. He was not a writer or a wrestler.
Anil reacted to the theft with silent forgiveness. He did not call the police or send Hari away.
'The Thief's Story' was written by Ruskin Bond.

scenes.text: A boy who learns to read gets his first proper job.
Hari sees education as the way to become a "big man".

steps.title: Themes
steps.body:
- **Trust and forgiveness** can reform a person.
- **Value of education** – Hari realises learning is worth more than stolen money.
- **Conscience and inner change.**

steps.title: Solved example: “Trust can change a person.” Explain (40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Trust:** Anil trusted Hari completely.

**Step 2 – Effect:** Betraying that trust troubled Hari.

**Step 3 – Change:** He returned the money and chose an honest life.

steps.title: Solved example: Why did Hari value education? (30 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Belief:** Learning to read and write could make him a respected, “big” man.

**Step 2 – Contrast:** Stolen money would bring only temporary gain.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Ignoring **education** as a theme.

statements.s: Anil reported Hari to the police.
Education is a key theme.
Hari returned the money.
The story ends with Hari leaving.

quiz.why: The key themes are trust and transformation, as Hari is changed by Anil's trust.

quiz.q: What did Hari want more than money?
quiz.why: Hari wanted education more than money, as he hoped to become 'a big man' by learning.
The ending is hopeful, since Hari stays and begins to change his life.
The story is narrated by the thief, Hari, in the first person.
Anil's forgiveness is silent: he never says anything, but shows it by his actions.

scenes.text: Hari decides to write to Anil, using the words he has learnt.
Writing becomes his way to say sorry.

steps.title: How to score
steps.body:
- Long answers (120 words): introduce → 3 points with evidence → value/lesson → conclusion.
- Use characters' names correctly.
- For creative tasks (diary, letter, speech), keep the format and stay true to the story.

steps.title: Solved example: Long answer: How did Anil's trust reform Hari? (120 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Start:** Hari, a thief, finds an easy target in trusting Anil.

**Step 2 – Kindness:** Anil feeds and teaches him.

**Step 3 – Theft:** Hari steals the money but cannot board the train.

**Step 4 – Return:** He returns it; Anil silently forgives.

**Step 5 – Conclude:** Trust and education transform him.

steps.body:
**Step 1 – Format:** Informal letter.

**Step 2 – Content:** Admit the theft, explain the change of heart.

**Step 3 – Promise:** To study and stay honest.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Retelling the whole plot instead of answering the question.
- Ignoring the word limit.

quiz.q: A long answer should end with
quiz.why: A long answer should end with a lesson or conclusion, which sums up the main point.
The main reformer is Anil, whose trust changes Hari. Police, a priest or a teacher do not reform him.

quiz.q: What did Anil give Hari next morning?
quiz.why: Next morning Anil gave Hari a fifty-rupee note, an act of kindness that touched him.
Hari's turning point happened at the railway station, where he decided not to board the train.

questions.q: The narrator calls himself
questions.why: The narrator calls himself Hari Singh, the young thief.

questions.q: Anil was
questions.why: Anil was a writer, not a policeman, doctor or cook.

questions.q: Where did they meet?
questions.why: Hari and Anil met at a wrestling match, where Anil first noticed him.

questions.q: Hari stole the money from
questions.why: Hari stole the money from under Anil's mattress.

questions.q: Why couldn't Hari board the train?
options: His conscience and wish to learn
questions.why: Hari could not board the train because of his conscience and his wish to learn, after Anil's trust.

questions.q: Anil's money came from
questions.why: Anil's money came from selling a book, which paid him a sum he kept under the mattress.

questions.q: Assertion: Anil knew about the theft. Reason: The note he gave Hari was still wet.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true: Anil knew about the theft, because the note he gave Hari was still wet. So the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Assertion: Hari left for Lucknow. Reason: He wanted to escape the police.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are false: Hari did not leave for Lucknow, and no police were chasing him.

questions.q: Hari studied his victims carefully. This shows he was
questions.why: Studying his victims carefully shows Hari was clever and experienced, a skilled thief.

questions.q: Anil's silent forgiveness preserved
questions.why: Anil's silent forgiveness preserved Hari's dignity. He was not shamed or accused.

questions.q: Case: A teacher gives a student who cheated another chance, and the student never cheats again. Which story?
questions.why: A teacher giving a cheating student another chance, who never cheats again, matches 'The Thief's Story', where trust reformed Hari.

questions.q: Why did Hari think he could become a “big man”?
questions.why: Hari thought he could become a 'big man' through education, not theft, cooking or wrestling.

questions.q: Which statement best sums up the story?
options: Trust and education reform a young thief
questions.why: The story is about trust and education reforming a young thief. He does not escape and Anil does not catch him.

questions.q: Which literary technique adds depth to the ending?
questions.why: Understatement adds depth to the ending: Anil says nothing yet shows forgiveness. The story has no poem or long speech.

questions.q: What did Anil promise to teach next?
questions.why: Anil promised to teach Hari whole sentences next, as Hari had learned to write only his first words.

questions.q: Author
questions.why: 'The Thief's Story' was written by Ruskin Bond, not Chekhov or Maxwell.

courses.title: Footprints · The Midnight Visitor (Robert Arthur)
courses.summary: A fat, unromantic-looking secret agent outwits an armed rival with nothing but quick thinking – and an imaginary balcony.
outcomes: Learners can narrate the plot and twist
Learners can analyse Ausable, Max and Fowler
Learners can explain how presence of mind wins
Learners can write exam answers
courses.note: chapter numbering may differ by edition

scenes.text: A man with a pistol waits in a hotel room for secret papers.
The fat agent who walks in has only one weapon – his imagination.

steps.title: Plot summary
steps.body:
- **Ausable**, a secret agent, is **fat**, speaks with an accent and does not look like a dashing spy. **Fowler**, a young writer, is disappointed – he expected romance and pistols.
- In Ausable's hotel room (sixth floor, Paris), they find **Max**, a rival agent, holding a **pistol**; he wants an important **report about missiles** that Ausable is expecting.
- Ausable calmly invents a story: Max must have come in through the **balcony** below the window – he says he complained to the management about this balcony because it lets anyone enter.
- There is a knock. Ausable says it is the **police**, whom he had asked to check on him. Max panics, threatens, then decides to escape via the “balcony”, swings out of the window and drops – with a scream – because **there is no balcony**.
- The visitor at the door is just a **waiter** with drinks Ausable had ordered. Ausable had invented both the balcony and the police.

steps.title: Solved example: How did Ausable get rid of Max? (40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Invention:** He made up a balcony below the window and a police visit.

**Step 2 – Effect:** When the waiter knocked, Max believed it was the police and jumped to the non-existent balcony.

steps.title: Solved example: Why was Fowler disappointed? (30 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Expectation:** Mysterious women, gunfire, romance.

**Step 2 – Reality:** Ausable was fat, ordinary-looking and dull.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying there really was a balcony – it was **imaginary**.
- Saying police came – it was a **waiter**.

items: Fowler meets fat Ausable and is disappointed
They find Max with a pistol
Ausable invents the balcony story
A knock – Ausable says it is the police
Max jumps out to the “balcony” and falls
A waiter enters with drinks

quiz.why: Ausable was fat, which surprised Fowler, who expected a thin, dashing spy.
Max wanted a report on missiles, which Ausable had in his possession.
The knock at the door was by a waiter, not the police, as Ausable made Max believe.
The balcony did not exist. Ausable invented it to trick Max into jumping.
Fowler was a writer, who came to meet a real spy.

scenes.text: In a crisis, the calm person often wins.
Ausable never loses his cool.

steps.title: Character sketches
steps.body:
- **Ausable:** looks dull but is **intelligent, calm, quick-witted** and a master of **presence of mind**; uses words, not weapons.
- **Max:** armed and threatening but **gullible** and easily panicked.
- **Fowler:** young, **romantic**, expects thrills; learns that real spies need brains.

steps.title: Solved example: Character sketch of Ausable (60 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Appearance:** Fat, unromantic, ordinary.

**Step 2 – Mind:** Calm, quick-witted; invents the balcony and police on the spot.

**Step 3 – Result:** Defeats an armed rival without violence.

steps.title: Solved example: Contrast Ausable and Max (40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Ausable:** Unarmed but clever and composed.

**Step 2 – Max:** Armed but nervous and easily fooled.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Judging Ausable by his looks – that is exactly Fowler's mistake.

quiz.why: Ausable's greatest weapon was presence of mind, as he outwitted an armed man with words.
Max was gullible, because he believed Ausable's lies about the balcony and the police.
Fowler's expectations were romantic, as he imagined spies to be thrilling and glamorous.
Appearance in the story can be deceptive; the fat, ordinary-looking Ausable was a clever spy.
'The Midnight Visitor' was written by Robert Arthur.

scenes.text: A quiz team with calm thinkers beats a loud team.
The story shows intelligence beats force.

steps.title: Themes
steps.body:
- **Presence of mind** and intelligence over force.
- **Appearances deceive.**
- **Suspense and twist ending** typical of detective fiction.

scenes.text: A thief opens a safe in a country house and is caught by a smiling lady in red.

steps.title: Plot summary
steps.body:
- **Horace Danby**, about 50, unmarried, a respectable **locksmith**, robs **one safe every year** to buy **rare and expensive books**; he has been to prison once.
- He plans to rob **Shotover Grange**, where jewels worth about **£15,000** are kept; he has studied the house; the family is away and the servants are at the cinema; he knows the dog's name, **Sherry**.
- He enters, calms Sherry, and is about to work on the safe behind a painting when a **young woman in red** appears. She pretends to be the lady of the house and says she must not call the police if he helps her: she claims she forgot the safe combination and needs the jewels.
- Horace, who suffers from **hay fever** (sneezes at flowers), is charmed and fooled; he **removes his gloves** and opens the safe for her. She takes the jewels and leaves.
- Two days later Horace is **arrested** – his **fingerprints** were on the safe. The woman was a **thief** who had tricked him. In prison he works in the library, bitter that people talk about “honour among thieves”.

scenes.text: Two boys in London see fresh muddy footprints appear on a step – with no one there.

steps.title: Plot summary
steps.body:
- **Griffin**, a scientist, discovered a way to make the human body **transparent** by swallowing certain rare drugs; he became **invisible**.
- In **London**, two boys saw fresh muddy **footprints** appear from nowhere.
- Griffin had **set fire** to his landlord's house in revenge after the landlord tried to evict him. Being invisible, he could move unseen but was cold and hungry in mid-winter, being naked.
- He entered a big **London store**, ate food, wore warm clothes and slept on a pile of quilts; in the morning assistants found him, and he escaped by taking off the clothes.
- He then robbed a **theatrical company's shop in Drury Lane**: took **bandages**, **dark glasses**, a **false nose**, **big bushy side-whiskers** and a large hat, and knocked down the shopkeeper and stole money.
- He went to the village of **Iping** and stayed at the inn (**Coach and Horses**), run by **Mrs Hall**. He was eccentric, rude and secretive; his room was full of bottles.
- When the vicarage was burgled (**Mr and Mrs Bunting** heard sounds but saw no one; money vanished), suspicion fell on him. Mrs Hall found his room empty and the furniture “flew” at her.
- When the constable (**Jaffers**) tried to arrest him, Griffin **threw off his clothes**, struggled invisibly, and escaped, leaving chaos.

courses.summary: How Richard Ebright's childhood passion for butterflies, his mother's support and a series of science-fair projects led him to become a scientist who proposed a theory of how cells read DNA.
outcomes: Learners can trace Ebright's journey from collector to scientist

scenes.text: A kindergarten boy in Pennsylvania collects butterflies – and doesn't stop.
Years later he proposes a new theory about how cells work.

steps.title: Plot summary
steps.body:
- **Richard H. Ebright** grew up in **Reading, Pennsylvania (USA)**; an only child. From **kindergarten** he collected **butterflies**, then rocks, fossils and coins; he became an eager astronomer too. By the second grade he had collected all 25 species of butterflies around his town.
- His **mother** encouraged him – took him on trips, bought telescopes, microscopes, cameras, mounting materials; she became his only companion after his father's death (when he was in third grade).
- She got him the book **“The Travels of Monarch X”**, which described how monarch butterflies migrate to Central America; at its end readers were invited to help study migration by **tagging butterflies** for **Dr Frederick A. Urquhart** of the **University of Toronto**.
- **Science fairs:** in **seventh grade** his project on frog tissues **lost** – winners had done real experiments. He realised he needed experiments, not just displays. In **eighth grade** he tried to find the cause of a **viral disease** that kills nearly all monarch caterpillars; next year he showed that **viceroy butterflies copy monarchs** (birds avoid monarchs, which taste bad).
- In high school he discovered that the **gold spots on a monarch pupa** produce a **hormone** necessary for the butterfly's full development; this project took him to the International Science and Engineering Fair, and he later spent a summer working at the Army's entomology laboratory.
- At college he and his roommate **James R. Wong** worked on a **theory of how cells “read” the blueprint of DNA**, published in the *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences*.
- He was also a champion **debater, public speaker, canoeist and outdoor person**, and an expert photographer.

scenes.text: A clerk's wife dreams of luxury; finally she is invited to a grand ball.
She borrows a friend's diamond necklace – and loses it.

steps.title: Plot summary
steps.body:
- **Matilda Loisel**, pretty and charming, was born in a family of clerks and married a **petty clerk** in the **Board of Education**. She suffered, dreaming of luxury.
- Her husband brought an **invitation to a ball** at the Minister's. She cried – she had no dress. He gave her **400 francs** he had saved to buy a **gun**.
- She still lacked jewels; she borrowed a **diamond necklace** from her friend **Mme Forestier**.
- At the ball she was a great **success**. Returning home, she found the necklace **lost**.
- They searched everywhere, then bought a similar one at the Palais-Royal for **36,000 francs**: her husband had **18,000** (left by his father) and **borrowed** the rest, ruining his life.
- For **ten years** they lived in poverty – she did all the housework, bargained, he worked nights – to repay the debt. Matilda became old, rough and coarse.
- One Sunday she met Mme Forestier and told her the truth. Mme Forestier, moved, said her necklace was **imitation (paste)**, worth **at most 500 francs**.

**Step 3 – Time:** Ten years of hardship.

steps.body:
- Saying the necklace was real – it was **imitation (paste)**.
- Mixing up amounts: dress **400**, replacement **36,000**, original worth **≤500 francs**.

questions.why: A person who borrows a costly item to show off, loses it and secretly borrows money to replace it mirrors Matilda's actions. Bholi, Fog and The Thief's Story have different plots.

questions.q: By how much did the replacement exceed the original's maximum value?
questions.why: The original was worth at most 500 francs and the replacement cost 36,000, so the difference is 36,000 − 500 = 35,500 francs. The other numbers are not this difference.

questions.q: Which best states the moral?
options: Vanity and false pride bring ruin; honesty saves
questions.why: The story shows that vanity and false pride led the Loisels to ruin, while a simple honest confession would have saved them. The other options are not what the story teaches.

questions.q: How did Matilda change over ten years?
options: From dreamy and vain to hard-working and worn
questions.why: Matilda began as a dreamy, vain woman longing for luxury. Ten years of hard labour left her rough, worn and hard-working, so she did not become rich or cruel.

questions.q: What fraction of the 36,000 francs did Loisel have from inheritance?
questions.why: Loisel had 18,000 francs from his father's inheritance. 18,000 ÷ 36,000 = 1/2, so he had half and borrowed the rest.

questions.q: Matilda's husband's first name is not given; he is called
questions.why: The husband is called M. Loisel; the story does not give his first name. Forestier is Matilda's friend, and Ausable and Ramlal belong to other stories.

scenes.text: In a village, a girl who stammers is called "Bholi" – the simpleton.
At school, a teacher's kind words change everything.

steps.title: Plot summary
steps.body:
- **Sulekha** was the fourth daughter of **Ramlal**, a prosperous farmer and village **numberdar**. She was called **Bholi** (simpleton). At **ten months** she fell off a cot, which damaged her brain; at **two** she had **smallpox**, leaving pockmarks; she **stammered** and was laughed at.
- Her sisters were married off; Bholi was neglected – parents worried no one would marry her.
- A primary school for girls opened in the village; the **Tehsildar**, who came to inaugurate it, asked Ramlal to set an example by sending his daughters. Ramlal's wife suggested sending Bholi (she had no marriage prospects).
- The **teacher** was kind; she gently encouraged Bholi to speak, told her she would lose her stammer with practice, and gave her books. Bholi felt hope.
- Years later, a proposal came from **Bishamber Nath**, a well-to-do grocer, **lame, middle-aged** with grown-up children. Her parents agreed, thinking it the best she could get.
- At the wedding, seeing her pockmarks, Bishamber demanded **₹5,000 dowry**. Ramlal begged and paid. **Bholi threw the garland** into the fire and **refused to marry** a mean, greedy man. She would look after her parents and **teach** in the same school.

**Step 3 – Hope:** Gave her books and a sense of self-worth.

steps.body:

**Step 2 – Self-respect:** She would not marry a mean, greedy coward.

**Step 3 – Courage:** Education gave her the strength to say no.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Bholi was born simple – her difficulties came from a **fall** and **smallpox**.
- Saying Ramlal refused the dowry – he **paid** it; **Bholi** refused the marriage.
