Her turning point was the kind teacher at school, who built her confidence. Smallpox and the fall were her early misfortunes.

options: threw the garland in the fire
quiz.why: At the wedding Bholi threw the garland in the fire, refusing the greedy groom. She did not cry silently or run away.
Bholi's plan was to teach at the school and look after her parents. She did not plan to move away or marry another.
The Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 makes giving and taking dowry an offence. POCSO, RTI and the Consumer Act deal with other matters.

questions.q: Bholi means
questions.why: Bholi is a nickname meaning simpleton. It was given to her because she was thought dull and slow.

questions.q: Bholi's father was a
questions.why: Bholi's father, Ramlal, was the village numberdar, a headman. The Tehsildar is a different person, and Bishamber is the grocer.

questions.q: Author
questions.why: The author is K.A. Abbas. Bond, Maupassant and Boiko wrote other lessons in the book.

questions.q: At what age did Bholi fall off the cot?
questions.why: Bholi fell off a cot at ten months and was injured; later smallpox left her face scarred. Her speech was affected too.

questions.q: Who asked Ramlal to send his daughters to school?
questions.why: The Tehsildar advised Ramlal to send his daughters to school, as a government officer setting an example.

questions.q: Bishamber was a
questions.why: Bishamber was a grocer, a shopkeeper, whom Bholi was to marry.

questions.q: Assertion: Bholi refused to marry Bishamber. Reason: He demanded dowry and mocked her.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Bishamber demanded dowry and mocked her, so Bholi refused to marry him.

questions.q: Assertion: Bholi was sent to school because her parents valued girls' education. Reason: The Tehsildar asked Ramlal to set an example.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: The assertion is false: Bholi was sent to school because she had no marriage prospects, not because of any belief in girls' education. The reason is true, since the Tehsildar asked Ramlal to set an example.

questions.q: Why did Bishamber demand dowry at the last moment?
options: It was custom to ask late
He saw her pockmarks and wanted compensation
questions.why: Bishamber saw Bholi's pockmarked face at the wedding and demanded dowry as compensation for marrying her. It was greed, not custom or poverty.

questions.q: The teacher's main gift to Bholi
questions.why: The teacher gave Bholi confidence and hope. That helped her find her voice, not a husband, a job or money.

questions.q: Case: A shy girl gets encouragement from a teacher, overcomes stage fear and later refuses an unfair demand. Which story?
questions.why: A shy girl who gains confidence from a teacher and later refuses an unfair demand matches Bholi. The other stories have different plots.

questions.q: Which order is correct?
options: Neglect → school → teacher's encouragement → proposal → dowry demand → refusal
questions.why: The order follows the plot: neglect, school, the teacher's encouragement, the proposal, the dowry demand and finally her refusal. The other orders put events before their causes.

questions.q: Which statement best sums up the story?
options: A girl marries a rich man
Education gives a neglected girl the courage to defy injustice
questions.why: The story shows how education gives a neglected girl the courage to defy injustice. The other statements describe events that are not its main message.

questions.q: Dowry demanded
questions.why: Bishamber demanded ₹5,000 as dowry, a large amount for Ramlal that he could not easily meet. The other sums are not in the story.

questions.q: Bholi’s difficulties began when she
options: fell off a cot at ten months and later had smallpox
questions.why: Her troubles began when she fell off a cot at ten months and later had smallpox. She was not born blind and did not lose her parents.

courses.title: Footprints · The Book That Saved the Earth (Claire Boiko)
courses.summary: A comic play set in the 25th century: Martians planning to invade Earth in the 21st century misread a book of nursery rhymes and flee in panic.
outcomes: Learners can summarise the play
Learners can analyse Think-Tank and Noodle
Learners can explain humour, satire and misinterpretation
Learners can write exam answers
courses.note: chapter numbering may differ by edition

scenes.text: Martians land in a library and find a strange book: Mother Goose.
Their leader, who looks like an egg, reads about Humpty Dumpty – and panics.

steps.title: Plot summary
steps.body:
- A **historian** of the **25th century** narrates how the **Martians** tried to invade Earth in the **21st century** and how a book saved it.
- The Martians are led by the vain **Think-Tank** (huge, egg-shaped head) with his apprentice **Noodle**. A space probe – **Captain Omega**, **Lieutenant Iota** and **Sergeant Oop** – lands in a **library** in Centerville, USA.
- They do not know what books are; they think they are sandwiches (Oop tries to eat one). Think-Tank tells them to use a **thought-wave** on the book: **Mother Goose** nursery rhymes.
- Think-Tank interprets the rhymes absurdly: **“Hey diddle diddle”** – Earthlings have trained cows to jump over the moon, so they must be advanced; **“Mistress Mary, quite contrary…”** – a code about silver bells and cockle shells (communication devices).
- Then they read **“Humpty Dumpty”** – Noodle points out Humpty looks just like Think-Tank, who falls and cannot be put together again. Think-Tank takes it as an **assassination plot** and orders a **retreat** – he orders the Martians to abandon the invasion and retreat far from Earth.
- The historian concludes that a simple **book of nursery rhymes** saved the Earth.

steps.title: Solved example: Why did Think-Tank call off the invasion? (40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Rhyme:** Humpty Dumpty described an egg-shaped being who falls and breaks.

**Step 2 – Fear:** Think-Tank thought it was a plan to destroy him.

**Step 3 – Order:** He ordered complete retreat.

steps.title: Solved example: How did the Martians misread “Hey diddle diddle”? (30 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Reading:** Cows jumping over the moon.

**Step 2 – Conclusion:** Earthlings are so advanced they train animals for space travel.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the story is set in the 21st century only – it is **narrated** from the **25th century** about events of the **21st**.
- Saying the book was a science book – it was **Mother Goose**.

items: Historian introduces the 21st-century invasion attempt
Martians land in a library
They mistake books for sandwiches
Think-Tank misreads Hey diddle diddle
He misreads Mistress Mary
Humpty Dumpty terrifies him
Invasion abandoned

quiz.why: The Martian leader is Think-Tank. Noodle is his apprentice and Oop is a sergeant.
The book was Mother Goose, a collection of nursery rhymes, not a dictionary or science book.
The Martians landed in a library, which is where they found the book.
Think-Tank was frightened by Humpty Dumpty, which he read as a warning about his own destruction.
The narrator is a historian of the 25th century, who tells the story as a past event.

scenes.text: A boss who thinks he knows everything gets everything wrong.
His sensible assistant is ignored.

steps.title: Character sketches
steps.body:
- **Think-Tank:** **vain, arrogant, self-important**, thinks he is the greatest mind; actually **foolish**; insults subordinates (calls Noodle names).
- **Noodle:** humble, sensible, polite apprentice; often closer to the truth; yet flatters his boss.
- **Captain Omega, Lt Iota, Sgt Oop:** obedient crew; Oop is comic (tries to eat the book).

steps.title: Solved example: Character sketch of Think-Tank (60 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Vanity:** Calls himself the greatest; demands flattery.

**Step 2 – Foolishness:** Misreads rhymes completely.

**Step 3 – Cowardice:** Flees when he imagines a threat.

steps.title: Solved example: Contrast Think-Tank and Noodle (40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Think-Tank:** Arrogant, wrong, fearful.

**Step 2 – Noodle:** Humble, sensible, polite – points out the Humpty resemblance.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Calling Think-Tank wise – his name is **ironic**.

quiz.why: Think-Tank is vain and foolish: he is proud of his intelligence yet misreads the rhymes. That is why his name is ironic.
Noodle, the apprentice, is humble and sensible. He is not arrogant or cruel.
Sergeant Oop comically tries to eat a book, thinking it is a sandwich. He does not lead the mission or read well.
The name Think-Tank suggests a great thinker, but he is foolish. Names that mean the opposite of the truth are ironic.
The play was written by Claire Boiko. Chekhov, Herriot and Wells wrote other works.

scenes.text: Misreading a message can cause huge mistakes.
Here, misreading saved the Earth!

steps.title: Themes
steps.body:
- **Humour and satire** on arrogance and false knowledge.
- **Importance of books** and correct interpretation.
- **Vanity leads to downfall.**
- **Science fiction + comedy.**

steps.title: Solved example: How did a book save the Earth? (40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Book:** Mother Goose rhymes.

**Step 2 – Misreading:** Think-Tank believed Earthlings were advanced and that Humpty Dumpty was a threat to him.

**Step 3 – Result:** Martians fled; invasion abandoned.

steps.title: Solved example: What does the play satirise? (30 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Target:** Arrogant leaders who ignore others and think they know everything.

**Step 2 – Lesson:** Humility and knowledge matter.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Missing the **satire** on arrogance.

statements.s: The Martians correctly understood nursery rhymes.
The play satirises arrogance.
The invasion succeeded.
Books are central to the plot.

quiz.why: The main theme is arrogance and misinterpretation: a proud leader misreads nursery rhymes and gives up an invasion.
It is a comic science-fiction play, with humour from Martians misreading rhymes. It is not a tragedy, biography or poem.
A book of nursery rhymes saved Earth, because the Martians misread it and retreated.
The lesson is that humility matters. Pride and arrogance blind Think-Tank to the truth.

quiz.q: The play is set (as narrated) in the
quiz.why: The historian narrates from the 25th century, recalling the Martian landing as a past event.

scenes.text: Class stages the Humpty Dumpty scene with an egg-shaped mask.
Timing makes the comedy.

steps.title: How to score
steps.body:
- Long answers (120 words): introduce → 3 points with evidence → value/lesson → conclusion.
- Use characters' names correctly.
- For creative tasks (diary, letter, speech), keep the format and stay true to the story.

steps.title: Solved example: Long answer: “Think-Tank's vanity saved the Earth.” (120 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Vanity:** Believed he knew everything.

**Step 2 – Misreading:** Hey diddle diddle, Mistress Mary.

**Step 3 – Humpty:** Took the rhyme as a threat to himself.

**Step 4 – Retreat:** Abandoned invasion.

**Step 5 – Conclude:** His arrogance and ignorance saved Earth.

steps.title: Solved example: Write Noodle's report to Martian headquarters (100 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Format:** Formal report: title, date, by.

**Step 2 – Content:** Landing, book, rhymes, Think-Tank's panic.

**Step 3 – Recommendation:** Study Earth's books properly.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Retelling the whole plot instead of answering the question.
- Ignoring the word limit.

activity.prompt: Have you ever misunderstood a message and overreacted? What helped you understand correctly?
activity.hint: Think of asking questions before acting.

quiz.why: A report carries a title, date and the writer's name. Rhyme, dialogue and a greeting belong to other forms.
Think-Tank's flaw is vanity. He trusts his own cleverness and misreads the book.
They read Hey diddle diddle literally and thought cows jumped over the moon, so they assumed Earthlings were very advanced.

quiz.q: Mistress Mary's silver bells were seen as
quiz.why: The Martians took Mistress Mary's silver bells as communication devices. It is another comic misreading.
The message is to read and understand carefully. Wrong assumptions can cause serious mistakes.

questions.q: The Martians' leader
questions.why: Think-Tank is the leader of the Martians. Oop is a sergeant and Noodle his apprentice.

questions.q: The book
questions.why: The book is Mother Goose, a book of nursery rhymes. The Martians misread it.

questions.q: Author
questions.why: Claire Boiko wrote the play. H.G. Wells and Chekhov wrote different works.

questions.q: Think-Tank's apprentice
questions.why: Noodle is Think-Tank's apprentice and is the sensible one.

questions.q: The Martians landed in a
questions.why: The Martians landed in a library, where they found the Mother Goose book.

questions.q: Oop thought books were
questions.why: Sergeant Oop mistook books for sandwiches and tried to eat one. It is a comic moment.

questions.q: Assertion: Think-Tank ordered retreat. Reason: He thought Humpty Dumpty described his own destruction.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Think-Tank feared that Humpty Dumpty described his own destruction, so he ordered a retreat.

questions.q: Assertion: Think-Tank was a wise leader. Reason: He interpreted every rhyme correctly.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Think-Tank was vain, not wise, so the assertion is false. He misread rhymes, so the reason is false too.

questions.q: Think-Tank's head was
questions.why: Think-Tank's head is described as huge and egg-shaped. It suits a vain leader who thinks of himself as a great thinker.

questions.q: The narrator of the play
questions.why: The narrator is a historian of the 25th century who tells the tale as past history, not a librarian or a character.

questions.q: Case: A boss refuses advice, misreads a report and makes a costly decision. Which character?
questions.why: A boss who ignores advice and misreads a report is like Think-Tank, who ignores Noodle and misreads the rhymes. Noodle is the sensible one.

questions.q: What made the Martians think Earthlings were advanced?
questions.why: Reading Hey diddle diddle literally, they thought a cow jumping over the moon showed advanced technology. They had not seen rockets or met scientists.

questions.q: Which statement best sums up the play?
options: A vain leader's misreading of nursery rhymes ends an invasion
questions.why: The play shows a vain leader misreading nursery rhymes and ending the invasion. The other statements are not the plot.

questions.q: Which device drives the humour?
options: Dramatic irony – audience knows the rhymes, Martians don't
questions.why: The humour comes from dramatic irony: the audience knows the rhymes are harmless while the Martians do not. It is a comedy, not a tragedy.

questions.q: Why is Noodle important?
questions.why: Noodle's observation about the book makes Think-Tank panic and decide to retreat. He is neither the attacker nor the historian.

questions.q: What did Think-Tank order after reading Humpty Dumpty?
questions.why: After reading Humpty Dumpty, Think-Tank feared the same fate and ordered a complete retreat. He did not attack or celebrate.

courses.title: English Grammar I · Tenses, Modals, Subject–Verb Agreement, Determiners
courses.summary: Exam-focused grammar for Class 10: the twelve tense forms and their uses, modals for ability, permission, obligation and possibility, subject–verb agreement rules, and determiners.
outcomes: Learners can choose the correct tense in context
Learners can use modals accurately
Learners can apply subject–verb agreement rules
Learners can use determiners correctly

scenes.text: Rohan writes for the school magazine: "The team has won… it was raining… they will celebrate."
Each verb shows a time and an aspect.

steps.title: The 12 tense forms
steps.body:
- **Simple:** present (She **plays**), past (She **played**), future (She **will play**) – habits, facts, completed actions, predictions.
- **Continuous (be + -ing):** is playing / was playing / will be playing – actions in progress.
- **Perfect (have + V3):** has played / had played / will have played – completion before a point; present perfect links past to now (experience, recent result).
- **Perfect continuous (have been + -ing):** has been playing / had been playing / will have been playing – duration up to a point (with *for/since*).

**Signal words:** *yesterday, ago, last* → past; *since, for, just, already, yet* → perfect; *now, at present* → continuous; *by the time* → perfect.

steps.title: Solved example: Fill in: “I ___ (live) here since 2015.”
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Signal:** “since 2015” = duration from past to now.

**Step 2 – Tense:** Present perfect or perfect continuous.

**Step 3 – Answer:** **have lived / have been living**.

steps.title: Solved example: Correct the error: “When I reached, the train already left.”
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Logic:** The train left before I reached – earlier past action.

**Step 2 – Rule:** Use past perfect for the earlier of two past actions.

**Step 3 – Answer:** “When I reached, the train **had already left**.”

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using present perfect with a definite past time: ✗ *I have seen him yesterday* → ✓ *I saw him yesterday*.
- Using *since* with a period: ✗ *since two years* → ✓ *for two years*.
- Using continuous with stative verbs: ✗ *I am knowing* → ✓ *I know*.

activity.text: She ___ (study) for three hours when the lights went out. By next June, we ___ (finish) the project. Water ___ (boil) at 100°C.

quiz.why: With the third person singular subject He in the simple present, the verb takes -s or -es, so goes is right.

quiz.q: “They ___ cricket when it started to rain.”
quiz.why: The rain interrupted an action in progress in the past, so the past continuous were playing is used.
Already goes with the present perfect, formed with have plus the past participle: have done.
Since is used with a point in time such as 2019. For is used with a period of time.
By a future time, an action will be complete, so the future perfect will have finished is used.

scenes.text: The sign says: "You must shower. You may use the slide. You should not run."
Each modal gives a different meaning.

steps.title: Meanings of modals
steps.body:
- **can/could:** ability (I *can* swim; he *could* read at four), permission (informal), possibility.
- **may/might:** permission (formal: *May I come in?*), possibility (*It may/might rain* – might = less likely).
- **must:** strong obligation (*You must wear a helmet*), logical certainty (*He must be tired*). *Must not* = prohibition.
- **have to:** external obligation; *don't have to* = no necessity.
- **should/ought to:** advice, duty (*You should rest*).
- **will/would:** future, willingness, polite request (*Would you help me?*), past habit.
- **shall:** offers/suggestions with I/we (*Shall we start?*).
- **need not / needn't:** no necessity.

Modals are followed by the **base form** of the verb (no *to*, except *ought to, have to*).

steps.title: Solved example: Choose: “You ___ not shout in the library.” (prohibition)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Meaning:** It is forbidden.

**Step 2 – Modal:** **must** not.

steps.title: Solved example: Choose: “You ___ bring lunch; it will be provided.” (no necessity)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Meaning:** Not required.

**Step 2 – Modal:** **need not** / **don't have to**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- ✗ *He can sings* → ✓ *He can sing* (base form).
- Confusing *must not* (prohibited) with *need not* (not necessary).
- ✗ *I must to go* → ✓ *I must go*.

activity.prompt: Match the modal to its meaning

quiz.why: May is the polite way to ask for permission. Must and need show necessity, not permission.
Should is used to give advice. Can and may do not recommend the action, and need not shows no obligation.
Can expresses ability, so She can speak four languages. Must and shall do not show ability.
Might expresses possibility, which fits the advice to take an umbrella. Must would show certainty.
A modal verb like must is followed by the base form without to, so He must go is correct.

scenes.text: "The team are/is winning" – Meera is unsure which to write.
Agreement rules decide.

steps.title: Key rules
steps.body:
1. Singular subject → singular verb; plural → plural.
2. **Each, every, either, neither, everyone, somebody** → singular (*Everyone is here*).
3. **Two subjects joined by and** → plural (*Ram and Shyam are friends*) – but if they refer to one person/idea → singular (*Bread and butter is my breakfast*).
4. **Either…or / neither…nor / not only…but also** → verb agrees with the **nearer** subject (*Neither the teacher nor the students were late*).
5. **As well as, along with, with, besides** → verb agrees with the **first** subject (*The captain, along with his players, is here*).
6. **Collective nouns** → singular when acting as one unit (*The jury has decided*), plural when members act individually.
7. **Amounts/time/distance** as a single unit → singular (*Five kilometres is a long walk*).
8. **The number of** → singular; **a number of** → plural.
9. **News, mathematics, physics** → singular; **scissors, trousers** → plural.

steps.title: Solved example: Choose: “Neither the players nor the coach ___ happy.” (is/are)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Rule:** Agree with the nearer subject.

**Step 2 – Nearer:** “the coach” – singular.

**Step 3 – Answer:** **is**.

steps.title: Solved example: Choose: “A number of students ___ absent.” (was/were)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Rule:** “A number of” = many → plural.

**Step 2 – Answer:** **were**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- ✗ *Each of the boys have* → ✓ *has*.
- ✗ *The news are good* → ✓ *is*.
- Agreeing with the noun in a phrase: ✗ *The box of apples are* → ✓ *is* (subject = box).

statements.s: “Everyone are invited.” is correct.
“The number of cars is increasing.” is correct.
“Mathematics are difficult.” is correct.
“The teacher, with her students, is coming.” is correct.

quiz.why: Each is a singular subject, so it takes the singular verb gets.
Bread and butter is thought of as one dish, so the singular verb is is used.
With either...or, the verb agrees with the nearer subject. The nearer subject is I, so am is used.
An amount of money is treated as a single unit, so the singular verb is is used.
Scissors is a plural noun, so it takes the plural verb are.

scenes.text: Ira writes: "I ate a apple" – her teacher circles it.
Determiners depend on sound and meaning.

steps.title: Types and use
steps.body:
- **Articles:** *a* before consonant **sounds** (*a university, a one-rupee coin*), *an* before vowel **sounds** (*an hour, an MBA*); *the* for specific/unique things (*the sun, the Ganga, the Himalayas*), superlatives (*the best*), ordinals (*the first*).
- **Demonstratives:** this/that/these/those.
- **Possessives:** my, your, his, her, its, our, their.
- **Quantifiers:** *much/little* (uncountable), *many/few* (countable), *some* (positive), *any* (negative/questions), *each/every*, *enough*, *several*.
- *few* = hardly any (negative); *a few* = some (positive); *the few* = all of the small number. Same for *little/a little/the little*.

steps.title: Solved example: Fill: “He is ___ honest man.”
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Sound:** “honest” begins with a vowel sound /ɒ/ (h is silent).

**Step 2 – Answer:** **an**.

steps.title: Solved example: Fill: “There is ___ milk left; buy some.” (very little)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Meaning:** Almost none – negative.

**Step 2 – Answer:** **little**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- ✗ *an university* → ✓ *a university* (sound /juː/).
- ✗ *much books* → ✓ *many books*.
- Confusing *few* (negative) with *a few* (positive).

activity.text: She is ___ European. I need ___ hour. ___ Ganga is a holy river.

quiz.why: An is used before a vowel sound, and umbrella begins with the vowel sound /ʌ/.

quiz.q: “I have ___ friends here; I'm not lonely.”
quiz.why: A few means some, a positive idea, and fits since the speaker is not lonely. Few would mean almost none.
Water is uncountable, so much is used. Many and few go with countable nouns.
The is used with the names of mountain ranges, such as the Himalayas.
The is used before a superlative like best, as there is only one best.

questions.q: “She ___ (write) a letter now.”
questions.why: Now shows an action happening at this moment, so the present continuous is writing is used.

questions.q: “We ___ the match last Sunday.”
questions.why: Last Sunday is a definite past time, so the simple past won is used.

questions.q: “___ I come in, sir?”
questions.why: May is the formal, polite word for asking permission, as in May I come in, sir.

questions.q: “The jury ___ given its verdict.”
questions.why: Jury here is one group acting together, so it takes the singular has.

questions.q: “He is ___ European.”
questions.why: European begins with a /j/ consonant sound, so it takes a, not an.

questions.q: “You ___ not pay; it is free.”
questions.why: Need not means there is no necessity, which fits since it is free. Must would mean it is required.

questions.q: Identify the error: “She have been waiting for an hour.”
questions.why: The subject She is third person singular, so the correct form is has been waiting, not have.

questions.q: Identify the error: “Neither of the answers are correct.”
questions.why: Neither of takes a singular verb, so the correct form is Neither of the answers is correct.

questions.q: “By the time we arrived, the film ___.”
questions.why: The arrival is a past event and the film started earlier, so the past perfect had started is used.

questions.q: “The Principal, along with the teachers, ___ attending.”
questions.why: With along with, the verb agrees with the first subject, the Principal, which is singular, so is is used.

questions.q: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.why: Know is a stative verb and is not normally used in continuous forms. With I, the correct form is I know.

questions.q: Choose the correct sentence.
options: He has gone to Delhi yesterday.
He had go to Delhi yesterday.
questions.why: Yesterday is a definite past time, so the simple past went is needed. The present perfect cannot be used with yesterday.

questions.q: Editing: “There is few water in the jug.” Correct word for “few”:
questions.why: Water is uncountable, so little is used instead of few. Many is only for countable nouns.

questions.q: Gap-filling: “If it rains, the match ___ (cancel).”
questions.why: This is a first conditional with if plus the present tense. The result takes will plus the passive, will be cancelled, as the match does not cancel itself.

questions.q: Gap-filling: “I wish I ___ the answer yesterday.”
questions.why: A wish about the past needs the past perfect, so I wish I had known is correct.

questions.q: “The number of applicants ___ grown.”
questions.why: The number of is singular, so it takes has. By contrast, a number of is plural.

courses.title: English Grammar II · Reported Speech, Editing, Omission and Gap-filling
courses.summary: Change direct speech to reported speech for statements, questions, commands and requests, and master editing, omission and gap-filling tasks with a step-by-step method.
outcomes: Learners can report statements with correct tense and pronoun changes
Learners can report questions, commands and requests
Learners can find and correct errors in passages
Learners can fill gaps using context

scenes.text: Dad says on the phone: "I am stuck in traffic."
Riya tells Mum: "Dad said that he was stuck in traffic."

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
- Reporting verb: *said / told + object* (*He told me that…*). Use *that* (optional).
- **Tense backshift** when the reporting verb is in the past: present simple → past simple; present continuous → past continuous; present perfect → past perfect; past simple → past perfect; *will → would, can → could, may → might, shall → should*; *must* often stays or → *had to*.
- **No backshift** for universal truths (*The teacher said that the earth revolves around the sun*) or if the reporting verb is present (*He says he is ready*).
- **Pronouns** change by speaker/listener; **time/place words** change: *now → then, today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, yesterday → the previous day, here → there, this → that, ago → before*.

steps.title: Solved example: Report: She said, “I am reading a novel now.”
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Verb:** said → said

**Step 2 – Tense:** am reading → was reading

**Step 3 – Pronoun/time:** I → she; now → then

**Step 4 – Answer:** She said that she **was reading** a novel **then**.

steps.title: Solved example: Report: He said to me, “I will meet you tomorrow.”
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Verb:** said to me → told me

**Step 2 – Modal:** will → would

**Step 3 – Pronouns/time:** I → he; you → me; tomorrow → the next day

**Step 4 – Answer:** He told me that he **would meet me the next day**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- ✗ *He said me that…* → ✓ *He told me that…* / *He said to me that…*
- Forgetting backshift with a past reporting verb.
- Backshifting universal truths unnecessarily.

options: He told that he was tired.
He said that he is tired.
He said that I was tired.
He said that he was tired.
quiz.why: When the reporting verb is in the past, the present tense backshifts to the past, so am becomes was. I also changes to he.
In reported speech today changes to that day, because the time reference moves to the time of the original speech.

quiz.q: She said, “The sun rises in the east.” →
quiz.why: A universal truth stays in the present tense in reported speech, so rises is unchanged.
In backshift, can becomes could.
Tell takes a person as its object, so told me is correct. Said, spoke and talked need a preposition such as to.

scenes.text: The interviewer asked: "Where do you live? Do you like music?"
Report it: She asked where I lived and whether I liked music.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
- **Wh-questions:** *asked + wh-word + subject + verb* (statement order, no question mark): *“Where do you live?” → She asked me where I lived.*
- **Yes/No questions:** *asked + if/whether + subject + verb*: *“Are you ready?” → He asked if I was ready.*
- **Commands:** *ordered/told/commanded + object + to + verb*: *“Shut the door.” → He told me to shut the door.* Negative: *not to*.
- **Requests:** *requested/asked + object + to + verb*: *“Please help me.” → She requested me to help her.*
- **Advice/suggestions:** *advised…to*; *suggested that we should…*
- **Exclamations:** *exclaimed with joy/sorrow that…*

steps.title: Solved example: Report: The teacher said to Ravi, “Why are you late?”
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Verb:** asked Ravi

**Step 2 – Order:** why + he + was

**Step 3 – Answer:** The teacher asked Ravi **why he was late**.

steps.title: Solved example: Report: Mother said to me, “Don't touch the stove.”
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Type:** Negative command

**Step 2 – Pattern:** told/forbade + object + not to + verb

**Step 3 – Answer:** Mother told me **not to touch** the stove.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- ✗ *He asked where did I live* → ✓ *where I lived* (statement order).
- Keeping the question mark in reported questions.
- ✗ *told me don't* → ✓ *told me not to*.

quiz.q: “Do you play chess?” he asked me. →
options: He asked me that I play chess.
He asked me if I played chess.
He asked me do I play chess.
He asked if do I play chess.
quiz.why: A yes/no question is reported with if or whether, and the word order is that of a statement, with the verb backshifted: if I played chess.
Please shows a request, so the reporting verb is requested, followed by an object and to plus the verb.

options: The guard told us don't run.
The guard asked to not running.
The guard told us not to run.
quiz.why: A negative command is reported with told plus not to plus the verb: told us not to run.
In reported speech the question becomes a statement, so it ends with a full stop.

options: She asked where the station was.
She asked where was the station.
She asked where is the station?
quiz.why: A wh-question is reported with the question word followed by statement order and a past verb: where the station was.

scenes.text: Before printing, Kabir checks each line for one error.
He looks at verbs, articles, prepositions and pronouns.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
1. **Read the whole passage** for meaning.
2. **Check each line** in order: tense consistency → subject–verb agreement → articles/determiners → prepositions → pronouns → word form (adjective/adverb, noun/verb) → conjunctions.
3. For **omission**, look where a sentence feels broken – usually a missing article, preposition, auxiliary or *to*.
4. Write **error → correction** (or *word before + missing word + word after*) as asked.

Common preposition pairs: *interested in, good at, afraid of, depend on, arrive at/in, different from, discuss (no “about”)*.

steps.title: Solved example: Edit: “Yesterday we go to the museum and saw a old coin.”
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Tense:** “go” → **went** (yesterday).

**Step 2 – Article:** “a old” → **an old**.

**Step 3 – Answer:** Yesterday we went to the museum and saw an old coin.

steps.title: Solved example: Omission: “She is interested music and plays the violin.”
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Gap:** interested ___ music.

**Step 2 – Rule:** interested **in**.

**Step 3 – Answer:** interested **in** music.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Changing correct words while missing the real error.
- ✗ *discuss about* → ✓ *discuss*.
- ✗ *He is senior than me* → ✓ *senior to me*.

statements.s: “She is good in maths.” is correct.
“We discussed the plan.” is correct.
“He arrived to Delhi.” is correct.
“She is afraid of dogs.” is correct.

quiz.why: Senior takes the preposition to, not than, so he is senior to me.
The subject She takes the third person singular form doesn't, so don't is the error.
We say going to the market. The words to the are missing.

quiz.q: Edit: “He speaks very good English fluently.” – best fix for clarity
quiz.why: An adverb like fluently is best placed after the object, so the better sentence is He speaks English very fluently.
Depend takes the preposition on, so we say depend on.

scenes.text: A notice has blanks: "The school ___ (organise) a trip, and students ___ bring water."
Context decides each word.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
- Identify **what part of speech** fits (verb, article, preposition, conjunction, pronoun).
- Look at **time clues** and **voice** (active/passive).
- Check **agreement** with the subject.
- Read the completed sentence aloud for meaning.

steps.title: Solved example: Fill: “The new library ___ (inaugurate) by the mayor last week.”
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Voice:** Library did not inaugurate itself → passive.

**Step 2 – Time:** last week → past.

**Step 3 – Answer:** **was inaugurated**.

steps.title: Solved example: Fill: “She was tired, ___ she continued working.”
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Relation:** Contrast.

**Step 2 – Answer:** **but / yet**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring passive voice clues.
- Using *and* where contrast is needed.

activity.text: The bridge ___ (build) in 1990. It is ___ oldest bridge in the city. People ___ (use) it every day.

quiz.why: The letter did not post itself and yesterday is past, so the passive past was posted is correct.
Working hard and still failing is a contrast, so the conjunction but is used.
Honest begins with a silent h, so it has a vowel sound and takes an.
For is used with a period of time such as ten years. Since goes with a point in time.
With neither...nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject. His friends is plural, so were is used.

questions.q: He said, “I like mangoes.” →
options: He told that he liked mangoes.
He said that he likes mangoes.
He said that he liked mangoes.
questions.why: With a past reporting verb the present tense backshifts to the past: like becomes liked, and I becomes he.

questions.q: “Yesterday” becomes
questions.why: Yesterday changes to the previous day in reported speech.

questions.q: “Please sit,” she said to him. →
questions.why: Please shows a request, so the reporting verb is requested, followed by to sit.

questions.q: “Are you hungry?” Mother asked me. →
options: Mother asked if was I hungry.
Mother asked me am I hungry.
Mother asked me if I was hungry.
questions.why: A yes/no question is reported with if and statement order: asked me if I was hungry.

questions.q: Omission: “He is fond ___ music.”
questions.why: The correct phrase is fond of.

questions.q: Correct: “We ___ the matter.”
questions.why: Discuss is a transitive verb and takes its object directly, so no preposition is needed.

questions.q: He said, “I have finished.” →
options: He said that he has finished.
He said that he had finished.
questions.why: In reported speech the present perfect have finished becomes the past perfect had finished, and I becomes he.

questions.q: The coach said, “Don't give up.” →
options: The coach asked to not give.
The coach told us don't give up.
The coach said not giving up.
The coach told us not to give up.
questions.why: A negative command is reported with told us not to give up.

questions.q: Edit: “Each of the students have a book.”
questions.why: Each takes a singular verb, so have should be has.

questions.q: Gap: “The results ___ (announce) tomorrow.”
questions.why: The results will be announced tomorrow, so the future passive will be announced is used. The results do not announce themselves.

questions.q: She said, “Where did you go?” →
options: She said where had I gone?
She asked where I had gone.
She asked where did I go.
questions.why: The simple past did you go becomes the past perfect had gone in reported speech, and the word order becomes that of a statement: where I had gone.

questions.q: He said, “I may come.” →
options: He said that he might come.
He said that he may came.
questions.why: May backshifts to might in reported speech, so he might come.

questions.q: Edit the line: “She is more taller than her sister.”
questions.why: Taller is already a comparative, so adding more makes a double comparative. Remove more.

questions.q: The teacher said, “Honesty is the best policy.” →
options: The teacher said that honesty is the best policy.
questions.why: A universal truth or proverb keeps its present tense in reported speech, so the teacher said that honesty is the best policy.

questions.q: “Let's go for a walk,” he said. →
options: He suggested that we should go for a walk.
questions.why: Let's is a suggestion, so it is reported with suggested that we should. It is not an order or a question.

questions.q: Omission: “I want ___ become a doctor.”
questions.why: Want is followed by to plus a verb, so the correct form is want to become.

courses.title: English Writing Skills · Letters, Analytical Paragraph and Reading Comprehension
courses.summary: Formats and model answers for formal letters (complaint, enquiry, order, letter to the editor), the analytical paragraph based on data, and strategies for unseen passages.
outcomes: Learners can write formal letters in the correct format
Learners can write a letter to the editor
Learners can write an analytical paragraph from a chart or table
Learners can answer comprehension questions using strategies

scenes.text: Ananya's new ceiling fan stopped working in a week.
She writes a formal complaint to the dealer.

steps.title: Format (block style)
steps.body:
1. **Sender's address**
2. **Date**
3. **Receiver's designation and address**
4. **Subject:** one line, specific
5. **Salutation:** Sir/Madam
6. **Body:** para 1 – purpose; para 2 – details (dates, bill no., problem); para 3 – request/action expected
7. **Complimentary close:** Yours faithfully/sincerely
8. **Name, signature (and designation)**

Word limit: usually ~120 words. Tone: polite, clear, factual.

steps.title: Solved example: Complaint letter (outline)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Subject:** Complaint regarding defective ceiling fan (Bill No. 4521)

**Step 2 – Para 1:** Purchased a ceiling fan on 2 March from your store.

**Step 3 – Para 2:** It stopped working within a week; humming noise, no rotation; under warranty.

**Step 4 – Para 3:** Request replacement within seven days, else will approach consumer forum.

**Step 5 – Close:** Yours faithfully, Ananya

steps.title: Solved example: Enquiry letter (outline)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Subject:** Enquiry about summer coding course

**Step 2 – Body:** Ask about duration, fees, timings, eligibility, certification.

**Step 3 – Close:** Request a brochure; Yours faithfully.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Missing the **subject** line.
- Informal tone or emojis.
- Writing “Yours lovingly” in a formal letter.

activity.prompt: Order the parts of a formal letter
items: Sender's address
Date
Receiver's address
Subject
Salutation
Body
Complimentary close
Name and signature

quiz.why: In a formal letter the subject line comes after the receiver's address and before the salutation.
A complaint letter should be polite and factual. Rude or emotional wording weakens the case.

quiz.q: Complimentary close for a formal letter
quiz.why: Yours faithfully is the formal close, used when the receiver is addressed as Sir or Madam. Bye, Cheers and Love are informal.
A complaint needs evidence such as the bill number and date so the problem can be checked.
An order letter lists the items, quantity and delivery terms, because the supplier needs those details to fill the order.

scenes.text: After rains, Kabir's street has dangerous potholes.
He writes to the newspaper editor to draw attention.

steps.title: Format and content
steps.body:
- Same formal format; receiver: **The Editor, [Newspaper], [City]**.
- Subject: the public issue.
- Opening: *Through the columns of your esteemed newspaper, I wish to draw the attention of the authorities to…*
- Body: describe the problem, its effects, causes; suggest solutions.
- Close: request publication/action; *Yours truly/faithfully*.

steps.title: Solved example: Letter to the editor on potholes (outline)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Subject:** Dangerous potholes on MG Road

**Step 2 – Problem:** Deep potholes after monsoon; accidents; traffic jams.

**Step 3 – Impact:** Two-wheeler riders injured; schoolchildren at risk.

**Step 4 – Solutions:** Urgent repair, better drainage, regular inspection.

**Step 5 – Close:** Request publication to alert authorities.

steps.title: Solved example: Letter on stray-dog safety (outline)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Issue:** Rising dog-bite cases.

**Step 2 – Balanced view:** Humane solutions – sterilisation, vaccination drives, shelters.

**Step 3 – Request:** Municipal action and awareness.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Addressing the authority directly instead of the **Editor**.
- Only complaining without **suggestions**.

activity.prompt: Before submitting your letter to the editor, check…
items: Addressed to The Editor
Clear subject line
Problem + effects described
At least two practical suggestions
Formal close and name

quiz.q: A letter to the editor is addressed to
quiz.why: A letter to the editor is addressed to The Editor of the newspaper.
It should suggest solutions to the problem it raises. Jokes, anger or gossip do not help.

options: Through the columns of your esteemed newspaper…
quiz.why: The usual formal opening is Through the columns of your esteemed newspaper...
Its purpose is to raise public awareness of an issue and draw attention to it.
Such letters use a formal and constructive tone. A casual or abusive tone would not be taken seriously.

scenes.text: A chart shows students' screen time from 2019 to 2023.
Riya must describe the trend in about 120 words.

steps.title: How to write it
steps.body:
1. **Introduction:** what the chart/table shows (topic, period, units).
2. **Overview:** the main trend (rise/fall/fluctuation) and biggest/smallest values.
3. **Details:** compare key figures with numbers; use linking words (*whereas, while, in contrast, similarly*).
4. **Conclusion:** summarise the trend; a short inference (no personal opinion beyond the data).

Useful vocabulary: *rose sharply, increased steadily, peaked at, declined marginally, remained stable, doubled, accounted for*.

steps.title: Solved example: Write an analytical paragraph (outline)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Data:** Average daily screen time: 2019 – 2 h; 2020 – 5 h; 2021 – 4.5 h; 2022 – 3.5 h; 2023 – 3 h.

**Step 2 – Intro:** The bar graph depicts average daily screen time of students from 2019 to 2023.

**Step 3 – Overview:** Screen time peaked in 2020 and declined thereafter, though remained above 2019 levels.

**Step 4 – Details:** It rose sharply from 2 to 5 hours (2.5 times) in 2020, then fell to 4.5 h, 3.5 h and 3 h.

**Step 5 – Conclusion:** Overall, screen time is falling but is still 50% higher than in 2019.

steps.title: Solved example: Calculate a comparison for your paragraph
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Data:** 2019 = 2 h, 2023 = 3 h.

**Step 2 – Change:** 3 − 2 = 1 h.

**Step 3 – Percent:** 1 ÷ 2 × 100 = **50% higher**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Listing every number without a trend.
- Adding opinions not supported by the data.
- Missing an introduction or conclusion.

activity.prompt: In 2018 a school had 400 readers in the library; in 2023, 500. What is the percentage increase?

quiz.why: An analytical paragraph begins by stating what the data shows, in a brief overview. Personal stories do not belong.
Peaked at means reached the highest point. It does not mean a fall or no change.
Whereas links two contrasting ideas. Also, and, and so add or show result.
A good analytical paragraph supports its points with numbers that show trends. Opinions alone are not evidence.
Analytical paragraphs are usually about 100–120 words. Twenty is too short and 500 or more is too long.

scenes.text: In the exam, Meena faces a 500-word passage on plastic pollution.
She skims first, then reads the questions, then scans for answers.

steps.title: Strategy
steps.body:
1. **Skim** the passage for the main idea (title, first and last lines of paragraphs).
2. **Read the questions** – note keywords.
3. **Scan** to locate answers; underline evidence.
4. For **vocabulary**, use context clues; replace the word in the sentence to check.
5. For **inference** questions, combine clues – don't copy whole sentences.
6. For **case-based/MCQs**, eliminate wrong options.

steps.title: Solved example: Vocabulary from context
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Sentence:** “The river, once pristine, is now choked with waste.”

**Step 2 – Clue:** “once” contrasts with “choked with waste”.

**Step 3 – Meaning:** pristine = **clean, unspoilt**.

steps.title: Solved example: Inference question
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Passage clue:** “Sales of cloth bags tripled after the ban.”

**Step 2 – Question:** What can be inferred about the ban?

**Step 3 – Answer:** It changed shopping habits – people shifted from plastic to cloth bags.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Copying long chunks instead of answering precisely.
- Using outside knowledge instead of the passage.

items: Skim for the main idea
Read the questions and note keywords
Scan the passage for answers
Use context for vocabulary
Write concise answers with evidence

quiz.why: Skimming means reading quickly to get the main idea. It is not slow reading or skipping the passage.
Scanning means looking through the text for specific information, such as a name or date.
Inference answers must rest on clues in the passage, not outside knowledge or copied lines.
For vocabulary questions, use the context clues, the words around the term. Random guessing is unreliable.
The first step is to skim for the main idea. Scanning and answering come after that.

questions.q: Which is NOT part of a formal letter?
questions.why: A formal letter has a salutation, subject and complimentary close. An emoji is informal and does not belong.

questions.q: A letter to the editor is addressed to
questions.why: A letter to the editor is addressed to The Editor of the newspaper, so that it can be published.

questions.q: “Rose sharply” describes a
questions.why: Rose sharply means a quick increase. Rose shows upward movement and sharply shows speed.

questions.q: In a complaint letter, the last paragraph should
questions.why: The last paragraph of a complaint should state the action expected, such as a refund or repair.

questions.q: An analytical paragraph should avoid
questions.why: An analytical paragraph should avoid unsupported opinions. It should rely on numbers, comparisons and trends.

questions.q: Skimming is done
questions.why: Skimming is done first, to get the main idea before looking for details.

questions.q: Which opening suits a letter to the editor?
options: Through the columns of your esteemed newspaper…
questions.why: A letter to the editor opens with Through the columns of your esteemed newspaper... Dear Mom and Hey there are informal.

questions.q: Which close suits a formal letter?
questions.why: A formal letter closes with Yours faithfully (or Yours sincerely). XOXO, Love and hugs and See ya are informal.

questions.q: Data: 2019 – 40, 2023 – 60. Percentage rise?
questions.why: The rise is 60 − 40 = 20. Percentage rise = 20/40 × 100 = 50%.

questions.q: Data: sales fell from 250 to 200. Percentage fall?
questions.why: The fall is 250 − 200 = 50. Percentage fall = 50/250 × 100 = 20%. Dividing by the new value would wrongly give 25%.

questions.q: Which sentence best states an overview?
options: Overall, usage rose until 2021 and then declined.
questions.why: An overview sums up the general trend. Overall, usage rose until 2021 and then declined does this, while the others give one fact, an opinion or a comment on looks.

questions.q: “Pristine” in “once pristine, now polluted” means
questions.why: Once pristine, now polluted contrasts with polluted, so pristine means clean and unspoilt.

questions.q: Which is the correct order?
options: Address, date, receiver, subject, salutation, body, close, name
questions.why: A formal letter runs: sender's address, date, receiver, subject, salutation, body, complimentary close and name. The other orders skip parts or mix them up.

questions.q: A chart shows A = 30%, B = 45%, C = 25%. Which sentence is accurate?
options: B accounted for the largest share, nearly half
questions.why: B at 45% is the largest share, nearly half. A (30%) is not double B, the shares are not equal, and C at 25% is the smallest.

questions.q: In an enquiry letter, you mainly
questions.why: An enquiry letter asks for information, such as price or availability. Ordering, complaining and apologising are other letter types.

questions.q: Inference questions require
questions.why: Inference questions need you to combine clues from the passage to reach an answer that is not stated directly.

courses.title: Class 10 English · Revision & Practice
courses.summary: Quick revision of all First Flight and Footprints chapters and poems, grammar rules and writing formats, followed by two mixed mock papers in the final test.
outcomes: Learners can recall authors, characters and themes of every chapter
Learners can recall poem themes and devices
Learners can apply grammar rules quickly
Learners can recall writing formats
Learners can attempt mixed mock questions

scenes.text: Tanvi revises all of First Flight in one sitting using a table of authors and themes.
She tests herself by covering the theme column.

steps.title: Prose
steps.body:
- A Letter to God – G.L. Fuentes – faith, irony.
- Nelson Mandela: Long Walk to Freedom – Mandela – freedom, courage, sacrifice.
- Two Stories about Flying – O'Flaherty / Forsyth – fear, help in crisis, mystery.
- From the Diary of Anne Frank – loneliness, wit, teacher–student understanding.
- Glimpses of India – Rodrigues / Abrol / Datta – diversity (Goa, Coorg, Assam).
- Mijbil the Otter – Gavin Maxwell – human–animal bond, humour.
- Madam Rides the Bus – Vallikkannan – curiosity, first encounter with death.
- The Sermon at Benares – Buddha – death is universal; overcome grief.
- The Proposal – Chekhov – farce, satire on materialism.

steps.title: Poems
steps.body:
- Dust of Snow, Fire and Ice – Frost – mood change; desire & hatred.
- A Tiger in the Zoo – Leslie Norris – captivity vs freedom.
- How to Tell Wild Animals – Carolyn Wells – humour.
- The Ball Poem – John Berryman – loss and growing up.
- Amanda! – Robin Klein – nagging and freedom.
- The Trees – Adrienne Rich – freedom; feminist symbolism.
- Fog – Carl Sandburg – metaphor of a cat.
- The Tale of Custard the Dragon – Ogden Nash – appearance vs courage.
- For Anne Gregory – W.B. Yeats – outer beauty vs inner self.

steps.title: Solved example: Quick theme answer: “The Ball Poem” (30 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Event:** A boy loses his ball.

**Step 2 – Lesson:** The poet lets him learn the epistemology of loss – some losses can't be replaced by money.

steps.title: Solved example: Quick theme answer: “A Letter to God” (30 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Faith:** Lencho's total faith in God.

**Step 2 – Irony:** He calls the helpful post office staff crooks.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing authors (e.g. Nash vs Wells).
- Writing themes without evidence.

activity.prompt: Match the work to its author

quiz.q: Author of “The Tale of Custard the Dragon”
quiz.why: The Tale of Custard the Dragon is a humorous poem by Ogden Nash. Frost wrote Fire and Ice.
Fire and Ice says desire (fire) and hatred (ice) can both destroy the world. It is not about nature's beauty or childhood.
Two Stories about Flying pairs His First Flight by Liam O'Flaherty with The Black Aeroplane by Frederick Forsyth.
For Anne Gregory is written as a dialogue between a young man and Anne. The other poems are not.
Kisa Gotami, who sought a cure for her dead son, appears in The Sermon at Benares.

scenes.text: Arjun makes a card for each Footprints character.
Name → trait → evidence.

steps.title: Supplementary reader
steps.body:
- A Triumph of Surgery – Herriot – Tricki, Mrs Pumphrey – pampering, irony.
- The Thief's Story – Ruskin Bond – Hari Singh, Anil – trust, education.
- The Midnight Visitor – Robert Arthur – Ausable, Max, Fowler – presence of mind.
- A Question of Trust – Victor Canning – Horace Danby, lady in red – irony, crime doesn't pay.
- Footprints without Feet – H.G. Wells – Griffin – science without ethics.
- The Making of a Scientist – Robert W. Peterson – Richard Ebright – curiosity, persistence.
- The Necklace – Maupassant – Matilda Loisel – vanity, honesty.
- Bholi – K.A. Abbas – Sulekha, teacher, Bishamber – education, dowry.
- The Book That Saved the Earth – Claire Boiko – Think-Tank, Noodle – arrogance, misreading.

steps.title: Solved example: Compare Horace Danby and Ausable (40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Horace:** Expert thief undone by misplaced trust.

**Step 2 – Ausable:** Unarmed agent who wins by wit.

**Step 3 – Lesson:** Presence of mind wins; blind trust loses.

steps.title: Solved example: Compare Anil and the teacher in Bholi (40 words)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Anil:** Trust and education reform Hari.

**Step 2 – Teacher:** Kindness and education empower Bholi.

**Step 3 – Common:** Mentors transform lives.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Confusing Mrs Hall (Iping inn) with Mrs Pumphrey (Tricki).

activity.prompt: Match the character to the story
pairs: The Book That Saved the Earth

quiz.why: In The Thief's Story, Hari Singh returns the money he stole, moved by Anil's trust. Horace, Max and Griffin are in other stories.
Ebright, in The Making of a Scientist, collected and studied butterflies. Tea, dragons and otters belong to other lessons.

quiz.q: Who refused to marry for dowry?
quiz.why: Bholi refused to marry a man who demanded dowry. Natalya, Valli and Matilda are in other stories.
Ausable, in The Midnight Visitor, used an imaginary balcony to trick Fowler.
Think-Tank misread the Mother Goose rhymes in The Book That Saved the Earth.

scenes.text: Before the exam, Ira runs through ten grammar rules.
She also checks letter and paragraph formats.

steps.title: Grammar rules
steps.body:
- Present perfect: no definite past time; *since* + point, *for* + period.
- Past perfect for the earlier of two past actions.
- Modals + base form; *must not* ≠ *need not*.
- Each/every/either/neither → singular; nearer subject rule for *either…or*.
- *a/an* by sound; *the* for unique/superlative.
- Reported speech: backshift; *told + object*; questions in statement order; commands *to/not to*.

steps.title: Writing formats
steps.body:
- Formal letter: address → date → receiver → subject → salutation → body (3 paras) → close → name.
- Letter to the editor: “Through the columns of your esteemed newspaper…” + suggestions.
- Analytical paragraph: intro → overview → details with numbers → conclusion.

steps.title: Solved example: Fix three errors: “She have went to the market since two hours.”
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Auxiliary:** have → has

**Step 2 – Participle:** went → gone

**Step 3 – Preposition:** since → for

**Step 4 – Answer:** She **has gone** to the market **for** two hours. (Better: She has been at the market for two hours.)

steps.title: Solved example: Report: “Can you help me?” she asked him.
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Pattern:** asked + if + subject + could

**Step 2 – Answer:** She asked him **if he could help her**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Last-minute changes that introduce new errors – trust the rules.

statements.s: “Since two hours” is correct.
Reported questions keep the question mark.
“An hour” is correct.
A letter to the editor should give suggestions.

quiz.why: In reported questions the word order is that of a statement and the verb backshifts: where I lived.

options: Each of them are a pen.
Each of them have a pen.
Each of them has a pen.
Each of them having a pen.
quiz.why: Each is singular and takes has: Each of them has a pen.
Unique begins with the consonant sound /j/, so it takes a, not an.
An analytical paragraph needs an overview of the trends, with supporting data. Dialogue, poems and signatures do not belong.
You need not worry means there is no necessity. Must would mean it is required, which does not fit.

lessons.title: Hindi grammar link and exam strategy

scenes.text: Class 10 students prepare English and Hindi papers in the same weeks.
A smart timetable rotates literature, grammar and writing.

steps.title: Exam-day strategy
steps.body:
- **Read the paper** fully in the first minutes; start with sections you know best.
- **Word limits** matter – practise 40, 60, 100 and 120-word answers.
- **Literature answers:** point + evidence + value.
- **Grammar:** do it early while fresh; check agreement and tense.
- **Writing:** format marks are easy – never skip them.
- Leave 10 minutes for **revision**.

steps.title: Solved example: Plan a 3-hour English paper
steps.body:
**Step 1 – 0–10 min:** Read paper; mark choices.

**Step 2 – 10–55:** Reading section.

**Step 3 – 55–90:** Grammar + writing.

**Step 4 – 90–170:** Literature.

**Step 5 – 170–180:** Revise.

steps.title: Solved example: Turn a weak answer into a strong one
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Weak:** “Lencho was a farmer who believed God.”

**Step 2 – Strong:** “Lencho's faith in God was unshakeable: even after the hailstorm he wrote to God and was not surprised to receive money – showing complete trust.”

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Spending too long on one question.
- Skipping format in writing tasks.

items: Revise authors and themes table
Practise one letter and one analytical paragraph
Do 20 grammar MCQs
Write two 120-word literature answers
Sleep 8 hours before the exam

quiz.q: Easy marks in writing come from
quiz.why: Easy marks in writing come from the correct format. Decoration or long stories do not earn them.
A strong literature answer backs its point with evidence from the text, not opinion alone.
About 10 minutes at the end is enough to check answers. One minute is too short and an hour is impractical.
Start by reading the paper fully so you know the questions and can plan your time.
Before an exam, sleep well. Rest helps memory and concentration, while panic and staying up do not.

questions.q: Mock A1 – Author of “Dust of Snow”
questions.why: Dust of Snow was written by Robert Frost. Nash, Sandburg and Yeats wrote other poems.

questions.q: Mock A2 – Mandela was inaugurated in
questions.why: Nelson Mandela was inaugurated as President of South Africa in 1994, after the first fully democratic elections.

questions.q: Mock A3 – “She ___ (go) to school every day.”
questions.why: She is third person singular, so the simple present verb takes -es: goes.

questions.q: Mock A4 – Who is Mij?
questions.why: Mij, in Gavin Maxwell's Mijbil the Otter, is an otter.

questions.q: Mock A5 – He said, “I am busy.” →
options: He told that he was busy.
He said that he was busy.
He said that he is busy.
questions.why: With a past reporting verb the present am becomes was, and I becomes he: He said that he was busy.

questions.q: Mock A6 – Assertion: Valli became quiet on the return trip. Reason: She saw the dead cow.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Seeing the dead cow upset Valli, which is why she became quiet on the way back.

questions.q: Mock A7 – Which is a metaphor?
options: The fog comes on little cat feet
questions.why: A metaphor states one thing is another without like or as. The fog comes on little cat feet does this, while the others use like or as and are similes.

questions.q: Mock A8 – Edit: “Neither of them are ready.”
questions.why: Neither takes a singular verb, so are should be is.

questions.q: Mock A9 – Case: A rich lady overfeeds her dog; a vet cures it with diet. The irony lies in
options: calling the cure “a triumph of surgery”
questions.why: The humour is in calling the vet's simple diet cure a triumph of surgery. The irony is the gap between the grand phrase and the plain cure.

questions.q: Mock A10 – Data: 120 → 150. Percentage increase?
questions.why: The increase is 150 − 120 = 30. Percentage increase = 30/120 × 100 = 25%.

questions.q: Mock B1 – Who wrote “The Necklace”?
questions.why: The Necklace was written by Guy de Maupassant. Bond, Wells and Chekhov wrote other works.

questions.q: Mock B2 – Bholi's real name
questions.why: Bholi's real name is Sulekha. Natalya, Valli and Matilda belong to other lessons.

questions.q: Mock B3 – “___ I come in?” (formal)
questions.why: May is the formal word for asking permission, as in May I come in.

questions.q: Mock B4 – In “Fire and Ice”, fire stands for
questions.why: In Fire and Ice, fire stands for desire. Ice stands for hatred.

questions.q: Mock B5 – Assertion: Griffin was a hero. Reason: He used invisibility to help people.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Griffin was selfish and misused invisibility, not a hero, so the assertion is false. The reason is also false, as he did not use it to help people.

questions.q: Mock B6 – “Don't be late,” the teacher said. →
options: The teacher told us don't be late.
The teacher told us not to be late.
questions.why: A negative command is reported with told us not to plus the verb: told us not to be late.

questions.q: Mock B7 – Which story shows presence of mind?
questions.why: In The Midnight Visitor, Ausable's quick thinking with the imaginary balcony shows presence of mind.

questions.q: Mock B8 – Which poem shows outer beauty vs inner self?
questions.why: In For Anne Gregory, the young man is loved for the yellow hair, but Anne wants to be loved for herself, so outer beauty is set against the inner self.

questions.q: Mock B9 – Matilda's replacement necklace cost 36,000 francs; the original was worth ≤500. Ratio of replacement to original (at most)?
questions.why: The ratio is 36,000 ÷ 500 = 72. Since the original was worth at most 500, the replacement cost at least 72 times as much, so 72 times is the answer.

questions.q: Mock B10 – Choose the correctly reported question: “Have you finished?” she asked.
options: She asked if I have finished?
She asked if I had finished.
questions.why: A yes/no question is reported with if, statement order, and the present perfect backshifted to the past perfect: if I had finished.

courses.title: हिंदी व्याकरण · रचना के आधार पर वाक्य भेद और वाच्य
courses.summary: कक्षा 10 के लिए वाक्य के भेद (सरल, संयुक्त, मिश्र), आश्रित उपवाक्य, वाक्य रूपांतरण, तथा वाच्य (कर्तृवाच्य, कर्मवाच्य, भाववाच्य) और वाच्य परिवर्तन – हल सहित उदाहरणों के साथ।
outcomes: विद्यार्थी सरल, संयुक्त और मिश्र वाक्य पहचान सकेंगे
विद्यार्थी आश्रित उपवाक्यों के भेद बता सकेंगे
विद्यार्थी वाक्यों का रूपांतरण कर सकेंगे
विद्यार्थी वाच्य पहचानकर उसका परिवर्तन कर सकेंगे
courses.note: grammar topics differ between Hindi A and Hindi B and by board – check your current syllabus

scenes.text: रिया ने लिखा: "भारत जीता।" फिर लिखा: "भारत जीता और लोग नाचने लगे।"
फिर: "जब भारत जीता, तब लोग नाचने लगे।" – तीनों वाक्य अलग प्रकार के हैं।

steps.title: तीन भेद
steps.body:
- **सरल वाक्य:** जिसमें **एक ही उद्देश्य और एक ही विधेय** (एक मुख्य क्रिया) हो। जैसे – *राम पुस्तक पढ़ता है।*
- **संयुक्त वाक्य:** जिसमें **दो या अधिक स्वतंत्र (प्रधान) उपवाक्य** समानाधिकरण योजकों से जुड़े हों – *और, तथा, एवं, पर, किंतु, परंतु, लेकिन, या, अथवा, इसलिए, अतः*। जैसे – *वह आया और बैठ गया।*
- **मिश्र वाक्य:** जिसमें **एक प्रधान उपवाक्य** और **एक या अधिक आश्रित उपवाक्य** हों; योजक – *कि, जो, जिसे, जब…तब, जहाँ…वहाँ, यदि…तो, क्योंकि, ताकि*। जैसे – *मैंने देखा कि वह रो रहा था।*

steps.title: आश्रित उपवाक्य के भेद
steps.body:
- **संज्ञा उपवाक्य:** प्रधान उपवाक्य की क्रिया के कर्म/कर्ता के रूप में; प्रायः *कि* से शुरू – *उसने कहा **कि वह कल आएगा**।*
- **विशेषण उपवाक्य:** संज्ञा की विशेषता बताए; *जो, जिसे, जिसका* से – *वह लड़का **जो कल आया था**, मेरा मित्र है।*
- **क्रियाविशेषण उपवाक्य:** क्रिया का समय, स्थान, कारण, शर्त बताए; *जब, जहाँ, क्योंकि, यदि, ताकि* से – ***जब बारिश हुई**, तब हम घर लौटे।*

steps.title: हल सहित उदाहरण: भेद पहचानिए: “यदि तुम मेहनत करोगे तो सफल हो जाओगे।”
steps.body:
**चरण 1 – योजक:** *यदि…तो* – आश्रित उपवाक्य का योजक।

**चरण 2 – प्रधान उपवाक्य:** *तुम सफल हो जाओगे*।

**चरण 3 – उत्तर:** **मिश्र वाक्य** (क्रियाविशेषण उपवाक्य – शर्त)।

steps.title: हल सहित उदाहरण: भेद पहचानिए: “सूरज निकला और अँधेरा मिट गया।”
steps.body:
**चरण 1 – योजक:** *और* – समानाधिकरण।

**चरण 2 – उपवाक्य:** दोनों स्वतंत्र।

**चरण 3 – उत्तर:** **संयुक्त वाक्य**।

steps.title: आम गलतियाँ
steps.body:
- *कि* आने पर हर बार संयुक्त वाक्य मान लेना – *कि* प्रायः **मिश्र** वाक्य बनाता है।
- एक से अधिक क्रियाएँ हों तो सरल वाक्य को भी संयुक्त समझ लेना: *वह खाना खाकर सो गया* – पूर्वकालिक क्रिया के साथ यह **सरल** वाक्य है।

items.text: मैं गया पर वह नहीं मिला।
जो परिश्रम करता है, वह सफल होता है।
माँ ने कहा कि जल्दी आना।

quiz.q: “वह आया और चला गया” कौन-सा वाक्य है?
quiz.why: इस वाक्य में दो स्वतंत्र वाक्य ‘और’ से जुड़े हैं, इसलिए यह संयुक्त वाक्य है। ‘और’ समानाधिकरण योजक है।

options: एक प्रधान और एक या अधिक आश्रित उपवाक्य
quiz.why: मिश्र वाक्य में एक प्रधान उपवाक्य और एक या अधिक आश्रित उपवाक्य होते हैं। सरल वाक्य में केवल एक उपवाक्य होता है।

quiz.q: “जो लड़का कल आया था, वह मेरा भाई है” में आश्रित उपवाक्य किस प्रकार का है?
quiz.why: ‘जो लड़का कल आया था’ संज्ञा ‘लड़का’ की विशेषता बताता है, इसलिए यह विशेषण उपवाक्य है।
इस वाक्य में मुख्य क्रिया एक ही है (सो गया) और ‘खाकर’ पूर्वकालिक क्रिया है। एक उपवाक्य होने से यह सरल वाक्य है।

quiz.q: कौन-सा योजक संयुक्त वाक्य बनाता है?
quiz.why: ‘इसलिए’ समानाधिकरण योजक है, जो दो स्वतंत्र वाक्यों को जोड़कर संयुक्त वाक्य बनाता है। ‘जब’, ‘कि’ और ‘जो’ आश्रित उपवाक्य जोड़ते हैं।

scenes.text: शिक्षक ने कहा: एक ही बात को सरल, संयुक्त और मिश्र तीनों रूपों में लिखो।
अर्थ वही रहे, केवल रचना बदले।

steps.title: रूपांतरण के नियम
steps.body:
- **अर्थ न बदले**, केवल रचना बदले।
- **सरल → संयुक्त:** पूर्वकालिक क्रिया (*-कर*) को अलग क्रिया बनाकर *और/इसलिए* से जोड़ें।
- **सरल → मिश्र:** किसी पद/पदबंध को उपवाक्य बनाकर *जो, कि, जब, क्योंकि* से जोड़ें।
- **संयुक्त ↔ मिश्र:** *और/इसलिए* के स्थान पर *जब…तब, क्योंकि, यदि…तो* का प्रयोग।

steps.title: हल सहित उदाहरण: सरल → संयुक्त → मिश्र: “परिश्रमी छात्र सफल होते हैं।”
steps.body:
**चरण 1 – संयुक्त:** *छात्र परिश्रम करते हैं **और** सफल होते हैं।*

**चरण 2 – मिश्र:** ***जो** छात्र परिश्रमी होते हैं, **वे** सफल होते हैं।*

steps.title: हल सहित उदाहरण: संयुक्त → मिश्र: “वर्षा हुई इसलिए खेल रुक गया।”
steps.body:
**चरण 1 – कारण पहचानें:** वर्षा = कारण।

**चरण 2 – उत्तर:** *खेल रुक गया **क्योंकि** वर्षा हुई।* या *जब वर्षा हुई, तब खेल रुक गया।*

steps.title: आम गलतियाँ
steps.body:
- रूपांतरण में **अर्थ बदल देना** (जैसे काल बदल देना)।
- मिश्र वाक्य में *जो* के साथ *वह/वे* का संबंध भूल जाना।

activity.prompt: सही रूपांतरण मिलाइए (सरल वाक्य → मिश्र रूप)
pairs: बीमार होने के कारण वह नहीं आया।
वह नहीं आया क्योंकि वह बीमार था।
सूर्योदय होने पर पक्षी चहचहाने लगे।
जब सूर्योदय हुआ, तब पक्षी चहचहाने लगे।
ईमानदार व्यक्ति का सब सम्मान करते हैं।
जो व्यक्ति ईमानदार होता है, उसका सब सम्मान करते हैं।
उसने माना कि उसकी गलती थी।

quiz.q: “मेहनत करके वह सफल हुआ” का संयुक्त रूप
options: जब उसने मेहनत की तब वह सफल हुआ।
उसने मेहनत की और वह सफल हुआ।
quiz.why: संयुक्त वाक्य में दो स्वतंत्र वाक्य ‘और’ जैसे योजक से जुड़ते हैं: ‘उसने मेहनत की और वह सफल हुआ।’ बाकी विकल्प मिश्र या सरल वाक्य हैं।

quiz.q: रूपांतरण में क्या नहीं बदलना चाहिए?
quiz.why: रूपांतरण में वाक्य का अर्थ वही रहना चाहिए। उपवाक्य, योजक और रचना बदल सकते हैं।

quiz.q: “जो गरजते हैं वे बरसते नहीं” कौन-सा वाक्य है?
quiz.why: इस वाक्य में ‘जो’ से आरंभ आश्रित उपवाक्य है, जो मुख्य उपवाक्य पर निर्भर है, इसलिए यह मिश्र वाक्य है।

quiz.q: सरल से मिश्र बनाने में प्रायः किसका प्रयोग होता है?
quiz.why: सरल से मिश्र वाक्य बनाते समय आश्रित योजक ‘जो’, ‘कि’, ‘जब’ आदि का प्रयोग होता है, जो आश्रित उपवाक्य को मुख्य से जोड़ते हैं।

quiz.q: “वह बीमार था इसलिए स्कूल नहीं गया” का मिश्र रूप
options: क्योंकि वह बीमार था, इसलिए स्कूल नहीं गया।
वह बीमार होकर स्कूल नहीं गया।
quiz.why: मिश्र रूप में ‘क्योंकि’ आश्रित उपवाक्य जोड़ता है और कारण बताता है: ‘क्योंकि वह बीमार था, इसलिए स्कूल नहीं गया।’ बाकी विकल्प अर्थ बदलते हैं।

scenes.text: "सीता पुस्तक पढ़ती है।" – यहाँ कर्ता प्रधान है।
"सीता द्वारा पुस्तक पढ़ी जाती है।" – अब कर्म प्रधान है।

steps.title: तीन भेद
steps.body:
- **कर्तृवाच्य:** क्रिया के लिंग, वचन **कर्ता** के अनुसार; कर्ता प्रधान। *लड़का गीत गाता है। लड़की गीत गाती है।*
- **कर्मवाच्य:** क्रिया के लिंग, वचन **कर्म** के अनुसार; कर्ता के साथ *से/द्वारा*; केवल **सकर्मक** क्रिया। *लड़के द्वारा गीत गाया गया।*
- **भाववाच्य:** न कर्ता प्रधान, न कर्म – **भाव (क्रिया)** प्रधान; प्रायः **अकर्मक** क्रिया; क्रिया सदा **अन्य पुरुष, पुल्लिंग, एकवचन**; प्रायः असमर्थता/निषेध के अर्थ में। *मुझसे चला नहीं जाता। बच्चों से सोया नहीं गया।*

steps.title: हल सहित उदाहरण: वाच्य पहचानिए: “मुझसे अब दौड़ा नहीं जाता।”
steps.body:
**चरण 1 – क्रिया:** *दौड़ना* – अकर्मक।

**चरण 2 – रूप:** अन्य पुरुष, पुल्लिंग, एकवचन; असमर्थता।

**चरण 3 – उत्तर:** **भाववाच्य**।

steps.title: हल सहित उदाहरण: वाच्य पहचानिए: “प्रधानमंत्री द्वारा पुल का उद्घाटन किया गया।”
steps.body:
**चरण 1 – कर्ता:** *प्रधानमंत्री द्वारा* – गौण।

**चरण 2 – क्रिया:** कर्म *उद्घाटन* के अनुसार।

**चरण 3 – उत्तर:** **कर्मवाच्य**।

steps.title: आम गलतियाँ
steps.body:
- अकर्मक क्रिया से **कर्मवाच्य** बनाने की कोशिश – कर्मवाच्य केवल सकर्मक क्रिया से बनता है।
- भाववाच्य में क्रिया को कर्ता के लिंग के अनुसार बदलना (✗ *लड़कियों से सोई नहीं गई* → ✓ *लड़कियों से सोया नहीं गया*)।

items.text: माली पौधों को पानी देता है।
माली द्वारा पौधों को पानी दिया जाता है।
दादी से अब बैठा नहीं जाता।

quiz.q: कर्मवाच्य में क्रिया किसके अनुसार होती है?
quiz.why: कर्मवाच्य में क्रिया कर्म के लिंग और वचन के अनुसार बदलती है। कर्ता पर नहीं, कर्म पर ध्यान रहता है।

quiz.q: भाववाच्य प्रायः किस क्रिया से बनता है?
quiz.why: भाववाच्य में भाव प्रधान होता है और यह प्रायः अकर्मक क्रिया से बनता है, जैसे ‘मुझसे चला नहीं जाता’।

quiz.q: “रीना गाना गाती है” किस वाच्य में है?
quiz.why: ‘रीना गाना गाती है’ में कर्ता प्रधान है और क्रिया उसके अनुसार चलती है, इसलिए यह कर्तृवाच्य है।

quiz.q: कर्मवाच्य में कर्ता के साथ लगता है
quiz.why: कर्मवाच्य में कर्ता के साथ ‘से’ या ‘द्वारा’ लगता है, जैसे ‘लड़के द्वारा पुस्तक पढ़ी जाती है’। ‘ने’ कर्तृवाच्य में आता है।
भाववाच्य की क्रिया सदा अन्य पुरुष, पुल्लिंग, एकवचन में रहती है, क्योंकि वह न कर्ता के अनुसार चलती है न कर्म के अनुसार।

scenes.text: प्रश्न: "कर्मवाच्य में बदलिए – माँ खाना बनाती है।"
अमन नियम लगाता है: कर्ता + द्वारा, क्रिया कर्म के अनुसार + जाना।

steps.title: नियम
steps.body:
**कर्तृवाच्य → कर्मवाच्य:**
1. कर्ता के साथ *से/द्वारा* लगाएँ।
2. कर्म को प्रधान बनाएँ (*को* हटाएँ यदि आवश्यक)।
3. मुख्य क्रिया को **सामान्य भूतकाल** रूप में बदलकर *जाना* धातु का रूप काल के अनुसार जोड़ें; लिंग-वचन कर्म के अनुसार।

**कर्तृवाच्य → भाववाच्य:**
1. कर्ता के साथ *से* लगाएँ।
2. अकर्मक क्रिया को सामान्य भूतकाल रूप में + *जाना* (अन्य पुरुष, पुल्लिंग, एकवचन)।
3. प्रायः *नहीं* के साथ असमर्थता।

steps.title: हल सहित उदाहरण: कर्मवाच्य में बदलिए: “माँ खाना बनाती है।”
steps.body:
**चरण 1 – कर्ता:** माँ → *माँ द्वारा*

**चरण 2 – कर्म:** *खाना* (पुल्लिंग, एकवचन)

**चरण 3 – क्रिया:** बनाती है → *बनाया जाता है*

**चरण 4 – उत्तर:** **माँ द्वारा खाना बनाया जाता है।**

steps.title: हल सहित उदाहरण: भाववाच्य में बदलिए: “घायल सिपाही चल नहीं सकता।”
steps.body:
**चरण 1 – कर्ता:** *घायल सिपाही से*

**चरण 2 – क्रिया:** चल नहीं सकता → *चला नहीं जाता*

**चरण 3 – उत्तर:** **घायल सिपाही से चला नहीं जाता।**

steps.title: हल सहित उदाहरण: कर्तृवाच्य में बदलिए: “बच्चों द्वारा पतंगें उड़ाई गईं।”
steps.body:
**चरण 1 – कर्ता:** *बच्चों ने*

**चरण 2 – क्रिया:** उड़ाई गईं → *उड़ाईं*

**चरण 3 – उत्तर:** **बच्चों ने पतंगें उड़ाईं।**

steps.title: आम गलतियाँ
steps.body:
- काल बदल देना (वर्तमान को भूत बना देना)।
- कर्मवाच्य में क्रिया को कर्ता के लिंग के अनुसार रखना (✗ *माँ द्वारा खाना बनाई जाती है*)।

activity.text: राम पत्र लिखता है। → राम द्वारा पत्र ___ जाता है। सीता गीत गाएगी। → सीता द्वारा गीत ___ जाएगा।

options: लड़के द्वारा पुस्तक पढ़ी जाती है।
लड़के द्वारा पुस्तक पढ़ा जाता है।
quiz.why: ‘पुस्तक’ स्त्रीलिंग है, इसलिए कर्मवाच्य में क्रिया भी स्त्रीलिंग रूप ‘पढ़ी जाती है’ में आती है। ‘पढ़ा जाता है’ पुल्लिंग कर्म के लिए होगा।
भाववाच्य में क्रिया अन्य पुरुष, पुल्लिंग, एकवचन में रहती है: ‘मुझसे हँसा नहीं जाता।’ ‘हँसी’ लगाने पर कर्म बन जाएगा और वाच्य बदल जाएगा।

quiz.q: “पुलिस द्वारा चोर पकड़ा गया” का कर्तृवाच्य
options: पुलिस से चोर पकड़ा नहीं गया।
quiz.why: कर्तृवाच्य में कर्ता प्रधान होता है, इसलिए ‘पुलिस ने चोर को पकड़ा’ सही कर्तृवाच्य है। बाकी वाक्य अर्थ बदल देते हैं या अशुद्ध हैं।

quiz.q: कर्मवाच्य बनाने में कौन-सी धातु जुड़ती है?
quiz.why: कर्मवाच्य बनाने में ‘जाना’ धातु क्रिया के कृदंत रूप के साथ जुड़ती है, जैसे ‘पढ़ा जाता है’, ‘पकड़ा गया’।
भाववाच्य में क्रिया सदा अन्य पुरुष, पुल्लिंग, एकवचन में रहती है और भाव (क्रिया का होना) प्रधान होता है। इसलिए कर्ता के साथ ‘से’ लगता है: बच्चों से दौड़ा जाता है।

questions.q: जिस वाक्य में एक उद्देश्य और एक विधेय हो
questions.why: जिस वाक्य में एक उद्देश्य और एक विधेय (एक ही मुख्य क्रिया) हो, वह सरल वाक्य है। उसमें कोई आश्रित उपवाक्य नहीं होता।

questions.q: “मैंने देखा कि वह रो रहा था” है
questions.why: ‘कि’ आश्रित उपवाक्य जोड़ने वाला योजक है। ‘वह रो रहा था’ मुख्य वाक्य पर आश्रित है, इसलिए यह मिश्र वाक्य है।

questions.q: कर्तृवाच्य में प्रधान होता है
questions.why: कर्तृवाच्य में कर्ता प्रधान होता है और क्रिया उसी के लिंग-वचन के अनुसार चलती है। कर्म या भाव प्रधान हो तो कर्मवाच्य या भाववाच्य होता है।

questions.q: “सूरज डूबा और अँधेरा छा गया” है
questions.why: इस वाक्य में दो स्वतंत्र वाक्य ‘और’ से जुड़े हैं और दोनों बराबर महत्व के हैं। इसलिए यह संयुक्त वाक्य है।

questions.q: “यह वही घर है जहाँ मैं पैदा हुआ” में आश्रित उपवाक्य
questions.why: ‘जहाँ मैं पैदा हुआ’ संज्ञा ‘घर’ की विशेषता बताता है और मुख्य वाक्य पर आश्रित है। इसलिए यह विशेषण उपवाक्य है।

questions.q: “जब घंटी बजी, तब छुट्टी हुई” में आश्रित उपवाक्य
questions.why: ‘जब घंटी बजी’ समय बताता है और ‘छुट्टी हुई’ क्रिया की विशेषता है। इसलिए यह क्रियाविशेषण उपवाक्य है।

questions.q: “उससे उठा नहीं जाता” किस वाच्य में है?
questions.why: ‘उससे उठा नहीं जाता’ में ‘उठना’ अकर्मक क्रिया है और असमर्थता का भाव है। इसलिए यह भाववाच्य है।

questions.q: “किसान खेत जोतता है” का कर्मवाच्य
options: किसान द्वारा खेत जोता जाता है।
किसान से खेत जोता नहीं जाता।
किसान द्वारा खेत जोती जाती है।
questions.why: कर्मवाच्य में कर्म पुल्लिंग ‘खेत’ के अनुसार क्रिया ‘जोता जाता है’ आती है और कर्ता के साथ ‘द्वारा’ लगता है। ‘जोती जाती’ स्त्रीलिंग रूप है, इसलिए गलत है।

questions.q: “ईमानदार लोग सम्मान पाते हैं” का मिश्र रूप
options: जो लोग ईमानदार होते हैं, वे सम्मान पाते हैं।
लोग ईमानदार हैं और सम्मान पाते हैं।
questions.why: मिश्र वाक्य में ‘जो…वे’ से आश्रित उपवाक्य जुड़ता है: जो लोग ईमानदार होते हैं, वे सम्मान पाते हैं। बाकी विकल्प सरल या संयुक्त हैं।

questions.q: भाववाच्य में क्रिया का रूप
questions.why: भाववाच्य की क्रिया सदा अन्य पुरुष, पुल्लिंग, एकवचन में रहती है। वह न कर्ता के अनुसार बदलती है, न कर्म के अनुसार।

questions.q: कौन-सा वाक्य कर्मवाच्य नहीं बन सकता?
questions.why: ‘सोना’ अकर्मक क्रिया है और उसका कोई कर्म नहीं होता। कर्मवाच्य में कर्म की आवश्यकता होती है, इसलिए ‘वह सोता है’ से कर्मवाच्य नहीं बन सकता।

questions.q: “वह आया पर उसने कुछ नहीं कहा” में योजक
questions.why: ‘पर’ दो स्वतंत्र वाक्यों को जोड़कर विरोध दिखाता है, इसलिए यह समानाधिकरण योजक है और वाक्य संयुक्त है।

questions.q: “हम पेड़ लगाएँगे” का कर्मवाच्य
questions.why: ‘हम पेड़ लगाएँगे’ भविष्यकाल में है, इसलिए कर्मवाच्य में क्रिया ‘लगाए जाएँगे’ होगी। ‘पेड़’ बहुवचन में है, इसलिए क्रिया भी बहुवचन होगी।

questions.q: “समय पर न पहुँचने के कारण उसकी गाड़ी छूट गई” का संयुक्त रूप
options: वह समय पर नहीं पहुँचा, इसलिए उसकी गाड़ी छूट गई।
जब वह पहुँचा तब गाड़ी छूटी।
questions.why: संयुक्त रूप में दो स्वतंत्र वाक्य ‘इसलिए’ से जुड़ते हैं: वह समय पर नहीं पहुँचा, इसलिए उसकी गाड़ी छूट गई। बाकी विकल्प मिश्र या सरल हैं।

questions.q: मिश्र वाक्य का योजक नहीं है
questions.why: ‘और’ समानाधिकरण योजक है, जो संयुक्त वाक्य बनाता है। ‘कि’, ‘यदि’ और ‘जो’ आश्रित उपवाक्य जोड़कर मिश्र वाक्य बनाते हैं।

questions.q: “माँ से अब काम नहीं किया जाता” में वाच्य
questions.why: ‘करना’ सकर्मक क्रिया है और ‘काम’ उसका कर्म है। कर्म की प्रधानता और ‘से’ के प्रयोग के कारण यह कर्मवाच्य है।
